events.title: Crude oil prices sell off more than 7% on Iran peace talk hopes ahead of U.S. midterms
events.summary: President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to make a deal. Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state media. The oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the U.S. midterm elections. Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as the presidents of the U.S. and Iran signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months. Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, lost 7.6% to close at $104.77 a barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate shed 7.3% to settle at $96.46 a barrel. President Donald Trump told reporters Monday that Iran wants to "make a deal and that could happen." U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said over the weekend that Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically. Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections, gaining more than 10% in October. The oil market has sold off during previous phases of the war on rumors of a possible settlement, only for the conflict to subsequently escalate and spike prices again. Trump "hasn't made a decision" on whether to strike Iran again, Rubio told reporters. "What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully." Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said Tehran is seeking to resolve problems through dialogue, according to state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency . Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has granted the government certain authorities to do this, Pezeshkian said. Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to IRNA. Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said. But Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response." Reports about diplomatic efforts will have a big impact on crude oil prices because much of the market's recent gains were risk premium in anticipation of a possible escalation, according to Ryan McKay, director of commodity strategy at TD Securities. "With that said, so long as there is no concrete conclusion to the war, and tanker and Houthi attacks remain prevalent, we do not anticipate a complete erosion of the risk premium via diplomacy headlines alone," McKay said. — CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

events.title: Intel foundry push faces critical test after stock's 45% plunge in October
events.summary: Intel's 29% drop on Friday left the stock down 45% in October, its worst month on record, according to FactSet. Intel sees the global market for server CPUs growing fivefold to $200 billion in the next five years, but the softening PC market is hurting legacy revenue. Intel is redirecting some 18A capacity in Oregon fabs to make Intel 3 chips for its server CPUs As Intel comes off its steepest stock drop since the 1970s due to a worsening outlook for the PC market, the chipmaker is facing intensifying pressure to get its flailing foundry business off the ground. It's been an elusive task for Intel. The company has spent half a decade, and a good chunk of its $108 billion in capital expenditures over that stretch, trying to challenge Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company . But it still has no marquee customer for its most advanced chips, and is primarily manufacturing chips for its own products. Wall Street is losing patience. After the U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, the stock started to shoot up, ultimately rising sixfold over 10 months before peaking in June. Intel was finally finding its niche in the artificial intelligence boom, delivering central processors used for agentic AI, while optimism simultaneously grew over its fab aspirations. Intel's story took a dramatic turn for the worse on Thursday, when the company said revenue this quarter will be between $1 billion and $2 billion shy of analysts' estimates as the PC market continues to suffer from soaring costs for memory and other components. Intel still counts on its PC segment for roughly half of its revenue, and consumers are increasingly choosing not to upgrade. The stock plummeted 29% on Friday, its worst day since the 1970s, capping off a 45% plunge in October, the steepest monthly drop on record, according to FactSet. It's down another 8% in Monday trading. Intel's investments in the future are supposed to be paying off. CEO Lip-Bu Tan said he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion. Intel's data center business recorded 78% growth in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.3 billion. However, Intel said it can't make enough chips to fill demand, pointing to industry-wide supply constraints for wafers, substrates and memory, many of the same factors hurting PC sales. That's forcing Tan to make some hard choices. In response to the capacity shortage, Intel said it's shifting some Oregon factory capacity away from making wafers for its advanced 18A chips to make make more wafers on an older node, known as Intel 3, which are used for its data center products. Intel is counting on 18A to attract outside foundry customers, so the shift in resources could complicate that effort. David Yoffie, a Harvard Business School professor who previously spent almost three decades on Intel's board, said the latest moves are hardly welcoming to prospective foundry customers. "They're concerned that if Intel doesn't actually have excess capacity beyond its own demand, that they're just not a very credible supplier," Yoffie said. If it doesn't find a large-scale foundry customer within a year, "then the stress on Intel's economics are going to start to show even more dramatically," he said. Intel didn't respond to a request for comment. Intel is best known for its industry-leading central processing units, or CPUs. Graphics processing units from Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices ruled the early AI boom because they excel at handling large workloads for training models and inference for chatbots, while CPUs like Intel's are crucial for running the virtual machines used by agentic apps like Meta 's Muse. As one of the only companies in the world capable of manufacturing and packaging the advanced chips it needs for its own products, Intel has "more control over their destiny" than most chipmakers, Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities, said in an interview. "If you don't have enough capacity, you leave revenue and money on the table," Klein said. Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger, who was ousted in late 2024, spent his four-year tenure at the company aggressively pursuing foundry investments to catch up after delays on its 7- and 10-nanometer technologies, advanced process nodes that aim to fit more transistors on each chip. Tan has taken a more cautious approach, limiting spending until customer demand is locked in. He said on Thursday that "a couple customers" would be announced in the coming two quarters. Intel's 18A chips, for its own use, are in high-volume production out of Arizona, with a second fab in the works. A first structural truss was just installed at Intel's new Ohio facility, although the project is nearly five years behind schedule .

events.title: Former Meta security chief says giving AI agents your financial logins is ‘totally insane’
events.summary: Alex Stamos is the chief security officer for the AI coding startup Cognition. Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile via Getty Images Meta's former security chief said that giving AI agents financial logins is "totally insane." People are giving agents like Muse and Instinct their entire 1Password vaults, Alex Stamos said. The dynamic has created a dilemma for banks as customers deploy bots to their accounts. It's plain nuts to hand over a personal AI agent the keys to your financial life, according to Meta's former security chief. Alex Stamos, now the chief security officer for the AI coding startup Cognition , called it "totally insane" that people are giving AI agent apps access to highly sensitive personal data. On a recent episode of the "Big Technology Podcast," Stamos said people are giving agents like Meta's Muse and Spear Street Technology's Instinct their entire 1Password vaults, then asking them to "go handle my finances for me" or "go file my taxes." This dynamic, said Stamos, has created a dilemma for banks that are now grappling with a growing wave of customer-authorized bot activity. "So that's what the banks are talking about is that they now see all of these interactions with them that are authenticated correctly — so they're not stolen credentials — but are clearly bots doing interaction," Stamos said. In Stamos' view, Instinct's popularity stems in part from what he said is its ability to bypass safeguards meant to prevent bots from operating in these cases. "That's why Instinct is useful because it will effectively bypass the safety protections that are in place at these companies to keep you from doing exactly what you're doing, which is to have your bot interact with the most important parts of your life," he said. Stamos said the result is a "crazy tension" between financial institutions trying to "prevent automated access" to systems and consumers who want to make life easier by turning over their logins and personal information "to a company that's existed for six months." Representatives for Instinct did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Stamos' remarks. A spokesperson for Meta declined to comment. Meta previously said in a blog post that Muse, launched in September, runs on its own computer in the cloud, so no other agent can access it. In recent weeks, some bank CEOs have sounded the alarm about consumers granting third-party AI agents access to their financial accounts. "If people are using them, they should understand the risk," JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said during an October earnings call. He added there's a "liability transfer" away from the bank, as well as risks that their data is "misused." Dimon said JPMorgan is developing its own agentic tools for clients, while guarding the bank from outside agents. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Anthropic's colossal pay packages cost the company more than $100,000 a month per employee
events.summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei speaks on a video at a conference. Giuliano Berti/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic keeps a relatively small head count, with 5,300 workers, its IPO filing says. New numbers show Anthropic's personnel expenses topped $322,000 per worker last quarter. Anthropic's IPO will be a multimillionaire minter, giving workers liquidity. America has a classic salary milestone: six figures a year. Anthropic's average employee has cost their employer that much every month. Anthropic's personnel expenses topped $1.7 billion for its 5,300 workers from July through September, according to an amended S-1 filing the AI company released Monday morning ahead of its initial public offering later this month. That means the expenses averaged over $322,000 per worker over the three-month span. The total indicates how a seat inside Anthropic became one of the 21st century's quickest pathways to extraordinary wealth. Its coming IPO will mint a new cohort of multimillionaires. Even employees who've only been around for a couple of years have seen their stock options multiply in value several times over. The AI juggernaut has used high salaries and a rapidly growing valuation to recruit skilled engineers, researchers, and other specialists. Over the first nine months of 2026, Anthropic's personnel costs totaled $4.8 billion, according to the S-1. The last quarter's $1.7 billion tally included cash salaries and bonuses, benefits, and employer payroll taxes. The largest chunk of the total came from Anthropic's stock-based compensation expenses, an accounting measure of the equity it recognized for employees — that came out to $1.1 billion in the three-month span. Against the high employee expenses, Anthropic's revenue has raced far ahead. Back in 2023, the company spent more than twice as much on personnel as it made in revenue. In the first nine months of 2026, personnel costs tallied just 15% of total revenue. The numbers could fluctuate. Anthropic wrote in its S-1 that, as of the end of September, it had more than $32 billion in stock-based compensation expenses that it had not yet included in its accounting. A successful listing on the stock market would increase Anthropic's personnel costs in the coming quarters. Anthropic quintupled in head count from the end of 2024 to the end of September 2026. It's still much smaller than its tech-industry peers. Meta is valued at around $1.6 trillion, a possible target for Anthropic's IPO. The social media giant has around 67,000 employees. Broadcom, worth about the same, has more than 30,000. This trim size makes Anthropic look especially efficient , as Business Insider reported last week. The company tallied $6.6 million in annual revenue per employee, compared with estimates that put Meta at $3.2 million per employee and Google at $2.5 million. "Talent density matters more than talent mass," Anthropic wrote in its S-1. Have a tip? events.title: Read the memo from Squarespace's CEO about laying off 19% of staff
events.summary: Squarespace founder Anthony Casalena said in a memo that the cuts would mostly affect product and engineering teams. Abbie Parr/Getty Images Website-building company Squarespace is laying off 19% of staff. In a memo, CEO Anthony Casalena said most of the cuts affect product and engineering teams. Casalena added that the changes would mean "more player coaches." Squarespace is laying off 19% of its staff in a move its CEO said would help it "adapt for the modern era" with leaner teams and "more player coaches." The website-building software company is reducing its head count by about 300 employees, according to a companywide memo sent by Squarespace CEO Anthony Casalena on Monday. Most of the cuts affect product and engineering teams, according to the memo, which was seen by Business Insider. "The way we need to work is changing faster than at any point in our history, and our operating model must adapt for the modern era," wrote Casalena. "This means smaller teams, more player coaches, and a simplified organizational structure." Affected staff will get a minimum of 16 weeks of base salary plus additional weeks based on tenure and benefits through May 2027. Employees would also be able to keep their company laptops, and those on work visas would get continued support, the memo said. A spokesperson confirmed the layoffs and memo to Business Insider, adding: "The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth." Later on Monday, Casalena hosted a livestream presentation about the layoffs for remaining employees. He reiterated the points made in his memo during the roughly one-minute livestream, which did not allow for comments. The company is planning a separate all-hands meeting, the spokesperson said. The cuts, first reported by The Verge, come after Squarespace has increasingly added AI features to its products. Squarespace joins a long list of companies that have laid off staff this year, some of which have cited the rise in AI. Last week, Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, though the company told Business Insider it expects only 3,000 or fewer to take the offer. Casalena also joins a list of CEOs who have cited leaner teams when discussing layoffs — in February, Block CEO Jack Dorsey emphasized a shift toward smaller teams in a post on X about cutting his company nearly in half. Read the Squarespace CEO's memo to staff: All — I am writing today to announce one of the most difficult decisions I've had to make in the history of our company. We will be reducing our workforce by ~19% and saying goodbye to around 300 of our colleagues, with most of these reductions affecting Product & Engineering. Within the next twenty minutes, impacted US employees will receive an email and personal meeting invitation and potentially impacted non-US employees will receive country-specific details. This is not a decision I arrived at lightly, and I'd like to explain why it was made and what we will be doing for those leaving Squarespace. The way we need to work is changing faster than at any point in our history, and our operating model must adapt for the modern era. This means smaller teams, more player coaches, and a simplified organizational structure. This is not an exercise designed to reach a financial target — it is about reshaping our organization around how we need to work going forward. Squarespace's core business has been about empowering people to establish themselves online in a world where technology was a major barrier. Technology still is a major barrier for many, but it has changed in ways we could not have anticipated before the past 12 months. Our product and industry is undergoing a fundamental change, and our organization must too. Those who will be leaving us have been an important part of getting us to where we are today, and I'm grateful for their contributions. To support their transition, we will be offering*: A minimum of 16 weeks of base salary, plus additional weeks based on tenure Payment of the November 20, 2026 vesting of the legacy RSU cash award, where applicable Continuation of benefits through May 2027 Career coaching, resume preparation, and job search assistance Additional support for employees on work visas Impacted employees may keep their Squarespace laptops To those staying, your department leaders will reach out to ensure you understand the changes specific to you and your teams and that you have the direction and support you need to work through them. We will also have a brief livestream presentation later today, which will be added to calendars shortly. After we have had time to absorb today's changes, we will come back together to talk about the opportunity ahead of us. Today, however, I want to say thank you to those who have been a part of this journey with us. Whether staying or leaving, I understand this decision will impact all of you emotionally. I would encourage everyone to take some time to reset and digest as we move forward. Anthony (Outside the US, we will communicate further with you, follow local processes and, where applicable, seek to provide comparable support.) Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Democrats weigh ‘lawfare’ against Trump
events.summary: David’s view Before there was the other Dan Sullivan, there was the other Mike Doyle. Four years ago, when longtime Pittsburgh Democrat Mike Doyle retired from Congress, a left-wing legislator named Summer Lee won the primary to replace him. Republicans nominated a local politician from the suburbs to face her who had a fortuitous name: Mike Doyle. Some voters were perplexed . The new Doyle’s lawn signs called him “the right Mike” without explicitly identifying him as a Republican — a moniker that would be a non-starter in the safely Democratic seat. Local Democrats got worried calls, asking why Lee was running against their beloved liberal congressman. The Democrat Doyle called an emergency press conference to clarify that he was not the Republican Doyle: “My name is on the ballot, but it’s not me.” Lee won, albeit by a smaller margin than other Democrats in her district had in the past. Nothing else came of the story. There was no federal investigation of the Doyle scheme; no demands not to seat Doyle if he won; no statement from the governor saying that he might not certify the election. All of that has unfolded in Alaska this cycle. The clandestine Democratic effort to recruit a candidate who shares the name of the state’s incumbent Republican senator could have major implications for what happens after Tuesday. The plot’s exposure damaged Democrat Mary Peltola, knocking her off-message, and now threatens her party’s chances of winning control of the Senate. President Donald Trump’s administration is investigating, and also sued to block the certification of the results should Sullivan lose — though a federal judge tossed out the suit over the weekend. Those efforts, along with the announcement of investigations into candidates within 60 days of the vote, show how the Trump administration is jettisoning unwritten norms at the Justice Department. The Alaska mess is weighing heavily on Democrats who hope to win control of Congress tomorrow. Victory in either chamber would mean a two-year license on oversight powers, empowering Democrats to subpoena the Trump administration and its allies in the private sector. There is a thirst for vengeance among some Democrats that is testing their public stance that they must restore standards blown up by Trump. There’s also a shared sense, among most Democrats, that following those standards has gotten them nothing, while Republicans have benefitted from bending the rules. “Donald Trump and [House Oversight Committee Chairman] James Comer have basically written a playbook on how to politicize investigations and attack political enemies and weaponize government,” said Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee in a Democratic majority. “[Attorney General] Todd Blanche? His whole job is just to grift for the president.” The argument over which party first used “lawfare” to get what it wanted is an old one. Democrats have long celebrated the Watergate investigation as an example of the Constitution and US legal system working as designed. Republicans are more likely to call the episode a coup against a president who’d just won a landslide. But the current debate begins, like so many irritating conversations, with the 2016 election. For all of Hillary Clinton’s errors, like telling coal miners that their jobs would vanish if she won, Democrats largely believe that she would have won the election against Trump had the FBI not abandoned its “60 day rule” and announced an 11th hour investigation into emails found on Huma Abedin’s laptop. Some believe that Barack Obama acted too timidly when Republicans refused to co-sign a letter warning of Russian interference in that campaign. Nobody has ever accused Trump of acting timidly. Ten years on, his Justice Department is still probing the origins of the Russia investigation into his first campaign. When Joe Biden replaced Trump, he kept on the US attorney who was investigating his son. When Trump replaced Biden, he sacked the prosecutors who’d worked on post-Jan. 6 investigations. Democrats felt like suckers. Biden publicly promised that his Justice Department would act independently. Privately, he was resentful of Attorney General Merrick Garland’s choices to hold off on investigating Trump until November 2022, after Republicans were more or less united in denouncing any Trump probe as “lawfare.” This is on many Democratic minds as they watch the Justice Department in Alaska — even though it’s not the only race where one party meddled in a way that might confuse voters. In Maine, a conservative PAC is sending out mail for a left-wing spoiler candidate for governor. In Ohio, a conservative PAC is doing the same for a socialist Senate candidate who could threaten Democrat Sherrod Brown’s chances. In Nevada, a conservative PAC… okay, you get the point. “They’re obsessed with meddling in elections,” Garcia said. “We have to put in place new rules and a new standard to get things back to a place where we don’t have the president trying to rig elections constantly.” In Pennsylvania, when I asked Gov. Josh Shapiro how Democrats should respond to Trump’s Justice Department, he was hopeful they would be the “party of law and order” — by showing that this was not the way to use the government’s bottomless resources. “I said every single day to our team and to the public that I enforce the law without fear or favor,” said Shapiro, referring to his six years as state attorney general. “That is not the case in the Trump administration.” Despite the ongoing debate of how far to go, Republicans are portraying a party intent on going after the president in order to rev up their base. “They’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress,” House Speaker Mike Johnson alleged . In reality, the impeachment articles filed by Democratic Reps. Al Green and Shri Thanedar failed to accumulate broad Democratic support, and neither man will be in Congress next year. I’d expect Democrats’ thinking to reflect what happens on Tuesday. To be sure, there will be investigations of the Trump administration and its allies. But the risk assessment of any new probe will depend on voters’ appetite for it. Voters haven’t really punished a party for launching an investigation that doesn’t go anywhere. At the same time, Trump hasn’t lost much support for pardoning corrupt politicians like Rod Blagojevich, Kwame Kilpatrick, or Chris Collins. I’m confident about one thing: No Democrat with a gavel is going to want to move on from Trump oversight. Notable For Fox News, Elaine Mallon looked at how Democratic investigations could do more financial damage to their Republican targets. In his Off Message newsletter, Brian Beutler argued that Democrats should treat Blanche’s investigations the way Trump treated Garland’s — as illegitimate electioneering.

events.title: Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December
events.summary: Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock from President and COO Gwynne Shotwell in December. The donation will go directly into about 2 million investment accounts of kids ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less. Elon Musk in October separately pledged to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX, which could come via Trump Accounts sometime in 2027. Eligible Trump Account holders will begin receiving donated shares of SpaceX stock next month, according to an X post on Friday. "Robert and I are thrilled that our gift of over 2 million shares of SpaceX stock will be distributed to children's Trump accounts in December!" President and COO Gwynne Shotwell wrote in the post. The gift from Shotwell and her husband will provide a share apiece to around 2 million Trump Accounts holders ages 11 to 17 who live in ZIP codes with median family incomes of $57,000 or less, or in ZIP codes with too few residents for a median family income to be reported by the U.S. Census Bureau. These families should receive a notice by Monday, Shotwell wrote on X. "In a few weeks, an additional gift will be finalized for eligible 11 to 17-year-old children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more children whose MFI is $90,000 or less living in counties near our home in the great state of Texas," she also wrote. Parents or guardians can check eligibility for the donation through Invest America, a nonprofit advocacy group, and track account activity with the Trump Accounts app . Children born from 2025 through 2028 may also receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the U.S. Department of the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria. In a separate funding announcement in October, Elon Musk wrote in an X post that he plans to give every kid in America a share of SpaceX sometime in 2027, which may also come via Trump Accounts . The U.S. Department of the Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold donated individual stocks, a change from previous guidelines that only allowed diversified, low-cost index funds . The move to permit stock donations could pave the way for more large-scale philanthropic gifts, Internal Revenue Service CEO Frank Bisignano told CNBC's " Squawk Box " on Oct. 8. On Oct. 29, Bisignano announced his own donation to Trump Accounts for eligible children ages 2 to 8 living in 11234, Bisignano's hometown ZIP code, according to The Bisignano Family Fund.

events.title: Germany says lawmakers’ iPhones may have been hacked with spyware
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. The German government is warning politicians and public figures that they were targeted by government-backed spyware, days after Apple began sending out notifications warning victims that their iPhones may have been hacked. Germany’s federal cybersecurity office, known as the BSI, said in a note over the weekend that it had become aware that members of the Bundestag, Germany’s parliament, and other unnamed notable individuals, had received warnings from Apple that they may have been targeted by cyberattacks. Per the Financial Times , German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said the government in Berlin was “taking the incident and the warning very seriously,” but he did not say who in the federal government had been targeted, including whether German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among them. Apple periodically sends out so-called threat notifications to people it thinks may have been targeted by spyware, which can steal messages, location data, and other sensitive information from their phones. This spyware often relies on zero-click exploits , which can hack individuals almost invisibly as they don’t require a victim to click on a link or open a file. Apple does not attribute attacks to specific governments or say whether someone’s phone has actually been compromised. For that reason, the BSI said that anyone who receives an Apple threat notification “should therefore assume that their device may have been compromised.” Others outside of Germany also received the recent threat alert from Apple. Radwan Mortada, a Beirut-based filmmaker, said in a post on X that he received a new threat notification warning that Apple had detected “another attack against your device,” after an earlier spyware attack targeted him in 2021. It’s unclear who is behind this latest round of spyware attacks, or which government may have orchestrated the targeting. Per the notice received by Mortada, Apple said its latest batch of threat notifications went out to users in 99 countries. The episode highlights again the murky business behind a growing number of attacks against members of civil society. Governments rarely build these tools themselves. Many buy them from private vendors, often called “mercenary spyware” makers, the best known being Israel’s NSO Group, which sells the controversial Pegasus spyware. Germany’s own central federal law agency, the BKA, reportedly bought access to Pegasus in 2019. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: HRW calls on Zambia to halt post-election crackdown
events.summary: Opposition figures arrested and disappeared since President Hakainde Hichilema claimed August victory. Human Rights Watch (HRW) has called on Zambia’s authorities to halt the vicious clampdown on the political opposition that was launched following President Hakainde Hichilema’s victory in disputed elections in August. The rights group demanded in a report released on Sunday that the authorities put a stop to the intensifying crackdown. list 1 of 4 Hakainde Hichilema sworn in as Zambia’s president after disputed election list 2 of 4 Zambia’s Hichilema begins second term after disputed election list 3 of 4 UN Human Rights Council elects 15 members in uncontested vote list 4 of 4 From Morocco to South Africa, Israel election watched closely across Africa It accused Zambia’s government of silencing government critics, with several members of the opposition, as well as journalists and lawyers, arrested and some having disappeared in recent months. “The post-election climate of intimidation, harassment, and repression has had a chilling effect on civic and political organizations, particularly on dissenting voices,” HRW said. The group said that Zambian police and military “forcibly disappeared, arbitrarily detained, beat, and threatened opposition members and supporters as well as lawyers, journalists, and government critics in the days before and after general elections in August 2026”. “Zambia’s government should break this dangerous cycle of repression,” added Ashwanee Budoo-Scholtz, deputy Africa director at HRW. “The authorities should immediately halt the ongoing post-election crackdown, allow access to lawyers and provide medical care for those in detention, release everyone arbitrarily detained, and ensure accountability for abuses by security forces.” Hichilema was sworn in for a second term as Zambia’s president following his victory in August. Critics have insisted that the election was marred by vote rigging. As he was inaugurated at the National Heroes Stadium in the Zambian capital, Lusaka, his main rival Brian Mundubile was in detention , accused of treason after claiming the opposition had won the election. Police raided Mundubile’s home the day after the August 13 elections. A former cabinet member, Mutotwe Kafwaya, was shot and killed during the operation. HRW called on the Zambian authorities to institute an independent, impartial and thorough investigation into the matter. About a dozen other opposition figures who have questioned the election results have been arrested. Meanwhile, authorities suddenly closed the country’s courts two weeks after the election, a move that Zambian police stated was an “intelligence-led and preventive measure”, without providing details. HRW noted that the closure prevents the opposition from filing legal challenges against the vote.

events.title: DOJ asks Supreme Court to block California counting disputed mail-in ballots
events.summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots of about 20,000 voters whom the Department of Justice suggests may not be U.S. citizens. The DOJ's petition to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's bid to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the ballots to be counted. The petition comes a day before Nov. 3, Election Day. The Supreme Court could act on the petition at any time, but there is no deadline. The Trump administration on Monday asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block California from counting mail-in ballots of about 20,000 voters whom the Department of Justice suggests may not be U.S. citizens . The DOJ 's petition to the Supreme Court came three days after the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals rejected the department's bid to overturn a federal district court judge's ruling that allowed the ballots to be counted. The petition comes a day before Election Day . The Supreme Court could act on the petition at any time, but there is no deadline. Alaska Gov. orders probe of Peltola Senate campaign's alleged recruitment of 2nd Sullivan Warren urges DOJ probe of Bank of America money laundering It's a 'socialist' bank — and North Dakota Republicans love it Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit The midterm elections will determine which parties hold majorities in both chambers of Congress. "In this case, this Office has been informed that the United States has identified more than 20,000 individuals who appear to be registered to vote in California based on publicly available information at the time that information was received, but who, in the United States' view, are likely not U.S. citizens," Solicitor General D. John Sauer said in application to the Supreme Court on Monday. Sauer said "the United States is likely to succeed on the merits of its appeal" of the lower court ruling denying the DOJ's request. "The district court concluded that the United States lacks Article III standing to bring this suit, but the United States suffers a judicially cognizable 'injury to its sovereignty' from the 'violation of its laws,'" Sauer said in the petition. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back." The DOJ sued California on Oct. 15 in U.S. District Court in Los Angeles. The complaint sought to prevent state election officials from tabulating mail-in ballots "from likely non-citizens in the upcoming federal election until the voter's citizenship status can be determined." The DOJ previously gave Los Angeles County officials a thumb drive containing names of voters the department suggested could be noncitizens, who by law are barred from voting in federal elections. Last Wednesday, Judge David Carter denied the DOJ's request that he order California officials to set aside mail ballots from alleged noncitizens named on a list prepared by the Department of Homeland Security, and not count their votes until their citizenship is confirmed. "This case is about the right of every American citizen to vote in a free and fair election," Carter said in his ruling. "Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Carter wrote. "In bringing this lawsuit, the Executive would have this Court believe that it reigns as a sole sovereign. But California and its people are sovereign, too." The DOJ then appealed that ruling to the 9th Circuit. A three-judge panel on that court denied the appeal in a 2-1 ruling on Friday "There is a material risk that granting the United States its requested relief would result in disenfranchisement," said the ruling by the majority, Circuit Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez. Bennett was appointed by President Donald Trump , and Sanchez was appointed by former President Joe Biden . On Sunday, a federal judge dismissed a DOJ lawsuit that sought to block Alaska election officials from immediately certifying the result of the U.S. Senate election there if incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses that race by a margin that could be attributable to voter confusion about another candidate with his name.

events.title: Trump to Axios: "No rush" to decide on bombing Iran again
events.summary: President Trump told Axios in a phone interview Monday he's "in no rush" to decide whether to resume fighting in Iran . Why it matters: The midterm elections have been seen as an inflection point for Trump on whether to unleash a massive bombing campaign to try to bring the war to an end. But it appears the president, at least for now, will continue on dual tracks — letting negotiations play out while preparing to go back to war if he concludes a deal isn't reachable. What he is saying: "One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially. They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it," Trump said in the interview. Driving the news: Qatari mediators have written a draft agreement outlining a three-day sequence of confidence-building measures aimed at resuming direct U.S.-Iran negotiations, according to regional sources. A diplomat with knowledge of the situation said the Qatari mediators are waiting for feedback from the U.S. and Iran. Trump is giving diplomacy a chance but is clear-eyed about the chances of reaching a deal. "We are talking to them. It's going fine. The problem with them is ... they try and tap tap tap [us along]. There's less urgency [on the Iranian side] than you think there would be, but they want to make deal more than they ever wanted," Trump said. Between the lines: Trump is weighing three courses of action, backed by three different camps: Make a deal: Vice President JD Vance and White House envoy Steve Witkoff are urging him to move toward a deal because a renewed war might not change the situation for the better. Most Gulf countries support this position and have communicated that to Trump, sources say. Go back to battle: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu wants to resume combat, as does Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. They argue that Iran can't be trusted to make a deal let alone abide by one, and that Trump should finish the job militarily. Maximum economic pain: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are advising Trump to maintain the "no war, no deal" status quo and allow the economic pressure campaign to continue, sources said. Ratcliffe told Trump that prolonged economic pain will induce Iran to make more concessions — or create enough instability inside the country that citizens revolt, a source with direct knowledge said. The CIA declined to comment. The other side: Iran's civilian leadership sounded hopeful on Monday about the prospects of reaching a deal. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei "granted the government certain authorities" to try to reach an agreement through diplomacy. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that the diplomatic exchanges "have become very intensive." "Qatar and Pakistan are playing very active roles as mediators. We have presented our conditions and our proposal, and everything depends on Washington's political rationality. If they choose genuine diplomacy, we are ready to engage. But if they intend to engage in deception and military operations, they will face a response more painful and severe than in the past," he said. Araghchi said that if the U.S. accepts Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, then "negotiations will resume." "Otherwise, the current situation will continue, and Iran will not bow down," he said. The big picture: Russia and China are taking an active role in the effort to reach a deal. Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke by phone Monday with Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Gen. Mohsen Rezaei. The two discussed the efforts to reach a diplomatic agreement. Rezaei, who is very close to Khamenei, was also the recipient of a letter Vance sent recently proposing to resume negotiations. Russia has also offered to be part of any nuclear agreement, including by receiving Iran's enriched uranium stockpile. At the same time, Rezaei's deputy visited Beijing on Monday and met with the Chinese foreign minister. China is also urging the U.S. and Iran to resume direct negotiations to end the war.

events.title: Lumentum CEO touts 'enormous' opportunity in massive AI connectivity deal with Marvell
events.summary: Marvell will acquire Lumentum in an all-stock transaction. The deal will expand Marvell's push into optical connectivity for artificial intelligence data centers. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026. Marvell Technology 's deal for optical components maker Lumentum will create an "enormous" opportunity to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout, Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston told CNBC on Monday. "You need scale-up technology that needs semiconductors and optical working seamlessly together," Marvell CEO Matt Murphy told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "We are going to create a new category of company here." Since the tie-up is a fixed-ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release. Marvell shares slumped 8% in trading Monday, while Lumentum's stock sank 13%. But both stocks have been huge winners in the artificial intelligence boom, with Marvell more than doubling in the past year, prior to Monday's sell-off, and Lumentum quadrupling over that stretch. Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models. "We're actually going to create solutions around those that are highly sticky, and the reason that they're sold out is because the demand is exploding, and we don't see that changing anytime soon," Murphy said. Humans are still doing the work behind some AI agents OpenAI pares fundraising goal, now seeking up to $20 billion in latest round Binance resumes withdrawals following $6.3 billion hack, says 90% of stolen user assets are covered Why AI is boosting Meta’s ad business while hurting Google search Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028. Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending. This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology. Marvell 's Murphy also shot down concerns about Nvidia's circular dealmaking, given the leading AI chipmaker's recent multibillion-dollar investments in both companies. In a bid to further support the data center infrastructure that houses its AI chips, Nvidia has positioned itself as a central cog in a network of related companies, investing in several technology companies that purchase its chips or neoclouds that rent out computing capacity. That's sparked criticism that companies like Nvidia are virtually funding themselves by taking stakes in customers. "This is a double down on supporting Nvidia, who is the ecosystem leader in this area," Murphy told CNBC. "We're very committed to that partnership, and I think having two of the key suppliers come together, that support that ecosystem, is going to be a big benefit for them." Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone. A previous version of this story incorrectly cited the Marvell CEO.

events.title: Residents campaign for curfew at new Sydney airport due to noise
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Blue Mountains residents unhappy at noise from Western Sydney International Airport David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo on the footsteps of the Blue Mountains for 44 years. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Residents living near the new Western Sydney International Airport are reporting increasing aircraft noise linked to the new Western Sydney airport. Blue Mountains resident David Lysiak says he worries about not being able to sleep at night as flights ramp up. An expert in air traffic managements says there are "no perfect options" when determining flight routes. Residents living in the Blue Mountains say they fear an end to the area's peace and quiet following last week's opening of the Western Sydney International Airport (WSI). The airport officially opened to domestic and international passengers on October 25 amid much fanfare. But a week later, concerns are being raised about aircraft noise. David Lysiak has lived in Warrimoo, a village in the lower Blue Mountains, for 44 years. Sydney's second airport officially opened on October 25. ( ABC News: Declan Bowring ) The retired grandfather and his wife raised four children there, and they have always loved the tranquillity. "It's just beautiful, quiet. Not many people. We have one shop, a general store," he said. "I just wander into the bush and go for a bushwalk, and take your bike down the trails … You ride through a blue gum forest and it's all accessible right from here." But he fears the serenity of the last four decades could be a thing of the past because his beloved town falls under the WSI flight path. Mr Lysiak is concerned for the future of Warrimoo. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) Freight flights began operating from the airport around the clock in July. Mr Lysiak said he has heard the noise of some freight aircraft "quite distinctly". That sound is only going to become more frequent . International airlines Air New Zealand, Singapore Airlines, Fiji Airways, Qatar Airways and Vietjet Air have so far signed up with WSI, with flights expected to ramp up over the next couple of years. The airport has one active runway. ( Supplied: Australian government ) WSI has one runway, designated as Runway 05 or Runway 23, depending on the direction of use. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west over areas in the city's west and Blue Mountains. Flights on Runway 23 arrive from the north-east and depart to the south-west. ( Supplied: Australian government ) When Runway 05 is used, flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west. Flights take off to the north-east and land from the south-west when Runway 05 is operational. ( Supplied: Australian government ) Weighing up if a trip from Sydney's new airport is for you The doors to Western Sydney International Airport are set to soon welcome commercial passengers. Airservices Australia has previously said that, where possible, Runway 23 would be prioritised during the day to minimise overflight and noise over residential suburbs to the north-east of the airport. Marek Bekier, a lecturer in air traffic management at the University of New South Wales School of Aviation, said there were always "trade-offs" when deciding on the best flight paths. "An air route connecting an airport to the wider airway system is not just a straight line in the sky," he said. "You have to think about it as a kind of three dimensional corridor that has to fulfil certain requirements. "No option is perfect. You will never find a new route that will basically satisfy the wishes and demands of everyone, so you always have to make some trade-offs." Community treated as 'collateral damage' Julius Timmerman, who moved to the Blue Mountains town of Lawson with his wife in 1996, said people in his community had been treated as "collateral damage". "I'm worried about not being able to sleep at night, just the effect on my amenity because we bought a house in the mountains in good faith that the area would remain quiet and peaceful," he said. "It's completely unfair that the people of Western Sydney and the Blue Mountains should be just treated as collateral damage for the sake of the airline industry." Julius Timmerman says he bought his house in the area thinking it would be quiet. ( Supplied ) He is one of hundreds of people in the community who want a rethink of the flight paths and have signed the Western Sydney Airport Community Impacts Alliance petition calling for a night-time curfew. "The main thing that we want is, as mentioned in the petition, a curfew from 11pm to 6am, which lines up with Kingston Smith Airport," he said.

events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Squarespace, the web company that helps customers build and host their own websites, is laying off about one-fifth of its workforce, in a move that will affect hundreds of jobs. Jeff Seedman, a public relations specialist representing Squarespace, confirmed the layoffs to TechCrunch. The Verge initially reported the layoffs. “Squarespace is restructuring its organization and reducing its global workforce by approximately 19%, representing around 300 employees,” said Seedman “The changes are intended to simplify how we operate, sharpen our priorities and enable the company to move faster as we position Squarespace for its next phase of growth.” Website building has changed immensely over the last few years as a result of the generative AI boom. So-called “vibe-coding” website builders, which only require simple prompts from users to spin up functional frontend designs, have largely upended the industry, making it possible for users to create sites with significantly less effort. These kinds of sites have become an increasingly central part of the website building business. Last year, web host rival Wix bought Base44 for $80 million . Similar offerings, like Lovable, have generated significant investor interest; Lovable raised a $400 million Series C round in August that valued the company at $13.3 billion. Google also recently launched Stitch , a feature that allows users to swiftly generate user interface designs. Squarespace has also begun a big push into AI. In 2024, the company launched an AI tool called Blueprint. The company also recently announced Forma, an upcoming AI native platform, which users can join its waitlist . Squarespace was founded in 2004 and went public in 2021 at a $10 billion valuation. However, the company struggled in the ensuing years to generate enthusiastic public market interest. Squarespace ultimately decided to go private again by way of a $7 billion private equity deal in 2024. events.title: Hardware Defense Blocks Memory-Dependent Prefetcher Leakage (KU Leuven)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at KU Leuven and EURECOM published “SecDMP: Provably Secure Data Memory-Dependent Prefetching.” Abstract Excerpt : “In this work, we address this gap by designing a defense that is both secure and efficient. First, we propose a classification of DMP leakage, categorize existing and novel attacks, and analyze which leakage classes are mitigated by existing defenses. We validate this analysis empirically by implementing the first open-source DMPs on a RISC-V processor, showing that the only existing defense that aims to preserve DMP performance fails to protect against entire leakage classes. Next, we propose SecDMP, a provably secure and efficient hardware-based defense. SecDMP requires secrets to be marked in memory and ensures that DMPs never encode these secrets in the microarchitecture—without compromising performance for public data. We formally prove that SecDMP introduces no leakage beyond a baseline semantics without DMPs. Notably, when combined with speculative-execution defenses, SecDMP restores complete microarchitectural security for constant-time code. Finally, our empirical evaluation shows that SecDMP prevents all DMP leakage while incurring minimal performance overhead and hardware cost.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: What we know so far about the Learjet 60 private plane that crashed in Florida
events.summary: Roads are closed after a jet crashed on November 1. Saul Martinez/Getty Images A private jet crashed in South Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people aboard. Weather data at the time of the crash shows thunderstorms and moderate turbulence in the area. NTSB officials said there is evidence of the jet breaking apart before impact. Nine people aboard a private jet were killed when it crashed and exploded in a fireball near Palm Beach, Florida, Sunday afternoon. The plane, a Learjet built in 2004 and registered as N722BD , had departed from Austin and was en route to the Bahamas. The identities of the passengers and pilots were not immediately available. Authorities have not said what caused the crash. "Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy wrote on X on Sunday. National Transportation Safety Board Member Tom Chapman said during a press conference on Monday that access to the crash site is challenging because of the bad weather on the ground, causing the impact crater to fill with water. Officials also said crash debris was scattered across fields, homes, and businesses. The crash occurred less than 10 miles from President Donald Trump's Mar-A-Lago resort. Trump left West Palm Beach around noon aboard Air Force One to attend a rally in Iowa, according to White House pool reports. What we know about the flight Aviation-tracking data from FlightRadar24 showed the plane descending from 41,000 feet to about 35,000 feet as it entered Florida, then crossed the state before plummeting about 27,000 feet in about a minute to the ground near Palm Beach. The plane was about two hours into the flight to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed. In the minutes before the accident, a pilot can be heard on air traffic control recordings reporting the air temperature outside as -47 degrees Celsius (about -52 degrees Fahrenheit), as well as icing, precipitation, and moderate turbulence. The pilot later declared "mayday," saying the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute, and moments later, reported an overspeed condition before impact. Video footage shared online of the crash shows that part of the Learjet's T-tail may have separated from the plane. Chapman said there is "some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact" and the NTSB is "still seeking to determine that." He also said the agency hopes to recover the cockpit voice recorder, but it's unclear if the particular jet had one installed. NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said during the briefing that the Federal Aviation Administration and the manufacturer Learjet, which is now a part of Bombardier, will assist the NTSB with the investigation. "We at Bombardier are deeply saddened by this tragic event and extend our sincerest sympathies to all those affected," Bombardier said in a statement. "We cannot comment on the potential cause of this accident until the investigation is complete and we will fully support the investigating authorities and cooperate as needed." What we know about the weather Widespread thunderstorms moved through South Florida on Sunday afternoon. Aviation weather data for the area showed heavy rain, low visibility, and turbulence around the time of the crash. "The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation," Chapman said. "You all saw what the weather was like here at the surface; what we have to determine is what the weather conditions were like at altitude." There were thunderstorms in the area at the time of the crash. Saul Martinez/Getty Images It's not yet known what caused the crash, but retired Delta Air Lines pilot Mark Stephens told Business Insider that icing can occur at any altitude and, in some circumstances, cause a wing to lose lift and an aircraft to stall. "If there was a failure on one wing, meaning that wing iced up, then the good wing would still fly, but the other would lose lift," he said. "You'd have such an uneven lift that it would basically do close to exactly what the Learjet did; it can flop out of the sky." Stephens warned against immediately placing blame on the pilots, adding that anti-ice and weather radar systems can fail and that a number of factors beyond human error could have contributed. 'She was doing her job' NASA administrator Jared Isaacman, who is also a pilot, shared his thoughts on the crash on X and urged the public not to criticize the woman pilot in the ATC calls. "She was the second-in-command (SIC), and while she was empowered to point out mistakes as part of good crew resource management, she was doing her job, communicating with ATC right to the end in a terrifying situation," he wrote. He added that she "likely knew before many of those calls that she was going to die," and the public does not know factors such as the jet's maintenance history, or whether there was structural failure and why. Isaacman also said that charter companies often hire commercial pilots "very early in their careers to gain experience," alongside airline-qualified captains. "She would still have the appropriate training, qualifications, and checkouts by an FAA examiner or designee," he said. "Let people investigate, learn, and share the facts. Be respectful to those who perished and the families who carry their memories." This is a developing story. Check back for updates. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Fed will vote on rates less often. What that could mean for borrowers
events.summary: After the Federal Reserve meeting in October, Chairman Kevin Warsh unveiled changes that would reduce the number of rate-setting votes. The move could mean consumers wait longer for their borrowing costs to come down. Economists say consumers may be even more affected by the lack of transparency, as Warsh also implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance. After the Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady last week, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh announced plans to reduce the number of rate-setting votes over the next two years. That move could potentially extend the timeline for everyday Americans to see borrowing costs adjust, some experts say. "Fewer Fed meetings in 2027 could mean consumers wait longer to see relief when borrowing costs are elevated," said James Vrachas, executive director at advisory firm Post Oak Group. Americans may feel somewhat removed from the Fed, but the central bank's moves have a ripple effect on many types of consumer products, including the borrowing rates for credit cards , home loans and auto financing. Midterm election: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing Trump Account holders to receive SpaceX stock from Gwynne Shotwell in December CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 For example, most credit cards have variable rates tied to the prime rate, which moves with the Fed's benchmark. However, even with the central bank holding rates unchanged, credit card rates are edging higher as issuers protect themselves from risk, according to LendingTree. Card issuers are mitigating their exposure from borrowers who may fall behind on payments or default in the face of stubborn inflation in everyday expenses, said Matt Schulz, LendingTree's chief credit analyst. Generally, card issuers are slow to bring rates down, unless prompted by the Fed's actions, said Schulz: "Issuers will tinker with rates a bit at the margins at other times, but the big moves tend to only come when issuers are pushed." On Oct. 28, the central bank voted to keep the benchmark borrowing rate at the current target range of 3.75% to 4% as policymakers deliberated next steps with inflation remaining well above the Fed's 2% goal. The Fed will keep meeting eight times a year, Warsh said at the news conference following the October meeting, but next year, one of the eight meetings will not entail a vote on interest rates or include a post-meeting statement. The "strategy" meetings will increase to two the following year, leaving just six opportunities to adjust rates — with the exception of emergency meetings, if necessary. "For consumers, that could mean longer periods of uncertainty around borrowing costs," said Jordan Ricciardi, a senior wealth strategy associate at UBS. "Our clients looking to buy a home, refinance a mortgage or finance a business could be impacted as fewer scheduled opportunities means the Fed isn't as quickly responding to changing economic conditions." Borrowing rates may stay elevated for longer With fewer scheduled opportunities to adjust rates, that means borrowing rates could remain stubbornly high even if economic conditions begin to improve, Post Oak Group's Vrachas also said. As it stands, financial institutions can adjust rates whenever market conditions warrant, regardless of the Fed's meeting schedule, he said. In the meantime, though, many consumers may continue to face elevated borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and credit card debt, among other financial products. "For consumers, the bigger concern isn't necessarily fewer meetings, but whether lenders pass along lower borrowing costs as quickly as they pass along increases," Vrachas said. 'Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest' Consumers may be even more impacted by the lack of transparency, economists say, as Warsh implements measures to curtail so-called forward guidance, or how the Fed signals its future rate moves. Although economic conditions have become more complicated and information is more widely available, "Warsh keeps his proverbial cards closer to his chest than his recent predecessors have," said Mark Hamrick, an economic analyst and founder of The Hamrick Brief, a weekly newsletter. "I wouldn't expect consumers to see the universe of market rates change simply because the Fed votes less often," he said. "But the public may have less opportunity to hear from the source about how and why the Fed is making the decisions that shape what they pay to borrow and what they earn on their savings." In the interim, "the best protection for consumers remains shopping around, particularly for the highest yields among savings accounts and [certificates of deposit]," Hamrick said.

events.title: Judge tosses DOJ case against ex-FBI officials accused of lying about Hunter Biden probe
events.summary: A federal judge in Washington dismissed the Department of Justice's case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden. The judge reportedly blasted the Justice Department, saying the situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization." He accused the DOJ of a "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, suggesting it rushed the case ahead of the midterm election. A federal judge on Monday blasted the Department of Justice for "weaponization" as he dismissed its case accusing two former FBI officials of lying to Congress about investigations into Hunter Biden , multiple news outlets reported. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui, in a hearing in U.S. District Court in Washington, reportedly tore into the DOJ over its "slapdash job" prosecuting ex-officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, saying he was "deeply troubled by what has happened here." Faruqui said the government lacked probable cause and failed to present evidence that the officials' statements before the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 were knowingly false, MS NOW reported. He also accused the DOJ of wrongly rushing the case ahead of the midterm election . The situation "cannot be described as anything other than weaponization," he said, according to MS NOW. Alaska Gov. orders probe of Peltola Senate campaign's alleged recruitment of 2nd Sullivan Warren urges DOJ probe of Bank of America money laundering It's a 'socialist' bank — and North Dakota Republicans love it Three media outlets seek full White House access in amended lawsuit The judge even apologized to the government's lawyers, calling it "incredibly unfair" that they were assigned to defend the flawed case. "This does not feel like an investigation," Faruqui reportedly added. "It feels like a broken one-wish willow obsession." The DOJ, in response to an email sent to its press office, said it "disagrees" with the decision. "We are evaluating all options but cannot comment further on an ongoing criminal investigation," the agency said in response to CNBC. "The Department's actions will continue to be guided by the facts, the evidence, and the law – not politics." Attorneys for Floris and Benavides praised the judge's decision outside the courthouse later Monday morning. "This case should never have been brought. The government had no case, as the judge just laid out," a lawyer for Floris said, slamming the prosecution as a "spaghetti-at-the-wall, Hunter-Biden-conspiracy fever dream." A lawyer for Benavides said they hope the DOJ will not try to keep the case alive by seeking an indictment before a grand jury "where they get to be behind closed doors and get to shape the narrative, and we are unable to present our side." The DOJ did not take that step when they unveiled the allegations against Floris and Benavides on Oct. 23. Rather, despite the alleged misconduct taking place years earlier, prosecutors acquired a criminal complaint, which only requires a judge's signature. Criminal complaints are often used to obtain arrest warrant in situations where prosecutors need to move quickly . Faruqui had flagged that circumstance as unusual, and last week refused to sign off on a superseding complaint that added an obstruction charge against the two ex-officials. "I'm concerned with your view as to what the law is," the judge told the prosecutors in a hearing last Tuesday. "Why today, on this one case, have you changed the entire history of how you charge cases?"

events.title: Lindsay Clancy in court to drop child murder charges after mistrial
events.summary: Defence argues juror misconduct and judge’s questioning impacted Clancy’s trial for strangling of her three children. Lindsay Clancy, the American mother facing murder charges for killing her three young children, has returned to court in a bid to get the charges dropped. Clancy’s lawyers urged Judge William Sullivan on Monday to dismiss the first-degree murder charges against her in the state of Massachusetts in the United States, saying retrying her for killing her three young children would violate ⁠⁠her constitutional rights. Prosecutors said they intend to retry Clancy if the case moves forward but have not decided if she would face the same first-degree murder charges. list 1 of 4 Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia election list 2 of 4 Suwayda remains in stasis as US signals differences with Israel on Syria list 3 of 4 Man targeted Muslims, Africans and North Africans, French prosecutors say list 4 of 4 Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy children’s murder case Monday’s hearing was her second time in court since September, when jurors were unable to reach a verdict at her trial. Clancy strangled her three children with exercise bands in 2023 at her home in Duxbury, a suburb of Boston in Massachusetts. Clancy then attempted to take her own life by cutting herself with a knife and was paralysed after jumping from a second-floor window. At Monday’s hearing, defence lawyer Martin G Weinberg argued that the judge should have investigated further after the jury foreperson sent two notes indicating that a juror was not following the rules. Further questioning could have revealed grounds to remove the juror, identified as Michael Desronvil, and continue deliberations, he said. After receiving the notes, Sullivan spoke with each juror, reminding them of their duties and explaining what constitutes reasonable doubt in a court case. He asked whether they could apply the law to the case, and all said yes. But Weinberg argued that Sullivan had not gone far enough. A juror who said he could follow the law could have been lying, Weinberg said, and the situation warranted questioning the foreperson separately to learn more about what was happening during deliberations. Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague argued there was no indication the holdout juror’s disagreement stemmed from personal bias or an inability to deliberate, rather than a different assessment of the evidence. Sprague said the judge handled the ⁠⁠jury impasse appropriately, saying the fact that one juror dug in his heels did not mean Sullivan should risk interfering with the deliberations by questioning him. “It is clear from the record this ⁠⁠juror did not refuse to deliberate,” Sprague said. “He refused to agree.” Defence lawyer Kevin Reddington accused the lone holdout juror of using a mobile phone to research terms related to the case and questioned whether he had been truthful during jury selection. Clancy has never disputed killing her three young children in 2023, but her lawyer has argued she had postpartum psychosis and was unable to control her behaviour. Prosecutors have acknowledged that Clancy, now 36, had mental health problems but said she acted deliberately and understood her actions were wrong. Sullivan did not immediately rule on the motion to dismiss. He scheduled another hearing for November 16 and suggested a retrial could begin in March. Another motion expected to be discussed is the state of Massachusetts’s request for a gag order barring lawyers and their supporters “from making extrajudicial statements to the media that would have a substantial likelihood of materially prejudicing the criminal proceeding”.

events.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to block 20,000 California ballots before midterms
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms California says the move to block ballots from suspected noncitizens could disenfranchise eligible voters. The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the Supreme Court to stop California from counting mail-in ballots from more than 20,000 voters it claims are not US citizens. The emergency request, filed on Monday, just one day before the midterm elections , is the latest development in a legal battle between the administration and California, a Democratic stronghold and the most populous US state. California says the move could disenfranchise thousands of eligible voters. The Department of Justice wants California to set aside ballots from voters on a list compiled by the Department of Homeland Security until after their citizenship status is confirmed. But California says the list is unreliable and could include thousands of US citizens. Voting has been under way since early October, and state officials say it would be nearly impossible to separate the ballots in question. Last week, a federal judge rejected the administration’s request, raising concerns about the reliability of the data on the list. “If the executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger,” Judge David Carter wrote. The administration has turned to the Supreme Court after a federal appeals court also rejected the request on Friday. The dispute comes as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress in Tuesday’s elections. Trump has repeatedly made false claims about widespread voter fraud, but studies and state audits have shown that ineligible voting, including by noncitizens, is rare.
