events.title: Shabana Mahmood softens immigration plans in face of cabinet backlash
events.summary: Exception for care workers will allow an estimated 280,000 people and their dependants to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years Shabana Mahmood rowed back on her most hardline plans to make care workers wait 15 years for settlement in the UK, but told MPs on Monday that many migrants would still face retrospective rule changes to make them wait a decade. Under pressure from a cabinet backlash and health unions, the home secretary has offered a carve-out for care workers to allow them to apply for indefinite leave to remain after five years. But most of the rigorous new rules drawn up by Mahmood’s office last year remain, including plans to force those who arrived in the UK by irregular means such as small boats to face up to 30 years before being able to apply for settlement. The changes drew cries of betrayal from the Conservatives and the Reform UK leader, Nigel Farage, who said it was “the beginning of the capitulation”. But Mahmood told the Commons she would still enact sweeping changes that will mean many migrant workers will wait double the time they had expected for settlement. She said settlement was “one of most valuable rights this country can offer. Until now it has been given almost automatically. From today it must be earned. Those who contribute will settle fastest. Those who don’t play by the rules will be refused or wait much longer.” In particular, the wait for those earning under £50,000 will double to 10 years. This was criticised by some Labour MPs who said vital workers such as research scientists and chefs would be caught by the changes. The Law Society said the changing rules could threaten the rule of law, saying it “retrospectively undermines the legal certainty that individuals, families and employers rely on”. Some MPs suggested they would continue to press the home secretary to rethink the retrospective nature of the changes – though the new policies do not require a vote in parliament, so MPs have limited means to block them. Abtisam Mohamed, the Labour MP for Sheffield Central, said: “Retrospectively uprooting someone’s plans, sometimes made at the most vulnerable time in their lives, is unfair. I’ll be pressing for those already here to be protected.” The former shadow home secretary Diane Abbott also criticised the retrospective changes. “You can come in legally, you can work legally and then have your residency rights turned upside down,” she said, warning of another potential Windrush scandal. The Walthamstow MP Stella Creasy said there was a “partial recognition” of the contribution migrants made but there were thousands of people “facing 10 years of limbo with many businesses unclear if talent will stay or not as a result”. She said: “The economic consequences of those people walking away from the UK will far outweigh any savings in entitlement to benefits, given many of them don’t claim anyway, so the home secretary still has work to do to make these reforms work for our national interest.” Refugees will also face a longer wait of 10 years, with an additional 10-year penalty for those who do not enter legally – and those who do not find employment will face a wait of up to 30 years. Andy Burnham, who promised voters in his Makerfield byelection that he would support Mahmood’s migration agenda, endorsed the plans and said the home secretary was “gripping this problem” by introducing the earned element. “People want to see an immigration system based on control, contribution, and which rewards those who play by the rules,” the prime minister said. “It is only fair that those who are making the most valuable contribution to our communities are given the opportunity to settle earlier. Those in other roles should expect to wait longer while people who abuse the system or arrive illegally will be refused or will also have to wait longer.” But migrant rights organisations accused the government of “moving the goalposts” for those who had played by the rules. “People who have built their lives around the government’s requirements deserve better than decisions that turn their own and their families’ lives upside down,” said Amnesty International. The key climbdown from the home secretary was an exemption for care workers – something which the housing secretary, Angela Rayner, had explicitly criticised. The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, also repeatedly refused to say she backed proposals to prolong the qualifying period for settlement. events.title: Defense, healthcare, crypto and AI: How the midterm election could affect stocks
events.summary: The midterm election could reshape the outlook for companies heavily exposed to Washington, especially in defense, healthcare, crypto and artificial intelligence. Democratic control of either chamber could bring more investigations and oversight, while giving the party leverage over federal spending and must-pass legislation. Even without control of the White House, Congress could influence billions of dollars in government funding and determine whether Trump-era regulatory changes become lasting law. Lockheed Martin gets about 70% of its sales from the U.S. government. Medicaid accounts for three-quarters of Molina Healthcare's premium revenue . Coinbase is waiting on Congress to finish writing the rules for cryptocurrency . For some of the biggest U.S. companies, Washington is part of the business model. Now, the midterm election could change who holds the leverage. A Democratic victory in either or both chambers of Congress would grant the party new leverage to investigate companies , challenge federal spending and demand legislative concessions. But their reach would have limits: President Donald Trump would retain his veto and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and federal regulation. Historically, stocks have performed well under divided government. Under Republican presidents, the S&P 500 has gained an average of 23% in the year after midterms when Congress was split, compared with 16% when Democrats controlled both chambers, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis published Thursday. Analysts often attribute the pattern in part to congressional gridlock limiting sweeping policy changes. Still, some analysts caution against assuming that pattern will repeat. "We don't think that blueprint holds up this time around, and we still see plenty of reasons to be constructive on the U.S. equity market," said Ariana Salvatore , head of U.S. public policy research at Morgan Stanley. For investors, the midterm election could reshape which businesses preserve their advantages in Washington, particularly in industries such as defense , healthcare , banking and artificial intelligence . "There are some policy changes that might be market moving, at least for certain segments," said Jeff Buchbinder , chief equity strategist at LPL Financial. Congressional oversight and investigations Control of either the House or Senate would give Democrats committee gavels and subpoena power, allowing them to demand documents, compel testimony and haul executives before public hearings. Companies are already getting a preview. On Oct. 21, Sen. Richard Blumenthal , D-Conn., the top Democrat on the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sought records tied to Trump's White House ballroom from donors including Cisco , Salesforce , ServiceNow and Kraken . Apple and Nvidia each committed $25 million to the project, according to records obtained by The Washington Post . Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., has separately sought records involving tariff exclusions, including communications involving Apple's former CEO, Tim Cook , as Democrats investigate whether Trump used trade policy to reward political allies and donors. While donations do not prove wrongdoing or favorable treatment, congressional probes still carry risks: subpoenas consume executive bandwidth, reveal internal communications and generate unpredictable news coverage. Few CEOs relish the idea of sitting at a witness table before lawmakers and television cameras. "It creates volatility because you get a negative headline," said Monica Guerra , Morgan Stanley's head of policy and geopolitical strategy, who expects Democrats to cast a wide net for their probes. Democrats have signaled interest in Trump family businesses, government contractors, firms tied to Donald Trump Jr.'s 1789 Capital , and companies associated with Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency . Then there is the most basic power Congress has: deciding where the money goes. Trump's 2025 tax cuts and spending law, known as One Big Beautiful Bill , is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by $911 billion through 2034, according to a KFF analysis of Congressional Budget Office estimates. KFF is a nonpartisan nonprofit that provides health policy information. Meanwhile, new work requirements for Medicaid enrollees are scheduled to take effect Jan. 1, or earlier in some states, while tighter state budgets could mean fewer people are covered and greater pressure on provider payments. Molina Healthcare generated $32.2 billion , or 75% of its 2025 premium revenue, from Medicaid, according to the company's annual Securities and Exchange Commission filing. In the same filing, Molina warned that losing government contracts or failing to renew them on favorable terms could materially reduce premium revenue.

events.title: I used to be a supermarket cake decorator. Here are 9 of my best tips for ordering a cake.
events.summary: Many supermarkets offer the option to walk in and grab a cake from their bakery case, as well as the option to order a custom cake. Molly Allen I worked as a supermarket cake decorator for two years before opening my own bakery . Ask for whipped cream if you want a less-sweet cake, or for two cake flavors to please more guests. It could be worth asking about free smash cakes or using your own toys for kids' birthday cakes . Supermarket cakes can be an easy, more affordable way to celebrate any occasion. However, not all of these cakes are served and created equally. Take it from me: I worked in the bakery section of a popular supermarket for two years, prepping treats and decorating cakes, before opening my own bakery. Here are my go-to tips for ordering the best cake from your local supermarket.  Place your order long before your party Some supermarkets bake cakes on-site, but many work with prebaked, frozen cakes. In these cases, the bakery will keep a stock of common cake flavors (vanilla, chocolate) on hand, and maybe a more limited selection of additional flavor choices (carrot, red velvet, marble).  To make sure you get the flavor you want, order your custom cake with two to three weeks' notice. This can help give the decorator and the bakery time to ensure your desired flavor is in stock. Ask for whipped cream if you think grocery-store cakes are too sweet Ask for whipped cream if the frosting on supermarket cakes is usually too sweet for you. Jasmin Merdan/Getty Images If you've stayed away from grocery-store cakes because the typical buttercream frosting is a bit too sweet for you, check if the bakery has other options.  Vanilla buttercream is often a default choice, but it's usually not the only one. Some supermarket bakeries can use fresh whipped cream for topping a cake. Other choices might include cream-cheese frosting , chocolate frosting, coconut-pecan frosting typically used for German chocolate cakes, and even chocolate ganache. Generally, you won't know for sure unless you ask. Check if the bakery can do half-and-half flavors You may not have to choose between chocolate or vanilla cake. When ordering, ask about doing half vanilla and half chocolate so everyone at your party can enjoy a slice of their preferred flavor. This is often possible with half-sheet cakes and two-layer round cakes. (And it might also work with other cake flavors, too.) Order with the cake decorator if you want something very specific Cake decorators can sometimes work early hours. gerenme/Getty Images You can generally speak with any bakery employee to order a cake, but if you have a specific or out-of-the-box request for decorations, ask when you can speak with the cake decorator by phone or in person. In my experience, they often work early shifts so they can begin preparing orders and items for the display case. Decorating is their specialty, and they can be the best person to tell you if tackling the specific design you're hoping for is achievable. And, if not, they may be able to help brainstorm an alternative. Consider bringing in your own toys for kids' cakes Supermarket bakeries usually have a look book of designs that cake decorators are trained to make, and children's cakes often include character toys from popular movies and shows. If the bakery doesn't have your child's favorite character, don't be afraid to ask staff what's possible. Depending on the store and decorator, you may be able to bring in small, washed figurines for the decorator to incorporate into the design. Or you can try asking the decorator to leave space for a specific toy when creating the design. Don't be afraid to order a plain cake if you want to dress it up yourself Remember that cake decorators don't have to dress up your cake with a border, sprinkles, and writing if you don't want them to. If you want a semi-customized dessert, just order a plain, frosted cake in your desired size. That way, you can take it home and turn it into anything you want. Add edible flowers to dress it up for a more formal occasion, or top it with candy and sprinkles in your desired shades. You can even try adding your own fun candles, toys, and knickknacks on top. Request a plastic cake container instead of a bakery box Premade birthday cakes can usually be customized. iStock / Getty Images Plus At many bakeries, custom cake orders are packaged in cardboard boxes for pickup. If you anticipate you'll have leftover cake, ask for a plastic cake container instead. This will provide an airtight solution for easily storing leftovers. Keep in mind that this tip may not work for every bakery, and it could depend on the supplies they have on hand. Ask about a free smash cake for kids If you're planning to order a birthday cake for a young child, ask if your supermarket bakery also offers free smash cakes. A smash cake is tiny, typically 4 inches in diameter, meant just for a kid to dig into on their birthday. These are usually served alongside a larger sheet cake meant for guests. Some bakeries will give you a free smash cake when you order a larger decorated cake or meet a minimum order size. Check last-minute options if you forgot to order ahead Even if you forgot to order a few weeks in advance, there may still be options the store's cake decorator can pull together for you. If it's a few days before your event, or the morning of, it doesn't hurt to ask. The decorator may be able to put together a simple design while you shop for other items in the store. Or you can grab a premade option from the bakery case and ask for writing on top and extra sprinkles along the edges to spruce it up. Just keep in mind that your options may depend on how busy the bakery is when you visit. This story was originally published on March 25, 2023, and most recently updated on November 2, 2026. events.title: Co-Optimizing Access Points Improves Analog Placement (UT Austin)
events.summary: Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Technical Papers Home '; AI/ML/DL Architectures Automotive/ Aerospace Communication/Data Movement Design & Verification Lithography Manufacturing Materials Memory Optoelectronics / Photonics Packaging Power & Performance Quantum Security Test, Measurement, Analytics tech papers Transistors Z-End Applications Videos & Research Videos Industry Research Newsletters & Store Newsletters Store MENU Home Special Reports Systems & Design Low Power-High Performance Manufacturing, Packaging & Materials Test, Measurement & Analytics Auto, Security and AI Knowledge Center Videos Startup Corner Business & Startups Jobs Technical Papers Events Webinars Industry Research Newsletters Store Special Reports Researchers at the University of Texas at Austin published “APPlace: Co-Optimizing Device Locations and Access Points for Routing-Aware Analog Placement.” Abstract “Analog layout automation remains challenging in Analog/Mixed-Signal circuit design, because parasitics and mismatches introduced during layout strongly affect circuit performance. Placement is especially critical among the layout stages, as it constrains the routing solution space and the achievable post-layout performance. Existing analytical placement methods optimize device coordinates under center-based wirelength proxies and leave access point (AP) selection to routing. In analog circuits, however, a routing pin is an extended piece of terminal metal rather than a fixed point, and the best AP on it depends on where the other connected devices are placed, so a coordinate-only placement optimizes for connection points that the router will not use. We present APPlace, a routing-aware analog placement framework that co-optimizes device locations and AP selections during global placement, followed by a legalization stage that preserves the structure established by global placement. Experimental results on four real-world analog benchmarks show that APPlace achieves better overall post-layout performance than representative baselines at comparable layout area. Ablation studies further show that removing AP co-optimization causes up to a 13 dB CMRR loss among the OTA benchmarks and a 23% increase in comparator delay.” Find the technical paper here . events.title: Senegal hosts Africa’s first Olympics
events.summary: More than 2,000 athletes from around the world are in Senegal for the Youth Olympic Games to compete in Africa’s first Olympic event. The head of the International Olympic Committee (IOC), Kirsty Coventry, says this is a milestone, not just for Senegal but for the continent, which has the largest youth population. The games, postponed four years ago because of the COVID-19 pandemic, are being viewed as a test for Africa to see whether it can handle major international sports events. She says this is a chance for Africa to show the world what it is capable of hosting such big events. Herself an Olympic gold medallist in swimming, Coventry tells Al Jazeera she hopes the games will empower young people and inspire them to dream big. But as the Olympic flame burns bright in Senegal – the future of the youth games is uncertain. Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye says hosting the event is a proud moment. However, the country is facing economic challenges, and some critics say the money could have been better spent elsewhere. Coventry says the IOC is re-evaluating its direction and examining how to reduce the costs of hosting. events.title: Texas governor race tightens in prediction markets, but Abbott remains favored
events.summary: Texas Republican Gov. Greg Abbott remains favored to defeat his Democratic opponent state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to prediction market traders, but his odds have slipped. Many are watching Texas to see if voters deliver a blow to data center development, which Abbott previously supported before turning more skeptical on the industry this year. Hinojosa has attacked Abbott for his previous support of data centers. Political observers are watching the Texas gubernatorial election for signs of an artificial intelligence data center backlash in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections on Tuesday, and prediction market traders see growing odds of the Democratic candidate pulling off an upset. Gov. Greg Abbott , a Republican seeking a fourth term, has a 60% chance of beating Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday, according to speculators on platform Kalshi. Hinojosa's odds to win have jumped from 8% in mid-July to 40% on Monday, with many of those gains coming in recent weeks as a series of polls have shown the race to be tightening . On Polymarket, Hinojosa has seen her odds jump from as low as 5% in late July to 39% on Monday. Contracts are resolved using data from the Texas Secretary of State's office. Odds and gambling platforms do not use methodologies used by traditional political polling, and therefore are not substitutes for political polls. Hinojosa is seeking to be the first Democratic governor in Texas in more than 30 years. She has used Abbott's previous support for data center development in the state as an attack against the incumbent . In November 2025, Abbott touted a $40 billion investment by Google — which included bringing three new data centers to the state — by saying that Texas will be the "epicenter of AI development." But Abbott has changed his tune as voters' opinion of data centers has soured over the past year. Abbott in August ordered an audit of data centers that sought to connect to the state's grid, and then in September halted the approval of all data center-related permits until an audit of the existing waitlist is conducted. Hinojosa is running on an immediate data center moratorium until the legislature puts guardrails on the industry, according to her campaign website. In-person early voting in Texas concluded on Friday, and more than 7.7 million Texans have already cast their ballots. events.summary: Tehran says plan has been condensed and can be implemented within two days as it continues talks with mediators. Iran has said it is trying to accelerate the ceasefire plan it has proposed to the United States, as the region braces for possible renewed fighting in the US-Israel war against the country. Officials in Tehran said on Monday that the seven-step plan they put on the table last month remains the same, but could now be implemented more quickly. The statement comes as Iranian officials continue negotiations with Qatari mediators in the latest effort to find a diplomatic path out of the eight-month conflict. US President Donald Trump has said the latest negotiations were “going fine” but has suggested several times that the United States could strike Iran after the November 3 US midterm elections. The offer from Iran remains on the table but has now been “condensed and can be implemented within two days” instead of seven, Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said . “If Iran’s demands are met, it is possible that both security will be restored to the Strait of Hormuz and the negotiation process will begin within a short period of time,” Baghaei said. “All of this depends on how the American side wants to proceed regarding the future of this process.” Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has reportedly granted “powers” to the government to accelerate talks with the US to end the regional war, the state IRNA news agency said. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated that Tehran is prepared for both diplomacy and military confrontation , as mediators ⁠Qatar and Pakistan continue to facilitate indirect talks. “By accepting these conditions, the Strait of Hormuz will be opened and negotiations will resume,” Araghchi told IRNA in Ashgabat, Turkmenistan. “Otherwise, the current situation will continue and Iran will not bow down.” Iran previously said the plan could be implemented within a week if the US met its conditions, which include lifting the naval blockade of its ports, the repeal of sanctions, and a guarantee of an end to strikes, and a complete regional ceasefire, especially in Lebanon. Baghaei gave no indication that Tehran had changed its demands or that Washington had accepted its proposal. Trump said the war on Iran will end “very soon one way or the other”, telling the Right Side Broadcasting Network (RSBN) on Sunday that Tehran would either “make a deal or we’ll just end it”.

events.summary: The expanded industrial action comes amid a wave of strikes and protests that have sparked unrest across Europe. Germany’s largest union has launched a wave of strikes as it pushes for higher wages and increased job security. The walkouts on Monday escalated a wage dispute affecting about 3.7 million employees in Germany’s metal and electrical engineering industries. The expanded industrial action comes amid myriad strikes and protests across Europe over the cost of living and conditions in workplaces and educational facilities, several of which have seen severe unrest. Major manufacturers including Audi, Mercedes-Benz and Tata Steel were affected by the strikes launched by the IG Metall union. The union is calling for a 5 percent pay rise amid cost-of-living pressures, as well as measures to protect jobs and production sites, and profit-sharing arrangements in sectors performing strongly. Employers have proposed a one-off payment equivalent to 1 percent of pay in July 2027, followed by a 1.3 percent wage increase from July 2028. The proposal would allow companies facing financial difficulties to withhold the one-off payment. IG Metall rejected the offer, saying it would amount to a pay cut in real terms, and called for the expansion of the industrial action. Strikes are expected to continue throughout the week. The union plans to release participation figures on Friday. During the previous bargaining round in 2024, more than 100,000 workers took part on peak days. The cost of living, housing costs, and education policy have provoked demonstrations across Europe in recent weeks. Students and unions have led mass rallies, and unrest has rocked Belgium, France and Spain among other countries. The wave of protest reached Germany over the weekend, with thousands of people rallying in Berlin and more than 30 other German cities on Saturday.

events.title: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years. Here's how much money is at stake for beneficiaries
events.summary: Social Security may have to cut retirement benefits in six years, according to the latest projections. Congress may act sooner to prevent those cuts, or lawmakers may opt to kick the can down the road. Putting off Social Security reform would have consequences for beneficiaries and the economy, experts say. Here's how much money may be at stake for individuals who rely on the program. Social Security retirement benefits may face an automatic, across-the-board cut in just six years . Without intervention before then, the Social Security retirement trust fund, formally known as the Old-Age and Survivors Insurance Trust Fund, which helps pay benefits to eligible workers and qualifying family members, will run out in the fourth quarter of 2032, the program's trustees said in a June report . At that time, the trustees project retirement benefits will be cut by 22%. The Congressional Budget Office has a more dire forecast, anticipating that the retirement trust fund may run out sooner, in mid-2032, and that retirees may see larger benefit cuts, at 26%, upon insolvency. Beneficiaries may receive an average $500 cut to their monthly benefits across the U.S. based on a 24% benefit reduction, according to a June report from the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. In 29 states, retirees would see even bigger average reductions, according to the nonpartisan organization focused on educating the public on fiscal policy issues. Senators elected this November will be in office in 2032, when the retirement trust fund depletion date hits. Their ability to right the ship is crucial for retirees and the economy. But it's not a sure thing given the political climate inside the beltway. "The attention on 2032 is appropriate in the sense that that is when beneficiaries and future beneficiaries will see and feel the consequences of inaction," said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a public policy think tank focused on promoting bipartisan cooperation. "Nothing gets Congress to move like that type of deadline," he said. Midterm elections guide: How affordability and the economy could affect voters' decisions These Senate races may help determine the fate of Social Security Social Security: How much money beneficiaries may lose if Congress does nothing Of course, brinksmanship and political deadlock may stymie efforts. Congress could opt to kick the can down the road, rather than enact changes to shore up Social Security — which may require tax increases, benefit cuts or a combination of both. If lawmakers decide to combine Social Security's retirement and disability trust funds, the depletion date may move to the third quarter of 2034, when benefits may be cut by 17%, according to Social Security's trustees. Akabas said any delay by lawmakers would have consequences: Social Security's shortfall would continue to increase. There could also be consequences for the economy, he said. In 2023, Social Security benefits generated $2.6 trillion in total economic output and supported more than 12 million jobs, according to 2025 research by the National Institute on Retirement Security, a Washington, D.C., based nonprofit, nonpartisan organization. A 19% benefit cut could reduce gross domestic product by hundreds of billions of dollars, according to the NIRS research . Moreover, failing to muster Social Security reform would prompt bond market strain, according to research published in June by George Mason University's Mercatus Center. Social Security is tied to the bond market because its trust funds are invested in special issue U.S. Treasury bonds. If Social Security reform is delayed, that may put upward pressure on Treasury yields, with investors wanting higher returns for long-term bonds. Delayed reform may either prompt higher interest rates and borrowing costs or inflationary adjustments that hurt the value of government liabilities, according to the Mercatus Center research. Those changes may affect household budgets through higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans and other types of consumer credit as well as student loans, according to the research. If interest rates and prices rise, that will interfere with economic growth, Akabas said. "Those effects are also ones that the American people feel, in addition to adjustments to their benefits," Akabas said. Heading to the midterms, some Democratic congressional candidates have said they would raise or eliminate the Social Security payroll tax cap so high earners pay more into the program. In 2026, the 6.2% tax paid by both workers and their employers applies to earnings up to $184,500. Yet it remains to be seen whether Washington leaders will have the political will to address the problem soon. Tax increases, in particular, may not be viewed as politically popular heading into the 2028 presidential election.

events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections Diesel prices ease to $6.29 per gallon, offering slight relief amid a global fuel demand squeeze. Petrol prices have dipped amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran, but remain high ahead of the United States midterm elections , as the cost of living remains a central issue for voters. On Monday, the average price for a gallon (3.78 litres) of regular petrol was $4.17, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices. That is down 12 cents from this time last week and 23 cents from a month ago. list 1 of 3 ‘Foreign policy is the economy’: How Iran war is shaping US midterm vote list 2 of 3 What to know about California’s midterm elections list 3 of 3 How US oil firms profit $130bn from Iran war as household bills surge By comparison, prices were $3.04 this time a year ago and $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran. Diesel fuel prices remain high at $6.29 per gallon, but that is down 6 cents from this time last week. Diesel prices climbed above $6 a gallon for the first time in September before topping out at $6.53. The average petrol price of President Donald Trump’s second term to date was set to exceed $3.46 a gallon on Monday, surpassing the previous record for a presidential administration set under former President Joe Biden, according to a Financial Times analysis of federal data. Oil prices are continuing to fall, down 6 percent on Monday as diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war on Iran continued following in-person talks in Qatar over the weekend. “Oil markets down significantly this morning after Trump signalled he favoured negotiations and not new attacks on Iran,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X. “Oil down [approximately] 5%, wholesale gasoline and diesel pointing to roughly 16 [cents per gallon] decline. ConocoPhillips was down 3.7 percent, Chevron 2.3 percent and ExxonMobil 3.3 percent. The major US indices more broadly were in positive territory. events.title: John Deere built an AI assistant to stop farmers from drowning in decades of field data
events.summary: John Deere announced its new AI assistant at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. Marcin Golba/NurPhoto via Getty Images John Deere's AI assistant, unveiled in September, helps farmers analyze data quickly. JD is embedded in John Deere's Operations Center, a digital farm management system. Farmers are warming to AI, but accuracy and data privacy remain concerns. Farmers have more data than ever about their fields, equipment, and crops. But turning it into a decision could take weeks. John Deere says its new AI assistant, JD, can do it in minutes. The agricultural manufacturing company announced the tool in September at the Farm Progress Show in Iowa. JD is integrated within John Deere's Operations Center, which is a digital farm management system that connects farmers' field and machine data into one platform. Farmers can ask JD questions on their mobile devices, such as the best time to harvest based on past trends, or which sprayer covers the most acres per hour. Melissa Neuendorf, the principal product manager for customer AI solutions at John Deere, told Business Insider that JD came about because farmers consistently said they were struggling to manage their abundant data. "We're now at a point where farmers have so much data that they have a difficult time finding the insights manually themselves," Neuendorf said. While smaller agricultural tech companies such as OneSoil, VisorPro, Arable, and AgZen are developing generative AI tools to give insights on specific equipment or crop metrics, Deere is among the first major agricultural-equipment makers to put a large language model AI assistant directly inside a platform that combines farmers' field, machine, and operational data. JD's launch shows how generative AI is becoming a central part of crop management. "Prior to John Deere's announcement, this didn't exist in the industry," said Matt Darr, a professor in the agricultural and biosystems engineering department at Iowa State University, who was in the room when Deere announced JD. Why farmers are considering AI tools more than ever Farmers have been collecting data for decades. But now, modern farm equipment is outfitted with additional technology and sensors, creating large volumes of data that are difficult to keep up with. It can be stressful for farmers who must also navigate tight margins, unpredictable weather , and limited planting windows. Plus, "most farmers aren't data scientists on the side," Darr said. Neuendorf said dissecting vast datasets is complex and time-consuming, sometimes requiring weeks. That's where AI can help farmers: "AI provides them the capability to do a lot of that analysis in minutes," she said. Before coming up with JD, Deere launched an AI tool last August that allowed farmers to ask questions in natural language about Deere's help documentation and operator manuals. This replaced the manual task of farmers flipping through pages of operator manuals. The tool received positive feedback, prompting Deere to broaden its application and launch JD to answer specific questions on the spot. Farmers can input data into the Operations Center from non-John Deere equipment if they use machinery from other manufacturers. Then, if they query JD, it can analyze all of that data to deliver answers. The Operations Center and JD are free to use, Neuendorf said. The AI assistant is available through an early access program, in which interested customers sign up for a waitlist and are considered for participation. John Deere will make JD broadly available in mid-November Neuendorf told Business Insider that the feedback from farmers so far has been positive. Neuendorf said she recently spoke to a farmer who was driving past a field and noticed it had lower weed pressure, or fewer weeds present, than other fields. Through JD, the farmer was able to open John Deere's mobile app right away, ask the assistant about previous years, and understand how he managed the field differently. Winning farmer trust in AI technology A McKinsey global survey of 5,500 farmers, published in September, found that 72% expect generative AI to impact operations within five years, but only 17% use the tech right now. One reason only a minority of farmers use AI is because they're worried about data privacy and how their information could impact commodity prices, Darr said. "These are competitive businesses," Darr added. "How information is used can influence global markets and what happens to global commodity pricing." John Deere said in its release announcing JD that it doesn't sell farm data or use it for agriculture commodity trading or speculation. Katya Kheistver, the chief product and operating officer of OneSoil, an agricultural technology company, said farmers won't trust AI if it delivers generic advice rather than insights tied to specific, real field data. Farmers often start their use of AI by checking the tech's outputs against what they already know. The farmer "watches whether the answer lines up with reality," and if it does so consistently, trust grows, Kheistver said. The stakes are high if farmers make decisions based on AI-generated answers because they have "one chance a year to grow a crop," Darr said. They need to be able to trust that an AI tool is accurate. JD meshes high-quality datasets with advanced LLMs, Darr added, which sets the AI tool apart and promises a high degree of accuracy. Neuendorf said JD is configured to notify farmers when field data is missing, rather than making inaccurate assumptions or generating false advice. This configuration also encourages farmers to input additional data, so JD can derive more insights and help farmers "make better decisions for the next season," Neuendorf said. events.title: The internet's latest obsession: The end of the world
events.summary: The world seems convinced the end is near — and social media is amplifying that belief, convincing people to stock up on food, water, generators and other items. Why it matters: Online chatter is fueling viral predictions of societal collapse amid growing unease about the future. But you're probably not going to die tomorrow. What they're saying: Michael Mills, a researcher at the University of Kent who has studied doomsday prepping for more than a decade, told Axios that modern doomsday fears aren't necessarily about a specific apocalyptic scenario. "It's an overall reaction to uncertainty in most cases," Mills said. He noted that whereas Cold War-era survivalists were often focused on nuclear conflict, modern preppers worry about terrorism, climate disasters, geopolitical threats and emerging technologies. He described the modern mindset as a "multifaceted concern with uncertainty." State of play: Viral posts have repeatedly urged people around the world to stock up on food and water, following similar recommendations from various governments and warnings from former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino. The situation has gotten so buzzy that President Trump was asked about it in an interview Monday. He said Americans don't need to stock up because the U.S. is "in good shape. We're strong. We have a great military and we will not have those kind of problems." Separately, conservative commentator Tucker Carlson — a man with 17.9 million followers on X alone — published a lengthy post Sunday evening alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring Trump to launch renewed attacks on Iran after the midterms, potentially with a nuclear weapon. For what it's worth, Carlson has been predicting similar doomsday scenarios for a while, and he's been wrong before. And the Pentagon's newly reported plan calls for U.S. military bases to prepare to operate without outside support for at least 90 days, terrifying some people into asking , "What's the government know that they're not telling us?" The big picture: Worries about financial insecurity , skyrocketing health care costs , a lack of rainy-day savings and younger generations' perceived inability to buy a house all contribute to the feeling that life is not okay. Then you've got AI , which could cut thousands of jobs, enable a cyberattack or help engineer a dangerous, and potentially deadly, biological disease. And then there's the geopolitical situation: wars, genocide and the possibility of global warfare as China continues to threaten Taiwan and rumors abound that the U.S. and Israel will reignite the Iran war with a fresh round of attacks. Zoom in: Political uncertainty can also fuel doomsday prediction culture, particularly around major elections . Mills described the prepper movement as historically right-leaning, with fears increasing during the Obama and Biden administrations and subsiding among some preppers after Trump's 2016 victory. During elections, "where it can often seem that everything is at stake... we don't know which way those contests are going to go and so naturally that uncertainty kind of flares up," Mills said. Reality check: Preparing for a catastrophe doesn't make you a conspiracy theorist. Governments commonly warn people about potential disasters, like advising them to evacuate before a hurricane. Mills distinguishes ordinary emergency readiness from prepping, which typically involves preparing for disasters lasting weeks or months, sometimes longer. The bottom line: Nobody knows what catastrophe, if any, might come next. But feeling prepared and stocking up for a couple of days without power can make sitting in the dark a little less scary. events.title: Owner of private Serbian bank detained and accused of siphoning money
events.summary: Serbian authorities have detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender BELGRADE, Serbia -- BELGRADE, Serbia (AP) — Serbian authorities Monday detained the owner of a private bank on suspicion he was siphoning money from the lender that was used for some public utility payments during the previous government of former President Aleksandar Vucic. Alta Bank rose to prominence under the rule of Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party that was ousted from power in a parliamentary election last week. The bank has handled all electricity payments by millions of users in the capital Belgrade, as well as public parking accounts. On Saturday, Serbia’s Central Bank revoked Alta Bank’s operating license and launched bankruptcy proceedings to protect the bank’s depositors, saying that its liquidity “has deteriorated significantly” and “could worsen further." Serbia’s Deposit Insurance Agency, which guarantees deposits of up to 50,000 euros ($56,000), will act as Alta Bank's bankruptcy administrator, the central bank said. Davor Macura, the bank owner who initially owned an exchange office before becoming a prominent banker, was given a 48-hour detention on Monday, prosecutors said. Macura’s lawyers told local media he was present at the bank headquarters in Belgrade and fully cooperated during an hourslong police search over the weekend. Lawyers added that Macura will be questioned by the public prosecutor on Tuesday. Macura, whose businesses also span retail and construction, is suspected of illegally moving 45 billion dinars ($428 million) out of Alta Bank’s vault. Two other persons were also held for aiding and abetting the crime. The moves against Alta Bank and its owner came as part of a wave of changes triggered by Vucic’s defeat in the Oct. 25 election that also included resignations in the state-run media, arrests of several officials and an announced review of long-standing corruption cases. Former central bank governor Kori Udovicki on Sunday criticized the Serbian Central Bank moves as too slow. She said on RTS television that the central bank “lost a week in which it could have limited the bank’s ability to transfer the money abroad or to the connected individuals.” Alta Bank is a rare Serbian lender that allowed tens of thousands of Russian émigrés to open personal and business accounts. Scores of Russians have moved to Russia-friendly Serbia since the start of the invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Alta Bank's troubles resonated outside Serbia. The Central Bank of North Macedonia put Alta Bank’s subsidiary into temporary administration and limited cash withdrawals to 160 euros ($179) per week, while Montenegro's banking regulator shut down payment processing company Alta Pay. Serbian investigative outlets in the past have described Macura as a tycoon whose political connections to Vucic and his SNS helped him win lucrative contracts with state agencies and public enterprises. In 2024, Macura’s Alta Group came under scrutiny by the European Central Bank, or ECB, when it attempted to acquire a 20% stake in Austria’s Addiko Group through two connected firms to avoid triggering the ECB’s approval requirement. The ECB spotted this and stopped the deal. It also questioned the anti-money laundering controls and the source of funds in Macura's network. The Association of Serbian Banks called Alta Bank's collapse “an individual issue” and said it would not affect other banks. The SNS, which has governed Serbia since 2012, lost the parliamentary election to the student-led Student List movement. The outgoing authorities remain in control until a formal transition of power, expected to take several weeks. Critics say the SNS has steadily taken control of state institutions since it came to power. It has been accused of corruption, cronyism, links to organized crime and pressure on the judiciary, police and media. events.title: Apple reports after the bell. Options traders expect a big move
events.summary: There are stocks. There are bonds. And then there is Apple . The tech behemoth is an asset class. The iPhone maker has a fortress balance sheet, a vice-like grip on its markets, and 20 years after the first iPhone release, still remains cool. But that doesn't mean the stock can get pushed around on earnings. Make no mistake, Apple remains a structural outlier in big tech, particularly regarding capital expenditures. While its megacap rivals are currently engaged in a relentless, capital-intensive arms race to outspend one another on infrastructure, Apple's relatively low capex stands out as a testament to its disciplined capital allocation. Yet, as we approach Monday's earnings, formidable fundamental hurdles remain. While iPhone average selling prices (ASPs) will likely rise, unit shipments are expected to fall under the weight of tougher year-over-year comparisons and recent price hikes. Furthermore, troubling reports are circulating regarding "issues" with Apple's highly anticipated foldable screens. For a device carrying an eye-watering ultra-premium price tag, design or durability problems are unacceptable. It is hard to imagine these manufacturing whispers won't be addressed on the earnings call. Adding to the top-line friction are potential foreign exchange headwinds, which threaten to eat into international sales growth. Combine these operational risks with Apple's current valuation, and the picture becomes precarious. AAPL now trades at a more than 40% premium to Amazon (AMZN) on a forward P/E basis, and a staggering 60% premium to Alphabet (GOOGL). That kind of multiple demands absolute perfection, and recent weeks have shown exactly what happens to heavily weighted tech names that fail to deliver a flawless quarter, Alphabet and Amazon among them. This brings us to the options market. Right now, the implied move for Apple by the end of the week is less than $16.50, or under 4.8% of the current stock price, considerably higher than the 3.25% median move over the last four quarters. In a season where earnings reports have punished some of the biggest names in the market, this relatively low options pricing suggests a long premium trade into the print is the most prudent play. Whether you are looking to hedge a long underlying equity position or simply want to speculate that Apple could become the latest casualty of a demanding earnings season, defining your risk is paramount. The Trade: Buy the November 6th expiration 345/325 put spread for $5.95. Important Housekeeping Note: Just two weeks ago , I outlined a moderately bullish setup for Apple using a diagonal call spread risk reversal—specifically, buying the February 360 calls while selling the December 310/375 strangle. The strategy was designed to capture positive carry while maintaining upside exposure. That position is cautiously optimistic, but after observing last week's earnings-related moves and options prices for AAPL expiring at the end of this week, if you didn't take that trade, the landscape heading into this week's quarterly earnings report may require a fresh look with a decidedly more defensive posture. events.title: Options traders are getting anxious on Palantir and Apple ahead of earnings
events.summary: It's not just the neoclouds and hyperscalers that investors are anxious about. Options data show a surge in bearish trading in anticipation of both Palantir and Apple earnings Monday afternoon. The two stocks have been on trajectories that are distinct from the broader AI trade – with Apple, in particular, trading almost inversely to the Nasdaq 100 Index – but that's not stopping speculators from betting on a reversal in their shares after earnings. Of the 620,000 options traded on Apple by midday, 385,000 were puts, with at least 113,000 puts likely initiated by buyers, compared to just 64,000 calls bought, Cboe LiveVol data show. At the same time, the price of puts reached the 86th percentile of the past year, compared to the 51st percentile for calls, according to data from Nations Indexes. Apple stock is up 25% this year and currently trading with a negative 0.65 correlation with the Nasdaq 100, ThinkOrSwim data show. Options are implying just under a 4% move for the stock, compared to the average 2.5% swing after earnings the past two years, according to LiveVol. Palantir options flows are also leaning bearish, with more puts trading than calls by volume and the price of puts at the 97th percentile of the past year, according to Nations Indexes. Calls are pricey, too, but not as much – they're in the 76th percentile. Traders should be ready for a big move in Palantir: market-makers are pricing an 11.5% implied move, compared to the 10% average the past two years. The stock rallied almost 30% after its last report, but sold off after earnings in May. The biggest trade in Palantir Monday was someone opening a new position buying about 750 in-the-money 250-strike puts expiring mid-February for a total $5.1 million.

events.title: Control of Britain’s 39m smart meters passes to non-profit startup
events.summary: The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence for Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, after years of spiralling costs and delays Control over Great Britain’s 39m smart meters has passed to a non-profit startup after its former owner presided over more than a decade of spiralling costs and delays in the troubled network. The company owned by crisis-hit outsourcing firm Capita has promised a “seamless transition” to its not-for-profit successor, which will take over running the data network connecting the smart meters from this week. The handover marks the end of a 13-year licence granted to Smart DCC, a subsidiary of Capita, to set up the country’s first smart meter data network, a process that has been dogged by costly delays while millions of households faced billing issues . Industry sources said Capita’s subsidiary was effectively blocked from tendering for a new licence to manage the smart meter network after Whitehall officials decided to replace the commercial framework established in 2013 with a not-for-profit public-interest model governed by an independent board. Instead, the network underpinning Britain’s smart meters will become a wholly owned subsidiary of the Smart Energy Code Company (SECCo) with “a greater focus on cost, transparency and customer and consumer needs”, the new operator said. Its board will include veteran energy and telecoms industry executives as well as Dame Gillian Guy, the former chief executive of Citizens Advice, which claimed in 2024 that households had been “let down” by the rollout because almost a third of smart meters weren’t working properly. Ministers had initially hoped that all households would have a smart meter before 2020 to help modernise Britain’s outdated energy system and make better use of renewable energy and innovative data-led energy tariffs . But the rollout has faced “serious reputational obstacles” , according to the government’s spending watchdog, which meant that three in 10 households still do not have a meter and another £1.7bn may be required to complete the rollout. The tender process for a new smart network operator ran last summer, at around the same time that the industry regulator opened an investigation into Smart DCC’s procurement contracts, which included deals that were awarded without a competitive process and one which was granted to its parent company, Capita. Smart DCC agreed in July to pay £200,000 into a consumer redress fund, in the same week that its parent company was forced to apologise for its role in administering the crisis-hit Civil Service Pension Scheme, which kept thousands of retired civil servants waiting for payments. Capita’s market value has plunged by 97% in the last decade after the outsourcing company once in charge of administering a string of government schemes revealed severely strained finances and mounting debts before undertaking an emergency restructuring of the business. A Capita spokesperson said: “Capita is proud of its 13-year stewardship of DCC. What began as an ambitious programme is now critical national infrastructure, connecting more than 39.2m smart meters across 23m homes and small businesses, with network availability of 99.6%. “We hand over a secure and resilient network that millions of consumers rely on every day and have been working with stakeholders to ensure an orderly transition to DCC’s next chapter.” A spokesperson for Ofgem said Smart DCC had “played a critical role” in delivering “an efficient and secure digital communication structure”, and that the new licence holder would be expected to “build on that solid foundation”.

events.title: The AI boom is facing another supply crunch. This time it’s the amount of capital available to feed Silicon Valley’s endless need for cash
events.summary: A new supply crunch is closing in on the AI boom as Wall Street starts to reach the limits of how much capital it’s willing to hand over to Silicon Valley. Hyperscalers have already been grappling with shortages of chips, materials and other physical inputs needed for AI infrastructure. They are also running out of political capital as voters push back on the aggressive data center build-out. Now the spigot of money is starting to dry up . OpenAI slashed the target on its latest funding round to $20 billion from $30 billion, sources told the Financial Times . That’s after securing about $11 billion in commitments, less than half of its original goal, according to the Wall Street Journal . A top credit rating agency also dented Silicon Valley’s appeal to debt markets. S&P Global cut its credit outlook on Meta to “negative” from “stable” late Friday, citing negative cash flow and uncertainty around capital expenditure ​plans. Meanwhile, the head of technology, media and telecom lending at a large European bank told Bloomberg last week that the bank is approaching the limit of what it can lend to the sector given its sizable exposure. But the latest earnings reports indicate the sector still plans to spend heavily, sending their stocks tumbling. A handful of hyperscalers are expected to invest $800 billion this year and more than $1 trillion next year. “Now, another concern is moving to the forefront: Does enough capital even exist to finance everyone’s ambitious AI spending plans?” Wall Street veteran Ed Yardeni asked last week. In a note last week, he pointed to a series of red flags: Broadcom CEO Hock Tan warned capital could become the biggest constraint on AI; BlackRock CEO Larry Fink said that competition for capital was the fiercest he had witnessed in his career; and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang observed that neocloud demand is “off the charts” but capital is scarce. Trillions more in financing will be in demand as AI businesses fall short on self-sufficiency. Market research firm Gartner estimated data center owners need $8.5 trillion in cumulative revenue by the end of the decade to justify their investments. But the data centers are expected to generate no more than $3.6 trillion of enterprise and consumer AI revenue by then. As a result, tech companies keep going to the well. On Monday, Oracle said it plans to raise $20 billion by issuing stocks and bonds. That’s after Elon Musk said SpaceX closed $40 billion in debt financing, Meta announced plans to raise $95 billion in equity, and Microsoft raised $25 billion in debt. For its part, the sector recognizes that the availability of money is tighter. Meta nodded to the “increasingly challenging environment for raising capital” in a recent filing and suggested it may have to speed up fundraising instead of slowing it down. “The Special Committee considered that, while the Company presently has sufficient capital resources for its current needs, in order to finance its funding needs going forward it would be prudent for the Company to do so before even more companies have absorbed available capital in the market,” it said. To be sure, Wall Street may also turn more selective about which AI companies to fund, allowing well qualified borrowers to obtain financing while shutting out shakier ones. Analysts at Bank of America said last week capital remains ample for investment grade firms and projects backstopped by suppliers, though such “circular” deals have also drawn more scrutiny. Still, BofA sees positive leading indicators for AI chipmakers into next year. But tech companies aren’t the only ones tapping Wall Street for cash. The federal government ran a deficit of nearly $2 trillion last fiscal year with no end in sight to its profligacy, putting more pressure on the bond market. “All those things combined basically means that at the moment we have a shortage of capital, and we have an abundance of good ideas that we need to invest in,” Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok told CNBC last month. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump administration turns to SCOTUS in California ballot case
events.summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to mandate that California separate ballots of more than 20,000 voters the government suspects are "likely" non-citizens. The big picture: A federal appeals court rejected the administration's bid to set aside mail ballots last week, erecting another roadblock in the DOJ's pre-election quest to demand the state root out claims of voter fraud in the final days of the midterm elections. Driving the news: "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the DOJ wrote in an application filed to the high court. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now," the application, signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, continued. The DOJ's initial lawsuit came after the administration threatened California officials with emergency court action unless it probed potential ineligible voters over 48 hours and set aside ballots. Catch up quick: A federal appeals court and a federal judge stymied the administration's bid. U.S. District Judge David Carter cast doubt on the government's voter lists in a late October order denying the administration's request for a temporary restraining order, citing the "vagueness" of the government's "descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states." And in last week's 2–1 ruling, a federal appeals court found that granting the request "would provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of the election." What they're saying: "We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement shared to X. The California Secretary of State's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

events.title: Judge dismisses charges against FBI agents involved in Hunter Biden case
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms The former FBI officials’ lawyers press for a dismissal of charges after a hurried and inaccurate case. A federal judge has dismissed a criminal case against two former senior FBI officials accused of lying to Congress about former President Joe Biden’s son, Hunter. On Monday, US Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui ruled that prosecutors, under the direction of the Department of Justice, lacked sufficient evidence to move the case forward and expressed concern that the investigation was rushed, overtly political and dogged by “critical mistakes”. list 1 of 3 Texas Republican group seeks to block certification of state’s election list 2 of 3 Trump slams ex-lawyer’s $50m deal with pardoned banker’s family list 3 of 3 US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks He said it “cannot be described as anything other than weaponization”. “I will not bury my head in the sand and pretend I cannot read a calendar,” Faruqui said in court, referring to its proximity to the midterms. “I will not lobotomize myself that way.” The case suggested that Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides misled Congress in 2023 by lying about their knowledge of and involvement in an investigation into a laptop the Justice Department said was dropped off at a Delaware tech shop in 2019 by Hunter Biden. An FBI agent who worked on the case testified that the investigation into Floris and Benavides began last July under the direction of FBI Director Kash Patel. The Associated Press news agency reported that the case echoed complaints by President Donald Trump and his allies that potentially damaging information about the Biden family was suppressed during the 2020 election, which Trump lost. The Justice Department may still have the chance to pursue a grand jury indictment of the former FBI officials. Nonetheless, Faruqui’s early ruling and concerns about the case hamper the Justice Department’s case. In a preliminary hearing last week, the judge pointed out that the Justice Department was not acting in accordance with legal procedure when it filed an amended complaint with an additional charge without first clearing the charge with the court — something he said he had never seen before.

events.title: Oracle files to sell $20 billion in new stock, bonds to finance AI buildout
events.summary: Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue $10 billion in stock and $10 billion in bonds, it said in a filing. The plans were outlined last week at its investor day. Oracle filed plans on Monday to issue new stock and more debt to finance its artificial intelligence buildout. The hyperscaler will sell $10 billion in common stock and $10 billion in senior notes, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. While the fundraising was already outlined at an investor day last week , shares tumbled more than 6% Monday. "This seems to be exactly what they previewed," said Rob Oliver, senior research analyst at Baird. "So I'm not sure why the market is freaking about it." Oracle said it plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes, which may include capital expenditures, repayments of debt and future investments. The hyperscaler's stock initially bounced after last Wednesday's investor day, when Oracle also issued a revenue forecast of at least $225 billion for fiscal 2030. At the time Oracle also said it was limiting its additional capital market funding for the fiscal 2027 to 2030 investment cycle to that $20 billion. "This is a major relief given concerns about the state of debt markets and the cost of capital (although UBS has argued that these debt market concerns have been over-stated)," UBS analyst Karl Keirstead said in a note on Thursday. Oracle plans to turn to vendor financing, customer-provided hardware and customer prepayments to help it transition to positive free cash flow, which it expects to reach in the second half of 2028. Stock and bonds in Oracle, co-founded by former CEO Larry Ellison, have been under pressure amid growing investor concerns about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure. Oracle shares are down 33% in 2026 and 50% over the past 12 months. The yield on its investment-grade 4.95% bond due in 2031 is currently 7.267%. The sentiment shift is also seen in Oracle's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default. The spread sits at 296, up 270% in one year. That's more in line with a high-end junk bond rating, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence's Gavan Nolan. While still an investment-grade credit, Oracle was downgraded by S&P to a BBB- in July, one rating level above high yield. It has $125.34 billion in debt, as of Aug. 31, with the bulk in senior notes. What ultimately matters for Oracle is execution, Pat Nerney, head of investment solutions at Dynasty Financial Partners, said in an email to CNBC Monday. "Can they do what they say they are going to do? We view this as the narrative across the AI space," he said. "If this gets executed according to plans laid out, they will be rewarded. If they have to come back to market in the back half of '27 after telling everyone this was the last of the capital needed ... look out." — CNBC's Seema Mody and Ari Levy contributed reporting.

events.title: Virgin Australia apologises after breaking young girl's $33,000 wheelchair
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Adelaide Tuimalealiifano relies on her specialised wheelchair for mobility. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) A six-year-old could not use her wheelchair after it was damaged on a flight she was taking for medical treatment. The incident is the latest in a number involving wheelchairs on Virgin Australia flights. Advocates want mandatory reporting for airlines on incidents involving damaged or missing mobility equipment. A girl with a rare bone disease was left without the use of her specialist wheelchair after it was damaged by an airline while she travelled to medical appointments. Adelaide Tuimalealiifano is one of about 60 people in the world diagnosed with multicentric carpotarsal osteolysis syndrome (MCTO), a genetic disorder that leads to the loss of the wrist and ankle bones. She can walk short distances but largely relies on her wheelchair which is worth $33,000. The damage to the wheelchair meant it couldn't be used. ( Supplied: Amanda Tuimalealiifano ) But during a flight from Townsville to Brisbane earlier this week, the wheelchair was broken when a bracket was twisted. "It actually took quite a significant force for that bracket to twist," Adelaide's mother Amanda said. The family discovered the damage when they arrived at Brisbane Airport. Without a working wheelchair, Adelaide's father Jaster carried his six-year-old daughter through the Queensland Children's Hospital. He later fixed the chair after buying some hardware tools, but Ms Tuimalealiifano said not everyone was so fortunate. Jaster Tuimalealiifano pushing his daughter in her wheelchair. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) "If our daughter was an adult and she was travelling solo and she couldn't walk any more … she wouldn't be able to leave the airport and she would be stranded. "It can be absolutely detrimental for people with disabilities." Ms Tuimalealiifano posted about the ordeal in a social media video that has been watched almost 100,000 times. She received many comments from people sharing similar experiences. The Tuimalealiifano family have shared their story of learning to live with disability on social media. ( Supplied: KZ Photography ) "Some people with disabilities completely refuse to travel on public transportation like airlines because their chairs are so complex … and they are so reliant on it that they can't even chance it getting damaged," Ms Tuimalealiifano said. "It is a systemic issue in the airline industry." The family received multiple apologies from Virgin Australia. In a statement, a Virgin Australia spokesperson said the airline extended immediate support and assistance to the family. "Virgin Australia is committed to improving our processes to provide an accessible and inclusive travel experience for all our guests," the spokesperson said. Ms Tuimalealiifano hopes the incident is a catalyst and "stepping stone" for conversations and meaningful change in the travel industry. The incident is the latest in a number involving wheelchairs on Virgin Australia flights, including in 2017 , two in 2023 , including when a former Queensland Australian of the Year was tipped out of a wheelchair , and another two in 2024 . In August this year, Shane Hryhorec was removed from a Virgin Australia flight in the Whitsundays because of issues with storing his portable wheelchair motor. Megan Spindler-Smith says incidents with personal mobility devices are far too common. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) People With Disability Australia (PWDA) chief executive Megan Spindler-Smith said damage to personal mobility equipment such as wheelchairs was a "long-standing issue". "It's so common that I'm not sure how it can continue to happen," they said. "How are airlines not sorting this out? "When equipment is actually damaged, passengers need more than just a 'sorry, we'll try and do this better'." Former Queensland Australian of the Year tipped out of wheelchair Dr Dinesh Palipana says a ground crew member at Brisbane Airport ignored his carers and manoeuvred his wheelchair sharply, tipping him onto the ground. They want mandatory reporting for airlines on incidents involving damaged or missing personal mobility equipment to better understand the scale of the problem and common causes. PDWA has been working with the federal government on proposed aviation disability standards. Public consultation closed on the draft standards earlier this month. Spindler-Smith wants the standards to become "practical, enforceable requirements" that change procedures at airports. "What really needs to change is the prevention of it happening," they said.

events.title: Stock market after midterm elections: What S&P 500 history shows
events.summary: The S&P 500 averaged a 13.7% one-year gain after 11 midterm elections since 1980. After divided-government outcomes, the index averaged a 15% one-year gain, compared to 11.5% under single-party control. Fed policy, earnings and the AI trade may matter more than the election result. Markets are sweating it out ahead of the midterm elections, but the event historically heralds strong performance for stocks — regardless of whether it's a red or blue wave, split decision, or status quo in Washington. The S&P 500 tends to perform well after both midterm and presidential elections. According to a CNBC analysis of S&P 500 returns after elections from 1980 through 2024, the index rose an average of 0.2% after one day and one week, and 1.1% after one month across both presidential and midterm elections. A year later, the index gained an average of 13.7% after midterms and 13.8% after presidential elections. Returns were positive in 91% of cases. And the S&P 500 was up after all 11 midterms from 1982 through 2022. Short-term returns were less reliable, particularly after presidential contests, which produced slightly negative average returns after one day and one week. "There's some anxiousness before these elections," Ryan Detrick, CNBC contributor and chief market strategist at Carson Group, told CNBC. "Once you are through it, it's a big relief and markets tend to do pretty well." Still, the market usually prefers divided government: one party in charge of the White House and the other holding at least one house of Congress. Across 10 midterm and five presidential elections that left no single party in charge, the S&P 500 rose an average 15% after one year. One-year returns were positive in 14 out of 15 cases. By comparison, the index gained an average of 11.5% over the year after elections that resulted in single-party control. "If you have a huge red wave or a big blue wave, markets actually kind of don't like that as much because you have too much spending one way and too much power," Detrick said. Leaving Democrats in control of Congress with a Republican in the White House — a scenario that may emerge from the elections on Tuesday — was also positive. A CNBC analysis found that after the three midterms (1986, 1990 and 2006) when Democrats controlled both houses and a Republican held the presidency, the S&P 500 averaged a 0.5% decline on the reaction day but was up 3.4% a month later and 10.9% after a year. Granted, elections may be coincident events to factors that matter far more for market performance. The S&P 500 plunged 22.1% in the year after the 2000 elections due to the dotcom bust, marking the worst post-election performance since 1980. Conversely, the S&P 500's best post-election year was a 38.3% gain after the 2020 elections, when markets mounted a massive comeback from the COVID-induced selloff. Investors should bear in mind that Federal Reserve policy and the corporate earnings cycle ultimately matter more than elections, according to Société Générale. Stocks declined in the aftermath of the 2018 midterms, for instance, when Democrats wrested control of the House during President Donald Trump's first term. More importantly, the Fed tightened monetary policy that year, raising interest rates four times, and the S&P 500 ended the year down 6.2%, though the market was up 11.7% a year after the election. The big swing factor now is AI and whether declines in tech will continue. As long as the AI wave is still moving and the economy keeps growing, "this bull market is probably still alive and well," Detrick says. But a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate would almost certainly pressure the AI infrastructure buildout and could lead to more retrenchment. The bond market is also skittish with yields rising globally and a mini debt crisis in France. And the war with Iran could get worse post-election if President Trump follows through on threats of more strikes or Iran escalates. "Seasonality isn't destiny, and worries around Iran, AI and France won't mysteriously vanish," said Jim Reid, Deutsche Bank's global head of macro and thematic research, in a note. If history is any guide, we could see a Santa rally and S&P 500 gains after the midterms. But this is still an AI-driven market, with geopolitics, the Fed, and bond market very much in charge. — CNBC's Chris Hayes contributed reporting.
