events.title: Anthropic reports $17 billion in Q3 revenue, purchase commitments of $895.4 billion in revised S-1
events.summary: Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, but the initial filing only included the company's financials through the first half of the year. Anthropic reported updated financials as part of an amended Form S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, giving investors a more comprehensive look into the state of its business. The artificial intelligence company said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic had a loss of $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025. Anthropic unveiled its highly anticipated prospectus last week, bringing the company one step closer to a potentially historic initial public offering . The initial filing only included the Claude maker's financials through the first half of the year. During its third quarter, Anthropic generated roughly $17 billion in revenue, up about 1,127% from the same period last year. Revenue growth slowed on a quarter-to-quarter basis, however. Third-quarter revenue increased around 47%, a steep drop from 144% growth in Q2 and 132% in Q1. The company reported a net loss of $23.29 billion during its third quarter. Anthropic's path to the Nasdaq just got a lot bumpier Chart: Anthropic’s cash pile towers over nearly every U.S. company Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei charts a new direction for tech philanthropy As the 5-year-old company prepares to kick off its roadshow, it will have to reckon with growing market jitters around the AI buildout. Wall Street has been worried that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds , and quarterly reports from Microsoft , Alphabet and Amazon last week added fuel to those concerns. The hyperscalers' aggressive AI spending is eating into their cash flows , causing some investors to worry that computing capacity may not come online quickly enough to meet Anthropic's demands. Anthropic gets much of its capacity from Amazon, Google and SpaceX , but it also relies on neoclouds for some compute as it races to expand as quickly as possible. In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure." Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year. "As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing. The company's CEO, Dario Amodei, co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. OpenAI confidentially filed its prospectus with the SEC in June, but its executives have signaled that it's aiming for a 2027 debut . Anthropic has worked to position itself as more safety-conscious than its competitors, and its S-1 includes more than 90 pages of risk factors . The company highlights risks, including potential political headwinds, its complex infrastructure needs as well as the difficulties that can come from balancing safety and commercial objectives. "We consider it our personal responsibility to help the world understand these risks, to prevent or mitigate them when they arise from our AI models, and to work with governments and the rest of the industry to address them at a societal level," Anthropic's co-founders said in the filing. events.title: Ruby on Rails creator has a warning for 'cantankerous' coders: Learn some people skills
events.summary: David Heinemeier Hansson said engineers will need to "learn some basic people skills" in the age of AI. LAT Images/Getty Images David Heinemeier Hansson said that AI agents will bring hard times for "cantankerous" engineers. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. Engineers on X chimed in to wave goodbye to engineers with bad attitudes. Don't be cantankerous. David Heinemeier Hansson has some advice for engineers as they adjust to AI. Often referred to as DHH, Hansson created the webapp framework Ruby on Rails and has fashioned himself into a software sage. On Monday, Hansson shared his prediction on X: "The age of agents is going to be amazing for most programmers, but it'll be hard times for the cantankerous ones." Hansson wrote that special abilities won't save those who are difficult to work with. That would be a dramatic shift in software engineering, where some so-called "cracked" coders can get away with large egos or social awkwardness. "Best learn some basic people skills," Hansson wrote. The prediction sparked a conversation among engineers about their social habits and professionalism. One pointed out the irony: agents "don't care how cantankerous you are," but your human coworkers do. One user wrote a eulogy to the "guy whose whole job security was 'only I know how this works.'" Dart cofounder Zack Swafford wrote that teams only tolerated bad attitudes because the staffers had "arcane tribal knowledge." Others questioned how new the change was. People skills have long been valuable, from networking your way into a job to landing that big promotion. "Been true in every company forever," one X user commented. "Skills get you hired, being easy to work with keeps you around. Agents just make it obvious faster." Hansson is committed to the future of AI coding. In September, he declared " pencils down " on handwritten code. Hansson explained that writing code was an "exceptional state," performed only when something went wrong with the AI-generated code. For some engineers, Hansson's post was a vocabulary lesson. "I had to search the definition of 'cantankerous,'" one engineer commented. "First time reading that word." For the record: cantankerous means bad-tempered and uncooperative. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: A National Geographic photographer taught me one easy tip for taking better nature photos with my phone
events.summary: Business Insider's reporter has been practicing photography for more than a decade, and now she wants to learn to shoot with her phone. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I used to focus on the background when taking photos of natural landscapes on my phone. A National Geographic photographer taught me to look closer. What's in front of a landscape matters as much as what's behind it, he said. Nowadays, people are "drowning in photographs," National Geographic photographer Kiliii Yüyan told me. But there are ways to make yours stand out — even if you're just shooting on your phone. Yüyan tells visual stories about how different cultures relate to the environment, from the Amazon to the Arctic seas. He gave me four useful tips for taking pictures with my phone , and one of them made me think about photographing nature in a whole new way. Put something between your camera and the scenery The author photographs a shoreline in Belfast, Maine. Joey Hadden/Business Insider When it comes to making phone photos stand out, Yüyan said natural landscapes are especially challenging since they've been photographed so much. His best advice is to find a foreground subject.  "Great backgrounds, such as mountains or waterfalls, are easy to find because we're always looking for them," Yüyan said. "On the other hand, a good foreground subject, such as blooming wildflowers or a craggy tree, can be much harder to find in the right location." Yüyan recommended searching for an interesting foreground subject and framing your shot so you can see the scenery in the distance.  The author photographs Jackson Hole, Wyoming. Joey Hadden/Business Insider "It'll give your images depth, intimacy, and make your photos unique," he said. I had never thought about foreground in this way before, but his tip reminded me of when I photographed a beach across the street from mountains in Santa Cruz, California. I started by photographing the beach from the shore. I thought the mountains looked nice, but the foreground was just sand, which made the bottom half of my image look boring.  Then I took my phone across some ocean rocks and into the tide pools. The rocks and the reflecting water spruced up my foreground, giving my image more layers. To me, this made my second picture feel more interesting and dynamic. The author photographs a beach in Santa Cruz, California. Joey Hadden/Business Insider I also thought about a time I took some photos on my phone during a hike in Prescott, Arizona. When I first arrived at the Watson Lake parking lot for my hike, I thought it looked stunning with rock formations I hadn't seen before. But photographing the scene from the lot didn't seem to do it justice.  Once I immersed myself in the landscape by hiking the trails, I found foreground subjects such as shrubs and trees that better framed the lake scene. The inclusion of these elements in the second image gave a better sense of what it was really like to be there because it had more layers showing what actually surrounds the lake. The author photographs Prescott, Arizona, in 2022. Joey Hadden/Business Insider Some images in my camera roll already seemed to support Yüyan's tip, but the National Geographic photographer helped me identify what makes certain pictures stronger than others. I'll go into my next nature trip feeling more inspired to shoot from my phone and scout for interesting foregrounds. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Readwise takes on Amazon’s Kindle and Goodreads with its new app for book lovers
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Readwise , the maker of a read-it-later app and digital reading companion that keeps track of your highlights across services, is now taking on Amazon’s e-book empire with its latest app, Readwise Books . The app is an e-book store also helps you track what you’ve read, similar to Amazon’s Goodreads. The bootstrapped startup described the new app as “a cross between Kindle and the Goodreads apps,” as it offers a single place to buy, read, and track books. However, Readwise Books aims to offer more detailed reading stats, than the dates you read a book and whether you finished it. It lets readers visualize richer reading data like words read, pace, depth, immersion, and sessions. Meanwhile, its new store offers “millions” of ebooks from the big five publishers and others, initially in the U.S., with more countries to come. Print books (fulfilled by Bookshop.org’s distributor) and some audiobooks are available as well, the company notes. The launch comes at a time when there’s been an explosion of new reading apps and book trackers, all hoping to challenge Goodreads by introducing new features like book clubs, widgets, improved discovery features, goal-setting, better lists and organizational tools, habit-tracking, and more. However, few indie developers have gone so far as to launch an alternative to Amazon’s Kindle e-books store, which remains the industry leader, with an 83% share of the market when Kindle+ (formerly Kindle Unlimited) is included in the stats. One of Kindle’s bigger advantages is that it offers an end-to-end solution for everything related to reading e-books, from the hardware devices to the book-tracking log. Readwise isn’t selling its own e-readers, but it is attempting to create its own community around reading, complete with tools for reading purchased and uploaded ebooks, tracking them (like on Goodreads), sharing your reading progress with friends, and more. It also offers a number of ways to track books outside its ecosystem. This includes a way to track reading sessions by using Kindle’s browser-based Cloud Reader and a feature that lets you snap photos of physical books to mark your progress. Plus, you can upload any DRM-free EPUBs (a common ebook file format without copy protection). The app can read your ebooks aloud via text-to-speech. Readwise believes its more in-depth metrics could be a big selling point, too, likening them to a “Strava for reading” — a reference to the metrics-heavy running app. “The desire to read books, like exercising and eating well, is laden with guilt,” the company explained in a blog post penned by co-founders Daniel Doyon and Tristan Homsi. “Many people feel like they should be reading more, but feeling bad about it tends to change nothing. The session tracking taps into a different psychological mechanism. It makes the reading you’re doing legible and, as the adage goes, that which is measured is improved.” The company adds that the most consistent feedback from users is that the app has led them to read more without willpower tricks like goal-setting, streaks, or scheduling. With publishers’ permission, the app will support AI-powered features as well, like session recaps, definitions and term lookups, word and phrase translations, and a location-aware ability to ask questions about the part you’re reading. (So far, only Harper Collins has opted in, though.) Unlike Goodreads’ locked-down ecosystem, Readwise is embracing open technology. This includes a public API and an MCP server. The latter supports AI agents that could be used to research book recommendations on your behalf, use your Readwise data to create a books page on your personal website, or even wire up your hackable e-reader to log your sessions automatically, depending on how involved your AI use cases may be. The new Readwise Books app will remain free, with some AI features later going behind a paywall. Its prior apps for reading and tracking highlights are either $7.99 per month each, or $9.99 per month for both. The Books app is currently in beta and requires an invite , unless you’re already a Readwise subscriber. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Europe's fridges are getting hacked. Could America be next?
events.summary: Cyberattacks are wreaking havoc on an unlikely target across Europe: supermarket refrigerators. Why it matters: Hackers are turning everyday, internet-connected equipment into physical hazards, spoiling food and causing costly damage. U.S. supermarkets use similar technology, and the Pentagon is already investigating suspected cyberattacks involving refrigeration systems at six military commissaries. Driving the news: Suspected cyberattacks sent refrigerator and freezer temperatures soaring at dozens of European supermarkets overnight, spoiling food and threatening costly losses. Grocery chains Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents affecting stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar disruptions, per Reuters . A Belgian company that operates Delhaize's refrigeration systems said hackers switched the units into defrost mode. Here's what to know. Supermarkets hacked in Europe Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported cyberattacks or IT disruptions, forcing some stores to discard spoiled food. Dozens of stores were affected, including an ICA supermarket in Sweden that said hackers set its refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 122°F, per ABC News . Authorities haven't shared who specifically is behind the attacks, per NBC News . Empty refrigerated shelves at a Proxy Delhaize supermarket in Maleizen, Belgium, following a refrigeration outage. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flashback: The incidents follow similar attacks in France last month, when hackers seized control of hundreds of refrigeration units, causing fires and spoiling food. It's unclear whether the attacks are connected. What they're saying: France's finance minister Roland Lescure said at the time that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. How fridges get hacked How it works: Hackers aren't opening up each individual fridge and setting new temperatures. Instead, they target computer systems that control the temperatures of multiple refrigerated units remotely. Many stores use internet-connected controllers — small computer-like devices, sometimes with touchscreens — that allow maintenance workers to remotely monitor temperatures without having to visit every store. Hackers can exploit software flaws or stolen login credentials to change temperatures or activate defrost functions. Case in point: Danish manufacturer Danfoss said it identified security flaws last year and had long recommended customers install updates, according to The Guardian . In the Netherlands, some affected refrigeration systems used default passwords and were connected to unsecured networks. A supermarket manager discards spoiled food following a refrigeration outage linked to suspected cyberattacks across Europe on Nov. 2 in Belgium. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images The cost of hacked refrigerators Spoiled food: If temperatures rise overnight, the stores end up finding ruined meat, dairy and frozen products the next morning. In some French supermarkets, the soaring hot temperatures lasted for six hours, per Reuters. Spoiled food becomes unsafe to sell. Overheating and fires: Refrigerators can also overheat and cause fires. French prosecutors confirmed that the October attacks caused fires and food losses. Supermarkets lose money: Some stores lost more than €130,000. Two markets in the French region of Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000, per The Guardian . Intermarché's parent company estimated its nationwide losses in the tens of millions of euros. Yes, but: Not every attack causes extensive damage. In Estonia, a refrigeration company said technicians responded to the breach within minutes and halted any massive losses, per AP . Fridge attacks in the U.S. Zoom out: Many U.S. supermarkets use refrigeration technology similar to that found in Europe. Danfoss markets refrigeration monitoring and management systems in the U.S. Copeland, a U.S.-based refrigeration technology company, sells controllers that manage the grocery store display cases and walk-in refrigerators. What we're watching: The Pentagon is investigating whether cyberattacks caused freezer malfunctions at at least six U.S. military commissaries in August.

events.title: After ProPublica Investigation, House Democrats Demand Answers on U.S. Citizens Detained by Immigration Agents
events.summary: Photo illustration by ProPublica. Source images: Congress and videos obtained by ProPublica. What Happened: Citing ProPublica’s recent investigation , House Democrats are again asking the Trump administration to explain why hundreds of U.S. citizens have been held by immigration agents and how the government verifies citizenship during immigration operations. In an October letter to Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, California Rep. Lou Correa and 39 other legislators demanded the administration share the number of citizens that immigration agents have detained and how the government is tracking such encounters. They also asked for more information about how agents are trained to verify citizenship and legal status. Why It Matters: ProPublica counted more than 500 Americans detained by immigration agents — almost certainly an undercount since the government is not transparently tracking the cases. Experts told us the cases collectively show federal agents running roughshod over the constitutional rights of citizens. We found more than 100 Americans who were questioned about their citizenship, 63 Americans detained while recording, 36 Americans held for at least a day without being able to contact a lawyer or their family and roughly a dozen citizens deported, mostly children. What They Said: “We remain concerned that the Department’s actions are violating American citizens’ constitutional rights to due process, equal protection, and freedom from unreasonable search and seizure, and request transparency regarding the Department’s actions,” the representatives wrote in their letter to DHS. DHS has long insisted it is not arresting U.S. citizens, and it defended its immigration operations as “highly targeted.” “These members of Congress have shown more concern for criminal illegal aliens who’ve broken our laws and destroyed any possibility of ever remaining in our country than they ever have for Rachel Morin, Laken Riley, Jocelyn Nungaray, and the true victims of illegal alien crimes in America,” a spokesperson wrote to ProPublica. Background: Democrats have been pushing the second Trump administration for more details about how immigration agents are interacting with U.S. citizens since early 2025 . Last year, congressional Democrats announced a wide-ranging investigation into immigration agents’ detention of U.S. citizens in response to our earlier reporting that found that more than 170 citizens were detained by immigration agents . Last month, Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, a New Mexico Democrat, introduced a bill, Justice for Citizens Wrongfully Detained by ICE Act, that would make it easier for citizens to sue immigration agents for wrongful arrests. events.title: British adventurer Karl Bushby returns home after 28-year walk around world
events.summary: The 57-year-old crossed jungles and frozen seas before an emotional homecoming in Hull, northern England. A British adventurer has completed a 28-year walking journey around the world, arriving at his childhood home after travelling some 50,000km (31,070 miles) across jungles, frozen seas and international borders. Karl Bushby, 57, was embraced by his mother, Angela, outside her terraced house in Hull, northern England, on Monday, beneath a banner reading “Welcome Home Son”. list 1 of 4 Al Jazeera condemns Israeli ban extension, calls for its immediate lifting list 2 of 4 Jake Paul returns to boxing after a year out to face MMA star in Dubai list 3 of 4 Carrick says United players are committed despite poor run list 4 of 4 Displaced in Hebron: Picking up pieces after Israeli siege Hundreds of cheering supporters had welcomed him in the city centre before he made the final stretch home. “Sorry to keep you waiting,” he joked to the crowd. “Is that it, is it done?” Bushby began what became known as his Goliath Expedition in Punta Arenas, southern Chile, in November 1998, carrying a tent, a few hundred dollars and a cheap plastic camera. His goal was to reach his home city by an unbroken route, without using motorised transport to advance his journey. The route took him north through the Americas, across the ice of the Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia, and onwards through Mongolia and China. He later swam across the Caspian Sea before continuing towards Europe. Along the way, he negotiated the dense jungle of the Darien Gap between Colombia and Panama, was detained after entering Russia, and faced repeated visa and funding problems. The global financial crisis in 2008 cost him major sponsors, adding to delays that stretched what he had expected to be a 12-year journey into 28 years. Last month, he finally swam across the English Channel, clearing the last major obstacle before beginning the final walk home. “They say it takes a village, but literally it took a world to get me here,” he said as he arrived in Hull. “The kindness of strangers, so many, from individuals to nation-states, to get me back here today. I didn’t do this alone. There was a big team. The biggest team. Earth.” A feature-length documentary about his journey is in production, while Bushby plans to begin a speaking tour around England in the coming weeks.

events.title: A prank meant to humiliate a Red Baron worker backfired—now strangers have given the dad of 4 more than $760,000
events.summary: The internet has a well-worn genre: Film a stranger at work, needle him until he snaps, post the meltdown for views. This time, the genre flipped. A video of a prankster faking an Apple Pay theft from a Red Baron Pizza worker as he stocked a grocery store freezer has made the prankster an online pariah. It has also turned the worker, a Michigan father of four identified only as Walt Z., into the beneficiary of a GoFundMe campaign that had raised $761,514 as of publication. Among the donors: Vivek Ramaswamy , the former Republican presidential candidate and GOP nominee for Ohio governor , who gave $38,000. What happened in the video The clip opens with the cameraman asking the worker, who is wearing a Red Baron shirt and loading frozen pizzas into a case, what time it is. When Walt pulls out his phone, the prankster holds up his own device, plays a sound mimicking an Apple Pay transaction, and claims he just took $10, NBC Chicago reported . No money actually changed hands. “Listen dude, I’m not in the mood for this crap right now,” Walt says. “You think this is funny, don’t you?” He tells the prankster he’s going to report him and walks away. The footage then shows him speaking with what appear to be store employees. When the cameraman approaches again, this time thanking him “for the $20,” Walt’s composure gives way. “My life is hard enough as it is” “It’s not a joke to me,” he says. “I don’t have time for this crap in my life. My life is hard enough as it is.” He explains that his kids went to bed without him, that he was supposed to be home an hour earlier, and that he has to be up at 5 a.m. to get to 10 more stores. When the prankster apologizes, Walt rejects it, wearing a smug look. Then comes the line that has been quoted across the internet: “You’re probably making money off this! I can’t even pay my goddamn mortgage! And I got four kids at home! So not funny!” Walt also worries aloud that the confrontation could get him kicked out of the store. Instead, the person behind the camera is the one who disappeared: The Instagram account that posted the clip has since been deleted , and the video now lives on through reposts on X and Reddit. Red Baron stands by its worker Schwan’s Company, Red Baron’s parent, told the New York Post that the encounter actually took place in August, months before the video went viral, and that the company had “ connected directly with our team member to check on his well-being, and we continue to offer our full support .” On Oct. 29, the brand’s X account went a step further. “He’s still here. He’s got a fan club. Including us,” Red Baron posted, alongside a graphic declaring that employee-of-the-month nominations were closed. “You know why.” A stranger started the fundraiser The GoFundMe, titled “Support a Harassed Red Baron Worker,” was launched Oct. 27 by Luke Oakenshield, who had never met Walt and set out to track him down. The campaign had raised about $5,500 by the next day . It crossed $100,000 a day after that, then $500,000 by Oct. 30 , as conservative commentators including Benny Johnson and Collin Rugg amplified it. As donations poured in, supporters learned that Oakenshield, a military veteran, says he is homeless and living out of his car . A friend has since launched a separate fundraiser for him. “I started all of this because I know struggle, and never thought it would explode like it did,” Oakenshield wrote. He has said GoFundMe is overseeing the campaign so the money goes directly to Walt. The displayed total reflects pledges, not confirmed payments. Striking a nerve The outpouring says as much about the economy as about prank culture. Walt is a full-time worker, still on the clock near midnight, who says he can’t cover his mortgage. Millions of Americans recognize that story. Some 63% of Americans say they are living paycheck to paycheck, according to a July 2026 CNBC|SurveyMonkey poll . As Fortune has reported, even six-figure earners increasingly say the same. Walt has stayed out of the spotlight. In an update on the GoFundMe page, he thanked donors and said the kindness shown to him and his family “meant more than I can put into words.” He added that he’s been keeping things private to protect his family, and that while being in the spotlight “isn’t something I would normally seek out,” he is considering sharing his story. For now, the total keeps climbing. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Shop freezers in seven European countries hit by cyber-attack
events.summary: 'All this food is now useless': Piles of rubbish after shop freezers hit by cyber-attack Published 2 November 2026, 11:21 GMT Dozens of supermarkets across seven European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their refrigerators and freezers. Around 40 Delhaize supermarkets in Belgium and Luxembourg were affected, while a smaller number of shops were hit in Sweden, Ireland, the Netherlands, Estonia and Finland. Sabcobel, a Belgian company that manufactures some of the affected refrigerators, said the units' evaporators were switched to defrost mode, causing them to warm up, in what is believed to be the same method used in last month's incident that hit hundreds of French supermarkets. Millions of euros worth of food had to be thrown away in October, local media reported at the time. Freezers have had to be emptied at several ICA grocery stores in Sweden after the cyber-attack Stephan Moelans, the CEO of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize's systems, on Monday told the Belga news agency that the incident was a cyber-attack and that the company had been "working all night and morning to disconnect the affected units from the network". He said since the French attack in early October, the company had been working to "protect our customers fridges against this vulnerability" but that the units needed physical modifications, not just software updates. Most supermarkets across Europe are linked to the internet, and maintenance and troubleshooting can be done remotely. "The simplest solution is to manage the fridges over a secure internet connection. Most of our customers switched to that after the attack in France," Moelans added. The temperature of freezers in several shops across Europe reportedly rose to as high as 50C (122F). It is unclear who is behind the latest apparent attack. In the US, authorities are investigating what caused refrigeration malfunctions at a number of American military bases in August and working together with French officials to examine whether the incidents could be linked. Both Belgium and Sweden's national cyber-security agencies said they were monitoring the incident. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre said it was working with international partners and industry to "fully understand details of an incident". No incidents have been reported in the UK. In Flanders, northern Belgium, a Delhaize branch in Hoeilaart told news website Het Laatste Nieuws it had lost €100,000 (£83,500) worth of produce. The manager said that estimate did not even take into account further losses that would result from closing the shop. Carrefour, a French-owned supermarket, said the incident had only affected 15 of its Belgian stores, adding that measures had been taken immediately to ensure all shops remained open. A spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates Spar stores in Belgium under a franchise system, told Reuters news agency five shops had their fridge systems attacked. Sweden's budget furniture retailer Ikea said refrigeration systems of its store in the western Belgian city of Mons were affected, with a spokesman quoted by Reuters as saying "we cannot rule out that additional locations may be affected". An employee at an ICA supermarket in Sweden's capital Stockholm was pictured throwing away bags of spoiled food In Sweden, several ICA and Coop shops were hit. A spokesperson for ICA confirmed the incident had affected a "small number of ICA stores operating outside ICA's central network". "ICA is currently supporting the affected stores in managing the situation," they said. One of the ICA branches located in Sjöbo, southern Sweden, wrote on social media: "Our refrigerators and freezers have been hacked overnight and they have set the temperature to 50 degrees." The store was closed earlier but has now reopened to customers. Seven out of the 800 Coop stores in Sweden were also affected but the "situation is currently contained and under control", the company told the BBC. In neighbouring Finland, refrigerator malfunctions were detected in some K-stores. The owner of the supermarket chain Kesko was quoted by Finland's Helsingin Sanomat newspaper as saying its security experts were investigating what caused the problem. The attack is also affecting shops in Ireland, the Netherlands and Estonia. In Ireland, it impacted 13 SuperValu supermarkets. A spokesman for the owner of the chain, Musgrave Group, confirmed to The Irish Times that a "cyber incident" affected its refrigeration systems, but added that the impact was limited to a "specific model" of refrigerator. A spokesperson for Danish manufacturer Danfoss told Dutch public radio channel NOS that the freezing and cooling systems of at least 17 companies in the Netherlands were attacked overnight, affecting butcher shops and small neighbourhood stores. A Selver supermarket in Estonia was also affected and there are reports of other affected companies in the country, according to ERR.

events.title: How Walmart heiress Alice Walton, the world's richest woman, spends her $135 billion fortune
events.summary: Alice Walton is the world's wealthiest woman. Wesley Hitt/Getty Images Walmart heiress Alice Walton is the richest woman in the world. She spends some of her fortune collecting art and opened a museum in 2011. Here's a look at her life, career, and fortune. Alice Walton, the daughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton, is the richest woman in the world. As of November 2026, Forbes estimates her net worth at about $135 billion, largely because of her inherited stake in Walmart. Including Walton's brothers Jim and Rob, Walmart is listed as the source of wealth of eight people in Forbes' 400 ranking of the wealthiest people in America. The 77-year-old Walton's fortune had grown $33 billion in the preceding 12 months as Walmart's stock rose 30%, Forbes estimated in March. She's the 14th richest person in the world. Despite the Waltons' high status, their personal lives remain largely private. Here's what we know about how Alice Walton spends her fortune, from collecting expensive art to building a medical school. Alice Walton, the only daughter of Walmart founder Sam Walton, is the world's richest woman. Rick T. Wilking/Getty Images Walton overtook L'Oréal heiress Françoise Bettencourt Meyers as the world's richest woman on Forbes' 2025 list, retaining the title this year. Unlike her brothers, Rob and Jim, Alice Walton has not played a major role in running Walmart and has instead become a patron of the arts. Members of the Walton family (L-R) Rob, Alice, and Jim speak during the annual Walmart shareholders meeting event on June 1, 2018 in Fayetteville, Arkansas. Rick T. Wilking/Getty Images Walton fell in love with the arts at a young age, according to a New Yorker profile. When she was around 10 years old, she bought her first work of art: a reproduction of a Picasso painting for about $2, she told the publication. After graduating from Trinity University in San Antonio in 1971, Walton briefly entered the family business, working for Walmart as a buyer of children's clothes, she told The New Yorker. But her career really began in finance, which led her to founding Llama Company , an investment bank, in 1988. She has been married and divorced twice and has no children. Walton has an immense private art collection that includes original works by legendary American artists. Alice Walton attends the American Federation of Arts 2017 Gala and Cultural Leadership Awards at The Metropolitan Club on October 26, 2017 in New York City. Sylvain Gaboury/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images "Collecting has been such a joy, and such an important part of my life in terms of seeing art, and loving it," she told The New Yorker in 2011. In 2011, she opened the Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas, with her private art collection. The Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in 2024. Hasan Akbas/Anadolu via Getty Images Walmart is also headquartered in Bentonville. Before the museum opened, it had four times the endowment of the famous Whitney Museum in New York, according to the New Yorker profile. In 2014, the Walmart heiress paid $44.4 million for a piece of artwork by Georgia O'Keeffe. 'Jimson Weed/White Flower No.1' by American artist Georgia O'Keeffe was briefly on display at Tate Modern in London in 2016. Rob Stothard/Getty Images At the time, it was the most expensive sale of a work of art by a female artist in history, the Observer reported. Walton later put it on display at her museum in Arkansas. Crystal Bridges underwent a major expansion this year. Crystal Bridges in 2024. Hasan Akbas/Anadolu via Getty Images The expansion grew Crystal Bridges' footprint by 50%, according to a press release. Walton has committed billions of dollars to philanthropy. Jim Walton, Alice Walton, and Rob Walton cheer at the annual shareholders meeting for Walmart in Fayetteville, Arkansas. REUTERS/Rick Wilking Walton has contributed more than $6 billion to five family charitable foundations, which had distributed an estimated $2 billion of her funds through 2024, Forbes reported. In 2017, the Walton Family Charitable Support Foundation gifted $120 million to the University of Arkansas to establish a School of Art . Walton also has her own charitable organization, the Alice L. Walton Foundation , which donates to causes including the arts, education, and health, according to its website. Walton has also put some of her money into politics. Justin Sullivan/Getty She has traditionally given to Republican candidates and PACs, though Walton donated $353,400 to the Hillary Victory Fund , a joint fundraising committee supporting Clinton and other Democrats, during the 2016 election cycle, according to Forbes. During the 2026 election cycle, she contributed to Republican senators including Bill Cassidy and Tom Cotton, as well as Democratic Sen. John Hickenlooper, according to Federal Election Commission data compiled by FundVoter . And she bought a two-floor condo on New York City's Park Avenue for $25 million in 2014. Park Avenue, New York City. Stockyme/Getty Images The condo, which had been owned by late financier Christopher H. Browne, has 52 large windows overlooking Central Park and the city, as well as a media room and a library. Walton was active in the horse-breeding scene in Texas, but in 2015, she said she would devote more of her time to Crystal Bridges. Alejo Benedetti talks with Alice Walton at the KAWS Director Reception at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in March 2025. Wesley Hitt/Getty Images "I've been stretched in too many directions, and I want to get focused," Walton said, according to the Fort Worth Star-Telegram in 2017. "I've got a house in Fort Worth, so I'm moving to town." In 2017, she sold her ranch in Millsap, Texas, for an undisclosed amount . The Rocking W Ranch had an initial asking price of $19.75 million but was later reduced to $16.5 million. Walton also listed her 4,416-acre Fortune Bend Ranch in Texas in 2015 for $28.7 million. Alice Walton in 2015. D Dipasupil/Getty Images She also cut its listing price to $22.1 million . In 2021, the Alice L. Walton School of Medicine was founded. Alice Walton speaks onstage during the Getty Medal Dinner 2022. Stefanie Keenan/Getty Images for The J. Paul Getty Trust The school welcomed 48 students in 2025 and welcomed its second class of 48 this year. Tuition was waived for these students and will continue to be for the next three cohorts. It is for students "devoted to transforming the health of medically underserved and rural communities in Arkansas, its surrounding states, and beyond," the school website says. The Alice L. Walton Foundation and Mercy are building a healthcare campus in Bentonville. Bentonville, Arkansas. Larry Fleury/Getty Images/iStockphoto Its first building, a 709,000-square-foot specialty care center , is expected to open in 2029. Along with other Walton family members, Walton is helping to fund a STEM-focused university in Bentonville. Bentonville, Arkans

events.title: Fanatics takes bigger NHL design role with all-32 team Hometown Remix jerseys
events.summary: Fanatics and the NHL debuted Hometown Remix, a special-edition uniform and apparel program covering all 32 teams. The program gives Fanatics responsibility for league-wide jersey design and execution, expanding its role beyond manufacturing and retail, the first such deal with one of its professional sports league partners. NHL teams will wear the jerseys during select 2026-27 games, while the NHL and Fanatics plan to evaluate fan response for future programs. In most professional sports arenas, rinks and stadiums across the globe, the gear that fans are now wearing to games is made and designed by sports merchandise giant Fanatics. But that isn't always the case for the jersey that the players are wearing on the field, ice or court. On Monday, Fanatics and the NHL debuted the Hometown Remix program, a collection of uniforms and apparel for all 32 NHL teams. The new designs and look of each jersey is focused on each team's city and fan base. It marks the first time that Fanatics has designed and developed a league-wide jersey program for one of its leagues partners, which include the NFL, NBA, and MLB. For some leagues, such as the NFL, while Fanatics may manufacture jerseys that fans buy in stores, other consumer-focused products and even what coaches wear on the sidelines, what players wear on the field may be manufactured and designed by a different company. In the case of the NFL, that is Nike. In MLB, while Fanatics manufactures player jerseys, Nike designs them. Fanatics has been a partner of the NHL since 2005, mainly focused on retail and e-commerce. But in 2023, as the league's jersey deal with Adidas lapsed, Fanatics expanded its partnership to include on-ice uniforms and authentic jerseys. When that deal began alongside the 2024-25 season, it marked the first time that Fanatics branding appeared directly on an official player jersey in a professional game, a massive evolution for the company. The new collection takes that a "giant step forward in our partnership with the NHL," according to Andrew Low Ah Kee, CEO of Fanatics Commerce, the company's merchandise business arm. "What's exciting to me about it is that not only is it all 32 teams, it's actually that Fanatics is singularly responsible and accountable for the design and execution of the program in partnership with the [NHL] and the clubs," Low Ah Kee said. "Whereas we work with Nike and others on other leagues and different programs." Low Ah Kee said the process for this collection began when its expanded deal with the NHL took effect in 2024, and Fanatics' design team has been working across the league, its teams and players since. Some of the process itself hasn't been totally new: Fanatics has designed jerseys in conjunction with the NHL and some of its teams for tentpole events like the Winter Classic, Stadium Series and the 4 Nations Face-Off. However, not every NHL team has participated in one of those events. But Low Ah Kee said doing it in the NHL, which he said has the "most complex construction of any sports jersey out there," while also adding new design elements, highlighting unique aspects of each team's fans and local culture, has been a big moment for Fanatics. "I don't think this will be a capstone, but this is certainly a big milestone in the relationship that we have," Low Ah Kee said. Brian Jennings, NHL senior vice president and chief partnerships and club strategy officer, said the league appreciates the legacy and reverence that hockey jerseys — often called sweaters — hold for fans of the sport. At the same time, Jennings said the league has been excited to create new designs around a league-wide platform that celebrates local team culture. "Each market and city is unique … we love to celebrate that uniqueness," Jennings said. Jennings said that each team will wear its jersey for a set of games throughout the remainder of this season, providing opportunities to highlight the designs and storytelling. While this is just set to be a program for the 2026-2027 season, Jennings said that if a team wanted to integrate some of the logos, colors or designs into a future alternate jersey or other products, the NHL and Fanatics would be open to it. This Hometown Remix collection is also setting the groundwork for future league-wide efforts with Fanatics, Jennings said. "In an ideal world, we'll start to ideate immediately around what is another version," he said. "Once we have the ability to collect some insights, what was successful, what wasn't, what do we want to turn the volume up on … we want to keep the design integrity really, really high and delight and excite fans." Jennings said these moments do boost the business side as well. While he declined to provide specific targets, he pointed to the bump that the league and teams see when new jerseys and merchandise are released for special event games like the Winter Classic.

events.title: Brickmaker’s woes deepen the UK housebuilding gloom
events.summary: Ibstock has issued a thumping profits warning, with sales 22% below expectations in the third quarter W ith John Healey’s Your First Home scheme on the way, is the mood improving in the housebuilding sector? A couple of the builders have results later this week, so can speak for themselves. In the meantime, though, here’s a thumping profits warning from Ibstock, the country’s biggest brickmaker, to spread a little more gloom. Demand hit a brick wall in the summer, as the company could have put it. Industry data, said Ibstock , show UK brick market volumes down 17% year-on-year in July and August. For the whole of the third quarter, it said, sales were 22% below expectations, forcing a one-fifth cut in its production volumes versus plans set out as recently as August. Cue an 11% fall in the share price to virtually its lowest level since the firm relisted on the stock market in 2015. Top-line earnings for the whole of 2026 will be “in the mid-£40m range” versus a figure close to £60m expected by the City. The short moral from Ibstock’s woes is that the sector’s slowdown is pretty entrenched. Across the board, we’ve heard shareholder-friendly vows from housebuilders of “financial discipline”, corporate-speak for saying expansion is off the table and the job is about hammering away at costs. Berkeley Homes, focused on the south-east of England, even said six months ago it will stop buying new land and hiring new staff . Everybody knows one deep cause: the turnaround in interest rate expectations with the Iran war. The Bank of England will probably raise rates this week (finally); then we’ll be on to wondering how many more increases will follow. In addition, housebuilders complain about costs of regulation that are harder to lose when the prices of new houses are going sideways. So is Healey’s Your First Home a reheat of Help to Buy, a gamechanger? From the point of view of housebuilders, the scheme is clearly welcome – they had been lobbying for action for ages. But there are a couple of caveats. First, the caps on the size of the transactions means it is not a copycat scheme for the very good reason that Healey can’t be seen to be adding too much inflationary pressure at a time like now. Second, it will only be launched next April, the chancellor said in his budget last week. The delay “may weigh on demand in the intervening period”, Ibstock chief executive Joe Hudson said, echoing others. He is surely right: for many qualifying buyers, it will make sense to wait five months for the discounted loans. Healey also said there will be no more changes to building regulations in this parliament (except where critical for safety), a nod towards the sector’s other grumble. On the other hand, he’s not proposing to remove existing regulations. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning So one suspects 2027 – a year of 1% growth in the economy, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts – is probably not going to move housebuilding volumes meaningfully. Your First Home should be “modestly helpful”, reckons Peel Hunt, but “lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity”. Yes, it all comes back to borrowing costs. And the upturn, when it comes, will surely be too late to save the government’s ambition of 1.5m new homes this parliament . The target isn’t officially rubble, but it may as well be.

events.title: Oil price falls amid hope of a breakthrough to end Iran war
events.summary: Brent crude drops by more than 6% to $105.55 a barrel, the lowest level in more than two weeks The oil price has fallen to its lowest level in more two weeks amid new hopes of a breakthrough to end the Iran war. Brent crude, the international benchmark, dropped by more than 6.5% to as low as $105.55 a barrel on Monday, the lowest since 16 October, sending shares in airline companies higher and pushing down government borrowing costs. Oil prices fell after Tehran revealed that contacts between Iran and the US to end their eight-month war were continuing. “Consultations through mediators are very ⁠intensive. We have presented our conditions and ⁠proposals and everything depends on the political ​rationality of Washington,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said, according to the state media outlet IRNA. Over the weekend, Qatari officials tried to negotiate the release of more than $6bn (£4.5bn) in Iranian assets , so that Tehran might allow the strait of Hormuz to reopen. Donald Trump had earlier taken a belligerent tone, telling voters in Iowa on Sunday that Iran would receive “the hammer” unless there was progress. “The only reason why I’m not finished with Iran is I want to be nice. I want to try and save all those lives if I can ... But at some point we’re going to have to give them the hammer,” he said during a campaign rally in the run-up to the US midterm elections. But investors were cheered by reports on Monday that Iran’s supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, had granted “powers” to his government in its talks with the US seeking to end the Middle East war. Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said: “The news is manna from heaven for stock markets, which have felt increasingly pressured by oil’s rise, but of course there is still a risk that Trump will try one last throw of the iron dice after the midterms.” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The drop in the oil price sparked hopes of a break in the inflationary pressures gripping the global economy. Government borrowing costs dropped, with the yield – or interest rate – on 10-year UK bonds down 10 basis points, or 0.1 of a percentage point, to the lowest since 22 September.

events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Republicans and Democrats hold last rallies from Washington to Michigan and Texas as polls point to a tight race for Congress. US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have begun their final push ahead of the November 3 midterm elections , with Republican and Democratic candidates spreading out across the United States for a last day of campaigning. Trump is scheduled to deliver his closing campaign message at 2pm ET (19:00 GMT) on Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC. list 1 of 3 Trump leans into Islamophobia and conspiracy in last-ditch campaign rallies list 2 of 3 US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks list 3 of 3 As Islamophobia ramps up in US midterms, Texas Muslims eye local stakes Republicans are trying to hold their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives despite Trump’s low approval ratings and polls predicting that the Iran war, high energy prices, and the affordability crisis could mean a strong night for Democrats. Closing the campaign at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, DC, is a departure from Trump’s recent strategy. The US president has staged more than 25 rallies in largely conservative areas over the past month, and wrote that Sunday’s rally in Kansas was the “last stop” of his 2026 midterm campaign tour. The reflecting pool is also politically awkward. Trump’s renovation of the historical landmark ran nearly three months late and cost more than 10 times the initial budget. The “American-flag blue” liner also began peeling after he declared the work complete, according to the Associated Press. In an interview on the New York Post’s Pod Force One podcast, Trump said that, in the event of having to work with Democrats, he’ll become “Mr. Veto”. “It wouldn’t be the first time [we] have a president and he doesn’t have the Senate. They set stuff up, you veto it. After a month or two of getting things vetoed, they come over, and you make a deal,” he said. Vance was due in Rome, New York, early Monday to boost Republican candidates for the House of Representatives Anthony Constantino and Kailee Buller at a rally that began at 9:15am ET (14:15 GMT). Constantino is running to succeed longtime Republican Representative Elise Stefanik, who is not seeking re-election. A Siena Research Institute poll shows the race could be close despite a Republican registration advantage of about 80,000 voters. “A new poll conducted by Siena Research […] shows that while voters in the district still favor Republicans more broadly, that sentiment does not necessarily translate to support for Constantino,” North Country Public Radio reported. In Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is holding a “Get-Out-The-Vote” canvass rally at Eastern Michigan University in Ypsilanti on his last morning of the campaign. He is then due in Flint at 1:30pm ET (18:30 GMT), Royal Oak at 3:30pm ET (20:30 GMT) and Detroit at 4:30pm ET (21:30 GMT) for a final rally. In Texas, Democrats James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa are making final pushes for Senate and governor, respectively, with a joint rally in Austin at 6:30pm CT (00:30 GMT on Tuesday). Talarico’s opponent, Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, is scheduled to appear in Conroe at 12pm CT (18:00 GMT) and Allen at 6:30pm CT (00:30 GMT). Polls show Talarico narrowly ahead of Paxton, while Governor Greg Abbott’s lead over Hinojosa has narrowed. More Democrats for your consideration In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson will make campaign stops in Yarmouth, Scarborough, South Portland, and Portland, with scheduled events starting at 9am (14:00 GMT) and ending at 6pm ET (23:00 GMT). In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek will be touring Harlan, Onawa, Le Mars and Sioux City to meet with voters, from 10am CT (16:00 GMT) to 6pm CT (00:00 GMT) In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton will be out from 7:30am CT (13:30 GMT) to 1pm CT (19:00 GMT), speaking to voters across Wichita, Topeka and Lawrence. The final event of the day has not yet been announced. Separately, a federal judge in Washington is due to hear a lawsuit early Monday over whether immigration agents can be present at polling places. Common Cause, UnidosUS, the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC) and the city and county of Denver are challenging the US administration’s position that armed agents from US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) may enter polling places for immigration enforcement. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in September that agents would not patrol polling sites but could enter to respond to threats or serve warrants on people. The plaintiffs argue that such operations would violate a federal restriction on armed personnel at voting places and could intimidate voters. The Department of Homeland Security has said ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations.

events.title: Raising the quality of insights in agentic analytics
events.summary: In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context. Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive. Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents. events.title: SpaceX reportedly wants to buy Boost Mobile to compete with AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. SpaceX is looking to buy Boost Mobile from EchoStar, according to a report from The Washington Post. If the deal goes through, it would help the Elon Musk-owned company build a hybrid cellular-satellite network that could help catapult it into fourth place among the top U.S. wireless providers. The space-launch company has been dabbling in cellular connectivity, rolling out satellite access to T-Mobile’s subscribers in 2024. Last year, SpaceX bought $17 billion worth of wireless spectrum from EchoStar for cellular services, which could help the company’s Starlink service reach inside buildings, for example, something it currently struggles with. “This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America,” Musk said on X at the time of the spectrum acquisition. Yet, if Musk is still looking to buy access to terrestrial networks, it apparently wasn’t the last piece. Elon Musk, SpaceX’s CEO, reportedly spoke directly with EchoStar chairman Charlie Ergen in October about acquiring Boost Mobile, the mobile virtual network operator. EchoStar has about 7.5 million customers between Boost Mobile and Gen Mobile, its other mobile service offering. Musk has also approached AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon about buying capacity on their networks. All three rejected Musk, and they may still have a say in a SpaceX acquisition of Boost Mobile. Boost doesn’t operate its own towers, instead leasing capacity from AT&T and T-Mobile, which might need to approve such a deal. Sources speaking to The Post said that network leases are usually nontransferable. The big three providers each have over 100 million subscribers, dwarfing Boost Mobile. But while the acquisition would give SpaceX an immediate bump in subscribers, the true value of the deal would be giving the company access to terrestrial cellular networks. Gaining access to towers leased to Boost Mobile would expand coverage significantly — Boost currently covers most of the 48 contiguous states in the U.S. — allowing Starlink to cover devices when they’re outdoors and relying on cell towers to handle devices when Starlink signals can’t reach them. events.title: Shop fridges and freezers across Europe hit by fresh suspected cyber-attack
events.summary: Chains in seven countries say cooling unit temperatures rose overnight in incident similar to hack of French shops Who is hacking Europe’s supermarket fridges and freezers, and why? Supermarket chains in at least seven European countries have said the temperatures of refrigerators and freezers in some of their shops soared overnight to as high as 50C (122F), echoing a cyber-attack last month that caused millions of euros of damage in France. Retailers in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg , the Netherlands and Sweden reported problems with their refrigeration systems on Monday, and several companies confirmed they had been hacked. The EU food and agriculture commissioner, Christophe Hansen, said the repeated cyber-attacks were deeply concerning, calling them “a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it”. The incidents follow an attack in France last month in which hackers seized control of cooling units in as many as 700 supermarkets, raising their temperatures as high ⁠as 50C (122F) and causing fires and food losses estimated in the tens of millions of euros. A growing range of devices, including refrigeration systems, can now be monitored and controlled remotely, leading authorities to particularly fear government-sponsored hybrid attacks ​in after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet that six of ​its shops ‌had been ​hit, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”. An ICA shop at Sjöbo in southern Sweden posted that its fridges and freezers had been hacked and their temperature set at 50C. Another in Stockholm said its freezers were broken “due to a 2am cyberattack” and that “everything was destroyed”. The head of Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, said it ‌was working on incidents around the country. It had established the country had “quite a lot of exposed operational ‌technology devices” that needed updating or patching, he told Reuters. The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​similar incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg had been hit. It did not specify the cause, but reporters visiting a shop north-east of Brussels saw refrigerators and freezers empty and a sign reading: “Due to cyberattacks, there will be no products on the refrigerated or freezer shelves. We offer our sincere apologies.” A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the range of fresh and frozen products was “temporarily somewhat limited” in affected shops, but that distribution centres were operating normally and there was no disruption to deliveries. Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of shops and supermarkets had been affected, including five Spar outlets, Shop & Go convenience shops attached to Q8 service stations and some smaller Proxy Delhaize mini-markets. “We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which operates Delhaize’s refrigeration systems, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations.” He told the Belga news agency the ‌incident had been a cyber-attack and that the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode. The Colruyt and Intermarché supermarket chains also said they had been hit by technical problems affecting fridges in five and 15 of their shops respectively, and Carrefour Belgium reported disruption in about 15 of its 700 shops. A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day “It’s a cyber-attack, there is no other reason,” said Mich Vergauwen, a Carrefour spokesperson. An Ikea Belgium spokesperson likewise told Agence France-Presse that a cyber-attack had caused the temperature of freezers in its Mons shop to rise suddenly. Ikea, famous for its in-store Swedish meatballs, said it had had to ‌remove some food products from refrigeration units ​as a precaution and expected some food waste as ⁠a result. In Finland, the Helsingin Sanomat newspaper said shops operated by the Kesko supermarket chain were investigating similar problems, while the Dutch public radio NOS reported that the systems of at least 17 mainly small local shops had been affected. At one Estonian supermarket chain, attackers accessed a computer controlling the refrigeration system and turned up the temperature to 50C, the refrigeration supply company Kitman Coldtech told the ERR broadcaster. “This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” its chief executive, Jann Mutso, said, adding that the attack was responded to within minutes and there had been no significant damage. The Selver supermarket chain said one of its outlets had been affected.

events.title: Villa Vie residents made a 'Hail Mary' effort to buy the Odyssey. Read the letter confirming the plan is dead.
events.summary: A drone view of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship docking at Sihanoukville Autonomous Port. SOVEIT YARN/Reuters A resident-led effort to buy the Villa Vie Odyssey has failed. Villa Vie's "never-ending" cruise came to a halt in Cambodia last Tuesday. One resident called the bid a "Hail Mary." Two days later, a letter confirmed it was over. A last-ditch attempt by residents of Villa Vie's Odyssey to buy and operate the ship is dead in the water. The Odyssey's final months were marked by signs of Villa Vie Residences' financial distress , culminating in the ship's abrupt halt last week in Cambodia. Residents — who bought cabins for between $119,999 and $439,999 in the hope of living permanently at sea — were given just eight hours to disembark on Tuesday. Paul Montoya, a member of the ship's seven-person Resident Council which was involved in securing resident pledges for the buyout, described the bid on Thursday as a "Hail Mary." Two days later on Saturday, a resident-backed group calling itself Sagar Capital told residents that the effort had ended, according to a letter reviewed by Business Insider. Three residents confirmed the letter's contents. The letter said the group had spent two months trying to negotiate a deal, but had been unable to do so. Montoya said in a call with Business Insider on Monday that the group had agreed to contribute a "fair amount" of capital toward the buyout to "get things rolling," while other residents were invited via WhatsApp or in person to pledge matching funds. Cambodian authorities said that 203 residents were on board when the ship docked in Sihanoukville. According to the letter, 169 residents made pledges, but the amount pledged was insufficient. "We were a little bit short, but we were pretty close," Montoya added, declining to say how much residents had pledged. He said that no money was collected from residents. In its letter, Sagar Capital cited a number of reasons for ending the bid, which several residents said was their only hope of keeping the Odyssey sailing. These included: An inability to reach an agreement with the ship's lender; Villa Vie having more debt than anticipated; Potential legal exposure; The cost of bankruptcy proceedings; The financial risk to residents' savings. "It was probably more exploratory than anything to see if the support would be there," Montoya said on Monday. "I think for the most part the support was there, but it would have been probably very tenuous in trying to move forward with those problems." In an interview with Business Insider on Friday, Petterson said the company was doing everything it could to keep the ship afloat after a potential deal with Oneil Khosa, the former CEO of Margaritaville at Sea, fell through earlier this month. Petterson said Villa Vie's focus was on recapitalization. "Preferably, we need an operational partner that can come in with a stronger hand and a bigger pocket," he said. Earlier last week, Petterson told Business Insider that the company was considering bankruptcy . Villa Vie, Petterson, and the company's cofounder Kathy Villalba did not immediately respond to requests from Business Insider for comment for this story. The resident-led effort was a final push to save the ship , Montoya said. Now, he said, residents are relying on "even more of a long shot," such as a "benevolent soul" stepping in. Cheryl Ethrington, a resident who had planned to pledge toward the buyout, said: "I haven't completely given up hope that someone will pick up the baton and run with it. If not, life goes on." You can read the letter from Sagar Capital to residents in full below: A Letter to our Fellow Odyssey Residents October 31, 2026 Dearest fellow residents and cherished friends, It is with profound sadness that we write sharing the difficult news that Sagar Capital has ended its efforts to lead residents in purchasing and operating the Odyssey. Sadly, this decision is final. Out of respect, we want to share a clear and candid explanation. Why we are bring this to a close: No agreement with the lender. We negotiated with the ship's lender for two months and could not reach terms. We understand the lender, with Columbia Ship management, has now taken control of the ship and intends to sell it at auction. More debt than we expected. We were given access to Villa Vie's records only last Saturday. Our review found substantially more debt than we had anticipated. Legal exposure. Taking over Villa Vie and changing its management would have exposed Sagar to significant liability from current and future lawsuits. The cost of bankruptcy. A Chapter 11 process would cost about $3 million for the first 60 days alone and could take much longer if lawsuits were filed. The risk to your savings. We could not find a monthly fee that both covered the ship's operating costs and stayed affordable. We could not in good conscience ask anyone to put their savings at risk on a plan that might not succeed. What we set out to do Our only aim was to keep the ship sailing for the people who call it home. It was never our intent to sell anything to anyone, or to press anyone into a decision. We tried to give you the facts as we learned them, and we are sorry the facts did not allow us to succeed. Profound Gratitude We received 169 pledges. To each of you who pledged, and to everyone who answered surveys, joined calls and offered ideas: thank you for your trust and your commitment. Your pledge: no money was collected. What we have learned over these months belongs to this community. If residents with the financial means to carry an effort forward ever come together, we will enthusiastically join in. We are bound together by this remarkable, unlikely adventure and will forever remain your neighbors and friends. We know this is a tender moment, and need to lean on one another for emotional and practical support. With that on our hearts, we would want to gather virtually in the coming days so we can share, reflect, and support each other as a community. The newly elected interim Resident Council is willing to serve or assist where needed. Though this chapter is closing, our community remains strong. Please reach out to one another as we always have, whether to talk, share resources, or navigate next steps together. We have been and will remain in this together, and we will continue to support one another. With respect and gratitude, Sagar Capital LLC Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Home Depot wants your AI agent to show some ID first
events.summary: Home Depot's CIO shares how she's thinking about AI agents, cybersecurity, and Anthropic's Mythos. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Have an AI agent? Need a hammer? Home Depot is thinking about how to make that palatable for the retailer. Angie Brown, the company's CIO, spoke to Business Insider about agents, the PHP cyber scramble, and AI fixes. She also talked about Home Depot's use of Anthropic's Mythos, and early attempts to join its Project Glasswing. Home Depot wants to roll out the welcome mat for your AI agent — so long as it's wearing a name tag and acting on your behalf. During a sit-down interview with Business Insider, Angie Brown , the company's executive vice president and chief information officer, said the retailer wants to support AI agents that can search and buy products on a customer's behalf. But Home Depot needs to be sure of two things first. "We want to know you're not a bot, and we actually want to know if it's you," she said. "That's something that Muse is working on right now, to self-identify." Her comments are the latest glimpse into how legacy retailers — and their tech staff — are thinking about the possible next generation of online shopping. Recently, several Silicon Valley companies have launched consumer-focused AI agents, such as Meta's Muse and Spear Street Technology's Instinct AI . They promise agents capable of scanning the internet, comparing products, filling carts, and buying items with little to no intervention from the person who sent them. Their rollout has been met with varying levels of resistance and buy-in from online retailers. Amazon barred Muse from shopping on its marketplace, saying the bots didn't properly identify themselves. Several other retailers — including Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora, and Shopify — have announced integrations or openness to AI agents. In October, Meta announced that it co-developed a personal agent protocol with Sierra AI to standardize AI agent identification. Brown said Home Depot is open to the idea of AI agents, but the retailer doesn't want to lose its connection with loyal customers. Frequent Home Depot shoppers, such as contractors and remodelers, are part of the company's Pro Rewards platform, where they're eligible for discounts. The retailer doesn't "want to lose contact with the customer," she said. "That's the next evolution," Brown added, confirming that Home Depot is in active conversations with Meta about how Muse should introduce itself to websites. "There's openness on both sides, because they want it to grow." Home Depot is already using AI to defend itself Brown said Home Depot is deploying AI amid a recent wave of cybersecurity worries. Last week, companies around the world raced to patch critical vulnerabilities in PHP , a programming language used in an estimated 70% of websites. The flaws were discovered with help from OpenAI and prompted US cybersecurity officials to urge affected organizations to update their systems or, in some cases, take them offline. Brown, whose remit includes Home Depot's cybersecurity, called the hours after the warning a "little hectic," but said the company's main website was not affected. "We had a couple of operating units — companies we've bought and things like that that are a little bit smaller — that had to plug a few vulnerabilities," she said, including an internal job application system that was taken down "in the middle of the day for about an hour to patch." Otherwise, she said, the company was largely spared from the sudden tech anxieties. Home Depot, Brown confirmed to Business Insider, has access to Anthropic's Mythos AI model, though the company wasn't granted early access via Project Glasswing, "despite our best efforts, and calling a lot of friends." Those slots were largely reserved for banks and cybersecurity firms, not major retailers. The Anthropic models "found a few things" for Home Depot to fix in its code — but the agents also found a few "false positives," Brown said. Home Depot, she said, has long ranked cybersecurity vulnerabilities, but AI is leading the company to rethink its desired time to deploy a fix. "The speed to fix a vulnerability has to be driven down to hours," she said. Update, November 2, 2026 — This story has been updated to reflect that Home Depot has not participated in Anthropic's Project Glasswing initiative. Read the original article on Business Insider
