events.title: OPay’s US IPO withdrawal casts shadow over African fintech
events.summary: The News OPay’s abrupt withdrawal of its $304 million US IPO on Friday cast a shadow over one of Africa’s most ambitious fintech listings, after an undisclosed foreign regulatory inquiry derailed its New York debut. On Friday, OPay had priced its American depositary shares at $19 each, the bottom of its target range, valuing the company at just over $4 billion. But trading never began: OPay and its underwriters terminated their agreement around 3.30 pm New York time, saying it was no longer prudent to proceed with the offering. OPay, which primarily operates its payments service in Nigeria, did not identify the regulator or specify the subject of the inquiry. It described the jurisdiction involved as “immaterial to its core business” and said it expected the inquiry to be “concluded satisfactorily in the near future.” The withdrawal represents a setback for Nigeria’s fintech sector and the wider African startup ecosystem, which has spent years trying to persuade global investors that its young companies can scale into major, publicly listed businesses that return funds to investors. Know More OPay, which launched in 2018 as a payments company, also outlined plans for a secondary listing on the Nigeria Stock Exchange after the NYSE debut to give local investors an opportunity to buy into a business that drives nearly nine-tenths of its revenue from Nigeria. But the F-1 filing warned investors that shares traded in Lagos may not be exchangeable for the New York-listed American depositary shares, potentially limiting liquidity and allowing prices to diverge. A key part of the IPO is a broader strategic relationship with Standard Bank Group, Africa’s largest lender by assets. Its subsidiary, Stanbic Africa Holdings, has agreed to invest up to $200 million, subject to a formula that caps its stake at 4.99% of OPay after the offering. Standard Bank’s Africa head Lungisa Fuzile is expected to join OPay’s board following the IPO. The two companies have also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to explore partnerships spanning payments, merchant acquisition, lending, remittances, and the distribution of selected banking and financial products. OPay suggested in the filings that it will use Standard Bank’s infrastructure, regulatory expertise, and presence to expand across Africa.

events.summary: Today, I’m talking with Matt Strauss, who is now chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. This is Matt’s second time joining me on the show, and there’s been a whole lot of organizational and structural change at NBCU since the last time he and I spoke just two years ago — pure Decoder bait. First, about a month after Matt was on the show, Comcast spun off most of the NBCU cable channels into something called Versant. That’s when Matt’s title changed from heading up just the direct-to-consumer offering — meaning Peacock, plus some other streaming services — to heading up the whole thing, across all distribution. And now, Comcast is spinning off the NBCU business entirely into a whole new standalone company. Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here . Not a subscriber? You can sign up here . That’s a lot to have going on all at once! And meanwhile, it’s only just this year that Peacock became an actual profitable business at all — and it’s still pretty far away from being anything like the juggernaut that Netflix is. But what NBCU has, and what Peacock has, that the rest of the streaming industry is still trying to wrap its head around, is live sports. Sports are huge. They held up the cable industry for years, they held up broadcast, and now they’re the big thing that could make streaming a winner for NBC. One thing before we start: You’ll hear me ask Matt about the red company and the blue company. That’s just my way of getting Matt to talk about Netflix and Skydance, the company that now owns both Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. I think he did a good job playing along. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Matt Strauss, chairman of the NBCU Media Group. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Matt Strauss, you are the chairman of the NBCUniversal Media Group. Welcome back to Decoder . Thank you so much, Nilay. It’s great to be back. I am very excited to talk to you. There’s a lot going on in the media. It is a tumultuous time in Hollywood. I have to tell the audience that you and I are speaking minutes after Anthropic filed its S-1 , and all of humanity is going to be turned into AI. Who knows what entertainment we’ll be watching in the future? There’s a lot going on. Let’s start at the very beginning of this. You have a new job since last time you were on the show. Last time, you were the head of Direct-to-Consumer — you were basically the head of Peacock and the other apps inside the family. Now you’re the chairman of NBCUniversal Media Group. What’s the new job? What does that mean? NBCUniversal Media Group is comprised of certain services within NBC. It’s the broadcast network, it’s Bravo, it’s Peacock, it’s NBC Sports. We also have NBC News and Telemundo. One of the things that we recognized, especially when we spun off some of our cable assets last year into Versant, was that the assets we had truly worked better together. NBC has been like a megaphone. Given the reach of NBC, it’s been incredibly strategic in growing Peacock, which is a bit ironic because I think so many people believed that broadcasting was a bit of a relic of the past in this digital world, but it’s actually proven to be the opposite. As things have gotten more fragmented, having a broadcast network is actually a superpower because we’re continuing to see ratings growth. That has been really helpful as we’ve been building out Peacock. But actually, Peacock was also finding new audiences, like cord cutters or people who maybe didn’t grow up watching NBC or some of our cable networks. So, Peacock’s also been really strategic in reaching and driving people back to NBC and Bravo. So, I think that flywheel is where we recognized that we needed to start operating differently. I’ve been a huge advocate of what I like to call “centers of excellence” in how I like to structure the business, which is, content first and platform second. How do we get maximum reach, maximum engagement? That really required us thinking differently about how we were running the business. Essentially, instead of having a programming group within broadcast and a programming group within streaming, we just collapsed the business. Now you’ve got one programming team, one marketing team, one product and technology team, one decision sciences and research team, and one advertising team. They’re all incentivized around continuing to grow the portfolio, get that maximum reach, maximum engagement, and drive top-line revenue. I think that structure, which we put in place about 18 months ago, is contributing to a lot of the success that we’re seeing now. Even if you look at 2026, NBC is the number one network in total viewers. We had an unbelievable early part of the year with “Legendary February,” which you might remember. That’s when we had the Super Bowl, the Milan Cortina Olympics, and the NBA All-Star Game. In 17 days, we reached over 225 million viewers. This summer, we had Love Island , which was the number one show of the summer for streaming. You had the World Cup, which was the number one Spanish-language sporting event in US history on Telemundo and Peacock. We had a show called The Five-Star Weekend , which was our number one scripted drama. Now, we’ve led ourselves into the fall, where we have Sunday Night Football, which has been the number one show for 15 consecutive years. We had a great kickoff with over 25 million viewers. We just had the NBA tip-off last week with the Knicks and the Sixers, which is the number one rated tip-off in NBA history. So, it does feel like we’re firing on all cylinders in how we’re trying to operate with this, again, content-first-platform-second mantra. But just to go one level deeper, a big part of this strategy is figuring out how do we move audiences across platforms. For example, when I mentioned that Love Island was the number one streaming show of the summer, 40 percent of those Love Island viewers also tuned in to watch the World Cup. So, migrating viewers back and forth across the portfolio is a critical part of how we see ourselves continuing to grow. But to effectuate that, you need to structure yourself in a way where people are incentivized along that vision. We’re still evolving as an organization, but I’m really proud of some of the milestones and accomplishments that we’ve made as a team. I love my job. events.title: Anthropic's amended IPO paperwork reveals soaring Q3 revenue and a stunning compute bill
events.summary: Anthropic's fresh S-1 updates complicate its profitability narrative. Oliver Contreras / AFP via Getty Images Anthropic filed an amended S-1 filing on Monday, giving investors a more recent picture of its financials. The update reveals Q3 revenue of nearly $17 billion and an overall operating loss for the period ending September 30. The company also disclosed $895 billion in compute and infrastructure commitments. Anthropic's revenue is soaring. So is the cost to keep Claude running. On Monday, the AI company filed an amended version of its S-1, the public filing that discloses its financials ahead of its much-anticipated initial public offering. The company filed the original paperwork last week. Monday's amendments include the third-quarter numbers that didn't make it into the initial filing: Anthropic generated nearly $17 billion in revenue during the period, a more than $5 billion increase from the prior quarter and roughly 12X year over year. But the compute required to power that growth weighed on the business. Anthropic swung back to a $567 million operating loss in the third quarter, after reporting $974 million in operating income in the second. Anthropic wrote in the filing that its Q3 operating loss was "primarily driven by $5.0 billion of compute under short-term commitments," which it said costs significantly more than comparable multiyear arrangements. The company also disclosed about $895 billion in committed spending on compute and infrastructure — nearly half of it expected by the end of 2030. Anthropic's fresh disclosure illustrates the often shifting economics of the AI race. While their increasingly capable AI products are spurring adoption, the frontier labs are also committing to enormous amounts of computing capacity — which can take years to build and come online — in an effort to meet anticipated demand. Anthropic's compute and infrastructure charges rose to $9.9 billion in the third quarter. That's a 4X increase in one year. Anthropic also reported $2 billion in non-cash charges related to its donation-matching program , where employees can pledge equity awards to charitable causes, and the company matches the pledge with nonvoting Class N shares. The company has not yet disclosed an IPO price range, number of shares, or the size of the offering. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: DoorDash enters the restaurant value wars with a $12 meal deal
events.summary: DoorDash is offering $12 meal boxes in some cities. Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images DoorDash is offering $12 meal deals in some cities. The value boxes include full meals from local restaurants — and no delivery fees. It's the latest entrant into the restaurant value-deal wars. DoorDash is getting into the meal deal game . The delivery service is offering $12 meal boxes in "select areas across more than 20 cities" including Atlanta, Chicago, and Philadelphia, it said on Monday. The meals will be filled by local restaurants and include a protein, vegetable, and carbohydrate. They also don't include a delivery fee and come with "reduced service fees," the company said. The boxes aren't just cheap eats. Like many value-priced options, they're meant to draw customers to restaurants, hoping to get them to order other items or come back later. "Meal Boxes are designed to drive a steady stream of everyday orders and introduce restaurants to new customers," DoorDash said in its statement. The deal is the latest value option for diners. Restaurant chains from McDonald's to Chili's have revamped their meal-deal offerings in recent years as food inflation has squeezed many consumers. Many customers have continued to order food for delivery while cutting their spending in other areas, despite added costs such as delivery fees and tips. DoorDash's $12 boxes might be an acknowledgment that some diners are seeking budget-friendly options and convenience simultaneously. Do you have a story idea about DoorDash? events.title: Bitcoin giant Strategy, unfazed by Binance hack, adds over $65 million BTC to its holdings
events.summary: Strategy, the publicly traded Bitcoin-holding company owned by billionaire Michael Saylor, is treating the market turmoil around last week’s massive Binance hack as a shopping opportunity. On Monday, Strategy announced that it had bought over $65 million worth of Bitcoin over the past week, its largest purchase since late September.  The company’s latest Bitcoin shopping spree ran from Oct. 26 through Nov. 1, when it bought 811 BTC at an average price of roughly $80,800 per coin. Strategy funded the purchases by selling shares of its common stock. It also spent $208 million from its cash holdings to repurchase roughly 2 million STRC shares, which pay investors regular dividends. Midway through Strategy’s buying run, hackers linked to North Korea began siphoning billions of dollars in crypto from Binance, the industry’s largest centralized exchange. They moved most of the roughly $6.3 billion in about 20 minutes, according to crypto intelligence firm TRM Labs. As news of the breach spread across social media Thursday, Bitcoin slid to a low of $76,600. A day before Monday’s announcement, Saylor, Strategy’s executive chairman and an outspoken Bitcoin bull, hinted that the company had added to its stash amid the sharp price drop. “We found room for even more orange,” he wrote in a social media post early Sunday morning, alongside a chart marking Strategy’s purchases against Bitcoin’s price.  Strategy’s purchases overlapped with a week of renewed concern about crypto security, though its disclosure did not specify whether it bought during the price dip. The breach, roughly four times the size of the 2025 Bybit hack—the previous record holder—was carried out by TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit, according to TRM Labs. It followed a string of North Korean crypto heists aimed at bankrolling the regime’s weapons programs . The unprecedented scale challenged the industry’s growing efforts to move beyond its history of hacks and failures. Although Binance moved quickly and publicly pledged to cover customer losses, users on social media questioned what the breach meant for the security of the broader sector. “If Binance can be hacked, then I seriously question how safe this entire industry really is,” one user wrote on X. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Following a sudden GOP slide, a top data scientist’s model gives Democrats 90% odds of taking the Senate as Kansas trends blue in major shock
events.summary: Data scientist Thomas Miller’s site handicapping outcomes for the U.S. Senate races now shows overwhelming odds that the Democrats will take control, numbers much more commanding than even the polls and prediction markets are showing. As of around 9 am ET on Monday, Miller’s site, Virtualtout.io, gave the Democrats a 90% chance of winning at least 51 seats. In recent days, the GOP’s chances of keeping control of the upper chamber have virtually collapsed, dropping from 23% on Oct. 26 to under 10% now. A major reason from the quick downdraft, and a sign of the blue wave’s strength: Democrats now hold the lead in longtime red stronghold Kansas, and have turned Iowa into a virtual tossup. Miller, a professor at Northwestern University, won kudos for correctly forecasting that Democrats would sweep the two Georgia Senate runoffs in early 2021, when the polls and pundits posited GOP wins in both. He scored again by calling a Trump win in 2024. His methodology: Miller starts by incorporating the “prices” posted on the two predictions markets boasting the highest volumes, Kalshi and Polymarket, and translates those numbers into probabilities of a Democrat or Republican. He then deploys multiple time series that examine 10-12 underlying factors that drive the prediction markets, and continually crunches the numbers to forecast their impact going forward. Miller updates the probabilities every 10 minutes, and the numbers stream across the top of Virtualtout.io in a continuous band resembling a stock ticker. The “NowCast” also displays the change over the last 24 hours. Hence, his figures are far more current than the polls. “They all relate to voters’ perception of the performance of the Trump administration,” Miller told Fortune . “That’s the thread running through all the races. The factors include affordability, the economy, and the war in Iran, the issues that motivate voters. The states don’t move independently of one another. When voters’ view of those issues turns more negative, the Republican numbers drop on all the races.” In other words, Trump has effectively nationalized the battle for the U.S. Senate. Miller added that the impact of Trump’s tireless stumping is harder to assess. “People have come to expect certain things from Trump,” he said. “The way he behaves is not a surprise, it’s a continuous thing.” Most of what the president says on the Senate campaign trail, according to Miller, simply reinforces the view of Trump and his party that voters already hold. “Still, there’s no evidence he’s helping,” Miller said. “It doesn’t appear that his appearances are a positive.” One instance where his model found that Trump’s rhetoric backfired: The POTUS’s defense of the ad Vivek Ramaswamy ran in Ohio featuring the mother of his Democratic opponent Amy Acton severely criticizing her daughter. “Following Trump’s praise of the ad, we saw a huge drop in the Republican percentage,” Miller noted. Republican numbers have dropped big time in almost all the key races He pointed out that in the last 10 days, “a lot of contests are moving a little bit” in the Democratic direction from day to day, but the cumulative gains are substantial. In the five elections where the Democrats have long harbored chances for a flip, the GOP stands below 30% in all of them, from a high of 28.4% in Alaska to a low of 2% in North Carolina. The Republicans’ best chance comes in Maine, where incumbent Susan Collins sits at 34.7%. In Michigan, the probability of a Republican flip via beating Abdul El-Sayed has faded from over one-third in mid-September to a current count of 24.5%. The Miller model now points to high possibility of Democratic wins in states that, until a few days ago, the GOP counted on as surely in their column. “Those are the races I’ve been watching closely and the move towards the Democrats in the last few days is surprising a lot of people,” says Miller. In the Iowa run for an open seat, Republican Josh Turek held an almost 62% shot at victory as of Sept. 17; now, he’s dropped to 51.6% as his opponent Ashley Hinson pulls almost even. In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall looked on track for easy re-election just two months ago at around 75%. His number’s dipped to 43.9%, and suffered a 7.1% drop just in the past 24 hours. Miller highlighted that Virtualtout.io and its NowCast will keep running all through Election Day, and will be first to call races, mainly based on its analysis of the swings in the betting odds. Of course, the Republicans could hang on by keeping Kansas and Iowa, winning Maine where their odds are still decent, and defying the probabilities in Texas or one other key state. It’s a narrow path that in recent days now looks far narrower as Midwestern strongholds swing blue. This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Ryanair CEO anticipates European airfare prices up as much as 20% next year
events.summary: The CEO for Ryanair expects European airfare prices may climb as much as 20% next year as jet fuel prices rise The CEO for Ryanair expects European plane ticket prices may climb as much as 20% next year with the conflict in the Middle East ongoing. “So we’re facing 2027 where we have much higher oil prices... I think they’re going to get passed on in significantly higher airfares,” CEO Michael O’Leary said in a Monday interview on CNBC. The price of jet fuel has been extremely volatile after the U.S. and Israel launched attacks on Iran . Jet fuel has risen even faster than oil during the war, reflecting both higher crude prices and tight supplies of the refined fuel that is one of the largest operating expenses for airlines. Carriers have cut some less profitable flights and raised fares and baggage fees, although major U.S. airlines said higher passenger revenue initially covered only part of their soaring fuel costs. Globally, jet fuel averaged about $99 a barrel on Feb. 27, the day before the war began , according to the International Air Transport Association’s Jet Fuel Price Monitor. Prices more than doubled to $209 by early April, fell for nearly three months and reached $195 a barrel in mid-September following their renewed ascent, IATA said, citing data from S & P Global Energy Platts. The global average jet fuel price is currently hovering around $196 a barrel. The IATA expects fuel to account for nearly one-third of airline operating expenses this year, up from about a quarter in 2025. Ryanair said Monday that it doesn't expect European short haul airfares to fully offset anticipated increases in its fuel bill for next year, so it is reviewing its costs and may have to impose temporary pay freezes, lower crew ratios and use more artificial intelligence to get further productivity for back office and support functions. events.title: China steps up Middle East diplomacy with Iran and Oman meetings
events.summary: Beijing urges dialogue on US-Iran war, sends envoy to Gulf as Xi hosts first Omani head of state visit since 1978. China is stepping up its diplomatic efforts in the Middle East, including over the US-Israel war on Iran , following a lapse in activity. Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Monday met a senior Iranian security official in Beijing, while President Xi Jinping hosted Oman’s Sultan Haitham bin Tariq for a landmark state visit. list 1 of 3 China’s political elite gather for talks on Communist Party discipline list 2 of 3 Iran’s calculations as US escalation looms: Trust, midterms, Hormuz list 3 of 3 How to stop the US-Israel war on Iran Wang told Ali Bagheri Kani, deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, that dialogue and negotiation remained “the only viable path forward” as conflicts in the region “drag on and risk further spillover”. He also reaffirmed China’s support for Iran’s sovereignty and security. Beijing has consistently blamed the US and Israel for starting the conflict. “China is very close to Tehran; it is the biggest trading partner of Iran, the biggest customer of Iranian crude,” said Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing. However, Beijing’s diplomacy efforts have recently been stalled, she noted. “It’s been a few weeks or even months [in which] China really hasn’t done much diplomatically towards … ending the war,” Yu said. The meetings on Monday appear to illustrate that China is growing impatient with the lack of progress. “I think China is very frustrated, and it wants to be seen to enter [the process],” Yu said. Reflecting the step up in activity, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs announced on Monday that Zhai Jun, Beijing’s special envoy on the Middle East, will visit Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia this month. Meanwhile, Xi received Sultan Haitham, the first Omani head of state to visit China since the two countries established diplomatic relations in 1978. The Chinese president said the Middle East and Gulf “should not become an arena for great-power rivalry and geopolitical conflict”. Sitting across from Iran on the Strait of Hormuz, Oman is a key player in navigation on the strategic waterway, through which one-fifth of global energy exports traversed before the US-Iran war restricted traffic. China is one of the world’s largest energy importers. Xi described bilateral ties with Oman as being at a “new historical starting point”. During the visit, China and Oman signed 14 cooperation documents, covering areas including artificial intelligence, green energy and supply chains, along with a currency swap agreement. In a joint statement, they called for safe navigation to resume through Hormuz and urged the US and Iran to restart dialogue. Yu said the conflict had made the relationship “more of a priority for both sides”, particularly given the disruption to China’s energy imports. “Oman is particularly important because many of its ports are outside the strait,” she said.

events.title: As Sergey Brin, Larry Page and the ultra-rich flee California, one 34-year-old tech billionaire is ‘not running’—he ‘wants to fight’ for the state
events.summary: California’s proposed billionaire tax has sent some ultra-rich residents flocking to other states—but tech entrepreneur Palmer Luckey is opting to stay put. While the 34-year-old cofounder of Oculus VR and Anduril opposes the bill, he still believes it’s worth it to stay.  “I think that this tax act, if you can call it a tax, is going to cause a lot of problems,” Luckey said during a press conference last week, reported by TechCrunch . “It’s causing a lot of people to run who I don’t want to be running. It’s going to cause companies that I work with to leave the state, which is a problem for me.” “As of right now, though, I’m not running. I am staying,” he continued. “I think California is something special. I want to fight for California.” The entrepreneur raised in Long Beach has nurtured all of his biggest career wins in the Golden State.  He founded his first company Oculus in Irvine, California back in 2012, joining the billionaire club just two years later when Facebook bought the virtual reality business in a deal estimated to be worth $2 billion. And one of his newer ventures, defense tech firm Anduril headquartered in Costa Mesa, California, was valued at $90 billion earlier this month following an employee tender offer.  Now, Luckey has a net worth of around $5.9 billion, according to Forbes —but he isn’t fleeing his home state to protect his fortune. Luckey said that he doesn’t mind the idea of paying more in taxes, but takes issue with the bill’s sponsor, a union under United Healthcare Workers, wanting to leverage the tax money “for their uses,” and questions how the bill would assess what is owed. Prop 40’s sponsors have stated that the money will be used to improve California’s “health care, education, and food assistance.” He is also concerned about illiquid and unsold assets being grouped into his fortune, likening it to a “seizure of future wealth.” The tax hike, Proposition 40, has caused quite a stir; while many successful peers like Google cofounder Sergey Brin and former CEO Eric Schmidt have flocked to tax-friendly states, others like Luckey still believe that staying in California is worth the hit.  “This has been a point of friction between me and some of my other billionaire friends,” the millennial founder said. “They’ve said things like ‘Palmer, you have to have solidarity for us. You can’t enable these really bad policies. If you stay and if you don’t leave, it’s going to show them that there’s no consequences.’ I empathize with that argument, but it’s not one that I’m going to participate in right now because I still believe that we can fix things.” Fortune reached out to Anduril for comment.  California’s Prop 40 has some billionaires fleeing the state Notable business figures in California have been waging war over Proposition 40: a one-time 5% tax on residents with assets over $1 billion. The coastal state hopes this will increase temporary revenue by tens of billions spread over several years to fund health care and education—and California is home to the highest number of billionaires in the U.S.  The fate of Proposition 40 will be decided by voters tomorrow during America’s midterm elections.  And some of California’s ultrarich have spent sizable fortunes to strike it down. Tech billionaires have raised more than $340 million and spent more than $1 million daily in a campaign to defeat Prop 40, according to The Guardian ; Palantir cofounder Peter Thiel, ex Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash leader Tony Xu, Stripe chief exec Patrick Collison all put money towards the opposition campaign.  Before Prop 40’s January 1 2026 residency cutoff, a slew of billionaires also fled the state. Google cofounders Larry Page and Brin moved their business entities to Florida and Nevada, and Travis Kalanick, the former CEO of Uber , also changed addresses to Austin.  Others like Palantir’s Peter Thiel and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg have already relocated from California to more tax-friendly areas. Jensen Huang is also choosing to stay: ‘I’m not afraid of paying taxes’ While Prop 40 has emboldened some to leave, there’s a vocal cohort of billionaires like Luckey choosing to stay.  Jensen Huang, the world’s ninth-richest person with an eye-watering $180 billion net worth, recently said that “the more you make, the more taxes you pay. And I’m okay with that.”  The leader of the world’s largest chip company reasoned that he’s the “American Dream,” and success wouldn’t have been possible without the opportunities the U.S. afforded him. He was able to pursue a high-level education, create a company, pursue his dreams, and meet the people that “made Nvidia possible.”  “The fact that I can afford to pay $8 billion in taxes over five years is a privilege,” Huang told CBS Sunday Morning last month. “I’m not afraid of paying taxes. I’m just afraid of being poor.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: OpenAI is already pitching 2028 hopefuls on how to talk about AI
events.summary: Chris Lehane, OpenAI Chief Global Affairs Officer, speaks during the 2026 Semafor World Economy conference in Washington, DC. Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images OpenAI is working to shape how White House hopefuls think and talk about AI. A memo from OpenAI's top lobbyist, obtained by POLITICO , argues that candidates need a governing philosophy for AI. Chris Lehane encourages candidates to show voters how they will keep humans at the helm of consequential decisions. OpenAI's top lobbyist is privately telling prospective 2028 candidates that artificial intelligence will define their bids for the White House. In a memo circulated among some contenders and obtained by POLITICO — which, like Business Insider, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — Chris Lehane argues that candidates need a governing philosophy for AI, not just talking points about key issues dominating the campaign. He warns that Democrats, in particular, could find themselves on the wrong side of the debate if they oppose the infrastructure needed to build the technology. A fight over data centers could have consequences far beyond local projects, Lehane warns. If the US loses its AI lead to China, he writes, "This could well be the 2028 version of the 2002 vote to go to war in Iraq." The memo , which has not previously been reported, is an attempt by the AI giant to shape how White House hopefuls think and talk about the technology as both parties begin preparing for the next presidential race. It was sent to about half a dozen prospective candidates alongside a few members of Congress and prominent political operatives, according to a person with knowledge of the memo granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. OpenAI declined to comment. Lehane, a veteran Democratic political operative who was press secretary to then-Vice President Al Gore, argues that candidates should offer voters a middle course between unchecked AI development and putting control of the technology in the hands of a "self-appointed elite." "The candidate who can articulate a compelling third path between those who would let AI advance without speed limits, and those who would keep control over the technology in the hands of a self-appointed elite, will have an opportunity to define a new contract for this new era." He compares the current era to the New Deal of 1932, saying the next president will have an opportunity to reimagine "the relationship between people and a transformative new force in their lives." Lehane thinks that AI is already showing up in the 2026 election with unpopular data centers serving as a proxy for affordability concerns that extend beyond the infrastructure build-out. He also sees the rapid technological progress as a driver of anxiety among an electorate who feel as though the social contract has been "fractured." But according to Lehane, the landscape will be different in 2028 as its capabilities continue to advance and Americans become more familiar with the technology. In the memo, he encourages candidates to show voters how they will keep humans at the helm of consequential decisions. He also urges them to address what the tax code should look like in the AI era, how children should be protected, whether AI can make life more affordable and whether the US can maintain its technological lead over China. "A world in which America leads will look very different from one in which the Chinese Communist Party sets the pace," Lehane writes. "That doesn't mean every data center is a good project or that communities should accept higher electricity costs. It means policymakers must solve those problems rather than treating infrastructure itself as the problem." With the shadow primary already underway and the race only expected to intensify in the weeks after the midterm elections, both parties will be forced to grapple with what their approach to AI is, and each party's eventual standard-bearer will help set the tone. "The successful candidates won't promise to stop the future or simply trust everything will work out," Lehane writes. "They'll show Americans how to shape that future and benefit from it." This story originally appeared on POLITICO and is courtesy of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network, which harnesses the resources of the company's newsrooms to publish ambitious scoops, investigations, interviews, opinion pieces, and analysis. It allows journalists — including those from POLITICO, Business Insider, WELT, BILD, Onet, and Fakt — to collaborate on major stories for an international audience of hundreds of millions across platforms. events.title: Lobster industry caught in Maine’s political headwinds before US midterms
events.summary: Importance of governor races in midterms Senator Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson clash over tariffs and their impact on Maine’s economy. For half a century, day after day, he has taken his boat and headed into the cold waters of the North Atlantic off the coast of the US state of Maine , hauling the crustaceans from the ocean and bringing them ashore. From there, they are loaded onto trucks, sent to processing facilities and shipped to restaurants around the world. list 1 of 4 US Senate nominee Platner halts campaign after assault allegations list 2 of 4 ‘Foreign policy is the economy’: How Iran war is shaping US midterm vote list 3 of 4 All you need to know about US midterms 2026 list 4 of 4 Tracking the money: The biggest donors in the 2026 US midterm elections Horner has voted for United States President Donald Trump three times and stands by his vote. He supports the president’s rollback of environmental regulations affecting commercial fishing operations like his own. While he supports Trump on one policy, however, he’s disappointed in another – the president’s antagonistic approach to Canada, which borders Maine and is deeply entwined with the state’s lobster industry. “I never heard anything about all this Canadian animosity in the campaign. I don’t know where that came from,” Horner told Al Jazeera. “As far as taking on Canada in this huge hostile trade war, I’m totally against it.” Horner has watched the price of bait climb along with the cost of the diesel needed to power his boat. Far beyond Maine’s rocky coastline, tensions involving the US, Iran, Russia and Ukraine have helped drive up global diesel prices, which hit record highs in September. Before the US and Israel began their war on Iran, diesel averaged $3.08 per gallon (3.8 litres) and has now more than doubled to $6.29. Horner’s business is just one small fish in a very big pond. Maine’s lobster fisheries brought in $461m in 2025, underpinning a seafood economy that is dependent on the crustacean. But that industry was put on edge when Trump announced sweeping tariffs on Canadian goods, prompting retaliation from Ottawa. In August, Trump imposed tariffs on $20bn worth of Canadian goods while alleging unfair treatment of US products. Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs , but lifted the levies on seafood later that month. Maine’s peak lobster season runs from late summer into early autumn, when catches surge and local processors can struggle to keep up. To handle the volume, much of the catch is sent to Canada for processing into lobster tails, meat and bisque before some of it returns to the US for sale. An estimated 60 percent of Maine’s lobster catch is processed in Canada. “As soon as those tariffs went out, the screaming, literally and figuratively, in Maine and Canada was quite loud,” Justin Snyder, who works in the Maine lobster industry and is also a Democratic strategist, told Al Jazeera. While seafood was ultimately exempted from the US-Canadian trade war, the tariff threat raised fears in the industry and put pressure on Susan Collins, the Republican senator who is in a close midterm election race with Democrat Troy Jackson. The race for the US Senate seat is tight. Jackson, the former president of the Maine State Senate, holds a very slight advantage. A recent CNN poll suggested Jackson was leading by four percentage points, and a Marist poll indicated he was leading by two points, which is within the margin of error. Collins has built a reputation in the Senate for voicing concerns about Trump’s policies and rhetoric but supporting his agenda when it comes time to vote. Collins has voted in line with Trump’s position on 92 percent of Senate votes during his second term, which began in January 2025. However, Collins has broken with Trump on tariffs on several occasions. In April 2025, she voted to overturn tariffs on Canadian goods. Later that month, she supported a resolution to end Trump’s sweeping global tariffs, and in August, she pushed back against the White House over tariffs affecting seafood. Beyond tariffs on Canadian goods and other imports, levies on foreign steel and aluminium have added costs for Maine’s lobster industry, which relies on the metals to manufacture the traps used by fishermen. Jackson has been an outspoken critic of Trump’s tariffs, arguing that Collins has not done enough to challenge the president’s trade measures. During their most recent debate, Collins touted her efforts to secure tariff exemptions for products such as road salt. Jackson pushed back, saying, “We can’t eat road salt.” Trump removed 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods, including certain machinery and packaging products, on October 30, ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. At the same time, his administration extended the tariffs to other Canadian goods, including certain waste products. “The Canada tariffs are just the dumbest thing in the world.

events.title: I turned 60 and realized I wasn't ready to retire. I became a flight attendant and started my third career.
events.summary: Richard Woulfe retrained as a flight attendant at 61. Courtesy of Richard Woulfe Richard Woulfe became restless soon after his 60th birthday and wanted a new challenge. He launched into the third chapter of his life as a flight attendant for a major US airline. Woulfe said that Gen X qualities , such as flexibility and a willingness to listen, have helped him. This story is based on an interview with Richard Woulfe , 63, a flight attendant from Fort Worth, Texas. It has been edited for length and clarity. I have always been in the travel business. Starting out in 1986, I worked at an event management company that often organized employee reward trips for large corporations. We offered VIP transportation, including meet-and-greets at airports, as well as luxury food and beverages. Have you got a story about launching a career in mid or later life? Please email Jane Ridley at jridley@businessinsider.com if you'd like to be interviewed by Business Insider. I enjoyed it very much, but I wanted to monetize my passion for scuba diving, which led me to become certified as an instructor at 19. Around 2008, I moved into my second career selling scuba diving trips. They were mostly done through high-end dive shops and targeted at affluent customers. I visited the Maldives more than 15 times They wanted to explore countries like Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, and the Philippines . It was fun to accompany them to places like the Maldives, which I must have visited more than 15 times. Woulfe traveled across the world in his previous jobs. Courtesy of Richard Woulfe Then the pandemic struck. My main markets shut down as destinations such as Thailand imposed travel restrictions. I returned to the city of Chicago , where I grew up, and took a little time off, spending time with my mom and dad. Dad, in his early 90s, was quite sick, and I wanted to be with him as much as possible. After I turned 60 in March 2023, Mom looked at me one day and asked if there was something wrong. I told her I wasn't depressed, but I was feeling restless. I texted my friend, who had been a flight attendant since 2018, for advice She encouraged me to get back to work. Life expectancies are long these days — I could live for another 35 years — and I didn't want to retire. I read that some of the major US airlines were hiring thousands of flight attendants. I texted my friend, who had been a one since 2018, for advice. His reply was two words long: "Do it!" he said. I'd been a passenger on countless flights and loved the transport industry since childhood. As a kid, I was more interested in the process than the destination. How about I drew on my experience of travel and hospitality for a third career as a flight attendant? Woulfe, pictured with his dad, had a long history of travel as a passenger. Courtesy of Richard Woulfe I applied to various airlines and had one face-to-face interview within 72 hours. However, there was a lot of back-and-forth in my personal life because of Dad, and it took me a while to make a solid commitment to a particular carrier. At 61, I started the six-week training program in April 2024. Language is important to me, and I don't like to refer to people as "Older than 50." Instead, I call people like me "Better than 50." Gen X is willing to acquire new skills I thought I was going to be the only "Better than 50" person. To my surprise, there were candidates ages 64, 67, and even 70. I believe that Gen-X has maturity, flexibility, and a strong work ethic. We're willing to acquire new skills to stay in the job market and make money. Woulfe, preparing for his duties aboard a flight. Courtesy of Richard Woulfe They also have life experience and the ability to listen. My mantra is to say, "I hear you," whenever a passenger raises an issue. People want to feel heard. The last two years have been amazing. I enjoy not knowing where I'm going next. It gives me an opportunity to learn about different locations. Flight attendant work is not for everyone I've been to international cities such as San José, Costa Rica; Guadalajara; Vancouver; and Montreal . Still, I've had fulfilling times in small, domestic places like Colombia, South Carolina, and Durango, Colorado. Flight attendant work is not for everyone. Still, my message for anyone considering a lifestyle pivot is this: If something is calling you — something you haven't done before — it's worth taking a risk. events.title: Billionaire investor Howard Marks lays out why valuing AI companies like Anthropic is so tricky
events.summary: Howard Marks is the co-founder and co-chairman of Oaktree Capital Management. Christopher Pike/Bloomberg via Getty Images Billionaire investor Howard Marks laid out why it's so difficult to value AI businesses. It's hard to predict what a company like Anthropic will be doing or earning in five years, he said. Marks said the AI boom's recent "stumbles" have "somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility." Howard Marks just highlighted one of the hardest parts of investing in AI companies. Value investors like him try to project a company's earnings five years from now to gauge whether a stock is attractively priced today, he said on "Bloomberg: The China Show" on Monday. "I don't think we can do that with much of AI," Marks said. He gave the example of Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude that recently filed to go public in what could rank among the biggest IPOs in history. "Can we really fool ourselves into thinking we know what it will do five years from now?" Marks asked. "And yet, that doesn't mean we don't want to be in it." Anthropic's cofounders wrote in its IPO prospectus that they "will be constantly seeking to reinvent our business, releasing new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones." They noted that advances in AI enabled chatbots in 2022 and coding agents last year, and this year have been gradually making it viable to use agents for broader knowledge work and scientific discovery. Marks, the billionaire cofounder and co-chairman of Oaktree Capital Management, said that in six decades of investing, he's never dealt with something like AI "in terms of its inscrutability, its novelty, its speed of progress , its autonomy, and its unpredictability." However, he noted the AI boom's recent "stumbles" — such as investors dumping Alphabet and Amazon stock last week on concerns about their AI spending — have "somewhat burst the bubble of infallibility." The Nasdaq 100 slumped by roughly 1,400 points, or nearly 5%, over the course of Thursday and Friday last week. But the tech-heavy index is still up about 13% this calendar year, and has soared by around 160% since the end of 2022, from under 11,000 points to just below 28,400 points. Marks, who's been sharing wisdom and advice in his memos for over 35 years, said it's "very healthy" that investors are trying to control their excitement and be a little more "thoughtful" and "skeptical." The distressed-debt investor said that instead of worrying about how a stock is performing on a single day, investors should " put together a portfolio of things that will work in the long run, and stay with it." "There is no reward in the investment business for hyperactivity," he said. One of Marks' key influences, Warren Buffett , has championed long-term investing for decades. The conglomerate he built, Berkshire Hathaway, finished building large stakes in Coca-Cola and American Express in the mid-1990s, and hasn't touched them since. Buffett, who stepped down as Berkshire's CEO at the end of 2025 and as its chairman this September, issued a similar caution about the AI boom in a July interview. "It's tough to find values when everybody is preferring gambling," the legendary bargain hunter said. He also emphasized that so-called hyperscalers such as Meta and Microsoft are spending hundreds of billions of dollars on microchips, data centers, and other AI infrastructure, describing that as "real money." Another prominent value investor, Michael Burry of "The Big Short" fame, has repeatedly warned that AI is a bubble destined to burst. He's made the case on his Substack that AI companies are overinvesting, and pointed to their aggressive accounting, hidden debts, and circular deals as red flags. events.title: I tried Chipotle's 'family meal' deal. It was a better value than I expected.
events.summary: I ordered Chipotle's family meal to see what I'd get and whether it would be a great value. Savannah Born I tried Chipotle's chicken family meal , which cost $52 and is meant to serve four to six. Although I wish we'd gotten more salad and that my chips hadn't been missing, I was impressed. Ultimately, we were able to make six well-portioned, tasty meals at home for less than $10 each. Even though I usually cook at home and avoid fast (and fast-casual) food whenever possible, I have a hard time turning down Chipotle. I build the same salad bowl every time I go, so I don't pay much attention to the rest of the menu. It wasn't until I saw Chipotle's strange fever-dream of an advertising campaign that I learned about its family meals. Simply put, it involved a 3-foot reusable version of its takeout bag. Bizarre, yes, but it worked. Curious about the details (and the "big ass" bag mentioned in the advertisement), I did some Googling. Turns out, Chipotle launched its family meals in August 2025. The build-your-own experience is a major appeal. Per Chipotle , "People can create any bowl, salad, or soft taco to their liking and dietary preferences." Nachos were also suggested. Since I love salads and my partner prefers bowls, it seemed like the perfect setup. Plus, family meals are designed to serve four to six people — which, in my two-person household , could mean dinners for days. So, I ordered a chicken family meal online, complete with all the default items. Here's how it shook out. My local Chipotle had a few options for family meals. Savannah Born Even though I set my sights on its $52 chicken meal, Chipotle also offered steak and sofritas meals featuring the same standard fixings: rice (white or brown) beans (black or pinto) cheese romaine lettuce large chips 10 soft-flour tortillas three dips (choices included sour cream and four different salsas) one premium side (either guacamole or queso). The meals ranged from $52 to $63, depending on the protein. It's worth noting that these family meals are all digital-only, so they have to be ordered through the app or website. Ordering online felt seamless. Savannah Born Since I stuck with the baseline, customization-free spread, ordering took only a few clicks. My lineup included white rice, black beans , cheese, romaine lettuce, large chips, and 10 flour tortillas, plus sour cream, pico de gallo, and hot salsa as toppings. Then, I scrolled to the "extras" section. I could add another protein and up to seven extra toppings, but they'd increase the total price. An extra protein portion, listed as serving two people, ranged from $7 to $10. Extra toppings like salsa and cilantro lime sauce cost an additional $2.35 to $3 apiece. For more so-called "premium" toppings like guacamole or queso, I'd pay a whopping $5.90 each. Since it was just my partner and me, I skipped everything additional. I'd only splurge on extras for a gathering. Then, I walked to pick up my order. Savannah Born I had the option to have my order ready in as little as 10 minutes, but I scheduled my pickup for half an hour out and then walked to the restaurant. When I arrived, I spotted two bags with my name on them (literally). Since I'd already paid online, I was in and out in under a minute. The food was still warm after a quick stroll home. The bags had everything needed for a six-person party. Savannah Born Inside the bags, I found five containers and four cups arranged neatly. They also included napkins, utensils, and six serving bowls — so I assumed the meal was prepared for six people, not four. The meal felt excessive for four and perfect for six. Savannah Born I'm not going to complain about too much food, but divided into four portions, the bowls would've been hard to finish. Six servings felt like the magic number … for the most part. Split into six bowls, each would get a moderate amount of chicken, rice, and beans. The same held true for the sour cream, guacamole, and salsas. The portion of shredded cheese seemed quite generous — probably enough for eight — though in my household, bonus cheese is never an issue. The amount of lettuce, however, felt somewhat meager for six. Making salads didn't seem very practical. The bowls were easy to customize. Savannah Born Salads are my go-to at Chipotle , but if I wanted to build more than two, I'd be out of lettuce. Even though the chain's press release mentioned creating salads , the shredded greens seemed more like a topping, not a base. Instead of depleting the entire container of greens on the first night, I followed my partner's lead and made a bowl. When reached for comment, a Chipotle representative said that the family meal includes 8 ounces of lettuce that's "intended as a topping for bowls rather than as a base for salads." He later said it could be used for a salad, but it's not intended to be enough for four to six salad entrées, which are usually served on a base of Chipotle's Supergreens mix. I created a bowl based on six servings, and the portion felt generous. Savannah Born I built my bowl using approximately one-sixth of each ingredient. The bowl came out about the same size as one I'd order at Chipotle , and to my delight, it tasted similar, too. Flavor and texture-wise, this at-home bowl seemed identical to the in-store version. The chicken was tender and well-seasoned, and the rice stayed firm, not soggy. As usual, Chipotle's black beans were beautifully spiced. It wasn't a big deal, but I needed a microwave for the tortillas. Savannah Born I didn't expect to need to use appliances for my takeout meal, but Chipotle's tortilla bag recommended a 60- to 90-second zap in the microwave. Thankfully, I was at home and therefore had access, but it seemed impractical for a portable meal. Hassle aside, I wasn't a huge fan of microwaving food that was in a plastic package — to get the proper experience, however, I followed the instructions. Unfortunately, my chips were missing. The chips were missing from my order this time. Savannah Born My only major gripe with this meal was the chips, or lack thereof. A large bag should have been included, and the receipt even listed one, but the crunchy snack was nowhere to be found. Honestly, I'm still disappointed. I wish I'd noticed when I was still in the store, as I'm sure it would've been an easy fix. If I'd had chips, we could've also used our toppings to build nachos and polish off more of the guac and salsa. Next time, I'd swap guacamole for queso. Savannah Born Chipotle's iconic six-ingredient guacamole tasted incredible, but without a lime on hand (if you know, you know), it began browning a few hours later in the fridge. Unfortunately, this is common for any fresh guac . Although it was still fine to eat, the oxidation made it unappetizing. Since my partner and I couldn't polish off an entire cup of guacamole in one go, we'd be better off with queso next time, which stores perfectly in the fridge. Overall, I'd order a family

events.title: Wall Street's Fear Index is doing something strange. Here's what it means for stocks
events.summary: Stocks wrapped their worst week since June on Friday, but a group of the most sophisticated options analysts agree the reaction in the options market was oddly calm. While the Cboe Volatility Index (VIX) , often referred to as a so-called fear index, did touch its highest intraday level since April on Friday, it quickly retreated and closed at 19.4. Its rollover came even as the S&P 500 finished the day down nearly 2%. For that size of a decline in stocks, the 2.2-point move in VIX was "relatively muted," according to SpotGamma's Brent Kochuba, whose analysis suggests VIX should have jumped closer to 2.6 points, based on a study of 126 selloffs since 2018. Even in the Nasdaq 100 Index , where implied volatility increased for most options contracts, there were key exceptions. Prices on put contracts that are between 20% and 50% out-of-the-money were higher on a volatility basis after the sell-off on Oct. 16, according to data shared by Nasdaq's Kevin Davitt. So not only did traders not pile into S&P 500 Index options on Friday, they were also especially choosy with which Nasdaq hedges they bought. For example, in the Nasdaq, puts were more expensive two weeks ago, according to Nations Indexes data. And out-of-the-money S&P 500 Index puts "just aren't being chased-into at this moment," writes Nomura managing director Charlie McElligott, indicating investor calm in the face of falling stocks. "Index options skew hasn't been particularly reactive to the few days of spot equities selloff this week, and even where it has, it's partially a function of call vol getting mushed," McElligot said in a note to clients on Friday. One explanation for the lack of hedging could be that asset managers are quickly selling stocks instead of using options to protect those stocks from further decline. One popular chart making the rounds over the weekend came from Morgan Stanley's prime brokerage. According to the firm's data on long-short active managers, total global gross equity exposure is down 8% from its most recent peak, the biggest drawdown in at least ten years. "Long/short has experienced a massive de-levering event," said Zed Francis, CIO of Chicago-based Convexitas. "Buy the shorts, sell the longs. If you were closer to cash than you were before, no need to hedge. I believe this is the main reason implied volatility has remained quiet during an increased-stress month."

events.title: AI didn't sink Weil. It could prevent the next Big Law failure.
events.summary: Clockwise from left: Barbara Melby, Oz Benamram, Greg Dickason, David Wang, Melia Robinson, Michael Zuckert, Erick Rabin, Logan Brown, Eric Greenberg, Bruce Karpati, Sharon Crane, Michael Gerstenzang, Sean Fitzpatrick, Avi Gesser, Ilona Logvinova, and Shermin Lakha. Carl Timpone/BFA A version of this story originally appeared in the Legal AI Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly Legal AI Insider newsletter here . Two stories have dominated the legal industry this year: artificial intelligence and lateral hiring. I tend to report on the first. But I gained a new appreciation for the musical chairs of Big Law while putting together the seating chart for a private lunch of lawyers I hosted last Thursday. I tried to make sure lawyers who had defected from one firm weren't seated next to their old boss. You know, to keep the peace. We came together at Business Insider's The Long Play event to talk about what law firm reinvention looks like in practice and how those experiments are changing relationships with clients. LexisNexis sponsored the lunch; I curated the guest list and led the conversation. We couldn't ignore the $2.1 billion elephant in the room. Sean Fitzpatrick is CEO of LexisNexis North America, UK, and Ireland. Carl Timpone/BFA Hours earlier, Weil Gotshal, one of the country's most storied law firms, had announced plans to wind down after an exodus of high-profile partners. The 95-year-old institution, which made its name handling some of the biggest bankruptcies in American history, couldn't find a way to save itself. The table seemed to agree: AI didn't kill Weil. But the firm's implosion exposed vulnerabilities that large law firms have always faced. And it raised a question: Could AI make those weaknesses worse? Or could it actually help law firms become less fragile? A spokesperson for Weil did not respond to a request for comment. AI-as-a-tourniquet Eric Greenberg is the general counsel of Cox Media Group. Carl Timpone/BFA Big Law is made up of enormously profitable institutions. Many have survived wars, recessions, and tectonic shifts in the technology that helps their lawyers work. Yet a handful of departures can set off a chain reaction that threatens to bring the whole thing down in months or weeks. Eric Greenberg, the general counsel of Cox Media Group, argued that law firms have always been vulnerable. But the white-hot lateral market is making them especially so. "This is really a case where you had a run on the bank and people didn't want to be the ones left at the firm," he said of Weil. David Wang, chief innovation officer of Cooley , saw Weil as a reminder that for all the talk about technology upending legal work, Big Law remains a business built on relationships. Star partners have outsize influence because of the clients they bring in and keep happy. When a rainmaker jumps ship, a firm doesn't just risk losing clients and revenue. It can also shed years of knowledge about their businesses and the work they've done together. Avi Gesser is a partner at Debevoise & Plimpton, where he leads its artificial intelligence practice. Carl Timpone/BFA Avi Gesser, a partner at Debevoise & Plimpton who leads the firm's artificial intelligence practice, suggested that the technology could act as a tourniquet for law firms. It might not stop a lawyer from leaving, but it could keep the firm from bleeding out when they do. His firm is increasingly building tools to capture the expertise locked in the heads of its litigators. The bet is that Debevoise can turn that knowledge into an asset belonging to the firm. Greenberg offered a way of thinking about how this might affect client loyalty. "It used to be, 'I got to stick with this person. I love him, and he knows my stuff,'" he said. "Now it's, 'I love them, and the firm knows my stuff.'" 'What do I take with me?' Bruce Karpati, Sharon Crane, and Michael Gerstenzang. Carl Timpone/BFA There's one problem. Why would a lawyer willingly give away the very thing that makes them valuable? Sharon Crane, the president of the Practising Law Institute, raised exactly that concern. "Once I give you everything I know, then if I leave, what do I take with me?" she asked. Gesser pointed out that partners aren't necessarily compensated for spending time teaching the firm's systems everything they know. For firms to make this work, they'll have to rethink how they reward that work. Oz Benamram, chief AI officer at the law firm Pillsbury, added another wrinkle. Partner agreements may need a rewrite, too. Departing partners might want to take the playbooks built from their expertise with them. And clients could stake a claim to that knowledge, too. Melia Robinson holds a copy of Oz Benamram's book, "Law, Reinvented." Carl Timpone/BFA Then Michael Gerstenzang, the senior partner at Cleary Gottlieb , introduced a twist. AI might make law firms less dependent on their individual lawyers. But it could also make those lawyers less dependent on the firms. Imagine you're a top M&A partner at Cleary Gottlieb. You have deep ties in the corporate world. You bring its biggest deals to the firm. But you can't execute those deals alone. You need tax specialists to structure transactions, antitrust experts to evaluate regulatory risks, and employment lawyers to handle compensation issues. "It's a team sport," Gerstenzang said. One of the biggest advantages of working at a large law firm is having all that expertise under one roof. Gerstenzang isn't sure that advantage will last. He imagines a future in which that M&A lawyer can use artificial intelligence to handle some of the specialized work they used to rely on colleagues to perform. Suddenly, the infrastructure of a large law firm might not look quite so indispensable. Which leaves Big Law with a paradox: The same technology that could make law firms harder to leave might make it easier for their most valuable lawyers to walk away. events.title: China rolls out support measures to aid struggling stocks
events.summary: China reels from sluggish consumption and property sector debt crisis. China rolled out support to steady weak stock markets after the CSI300 fell 8.5% in October, its worst month since early 2016. The PBOC will use swap operations to inject more than 100 billion yuan, and cut the buyback lending rate to 1% from 1.25%. The CSRC urged big index and tech firms to buy back shares, while the Shanghai Composite rose 1.1% as investors welcomed the measures. BEIJING/SHANGHAI – Chinese regulators have rolled out a handful of measures, from conducting swap operations to upgrading a lending facility for stock buybacks by listed companies, as part of efforts to stabilise struggling capital markets. The authorities also prodded index heavyweights and leading tech firms to try to stabilise their share prices, and are studying plans to ease margin rules to increase market liquidity. China’s central bank and securities watchdog made their announcements on Nov 2 after the benchmark CSI300 Index slumped 8.5% in October, its worst month since early 2016. Persistent weakness in the world’s second-largest economy, reeling from sluggish consumption and a prolonged property sector debt crisis, and sharp falls in tech stocks have hit investor confidence. Local media first reported that regulators had met financial institutions on Nov 2 to discuss tools to support capital markets. Share prices regained ground on Nov 2 in expectation of supportive policies. As part of the measures, the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) said on Nov 2 it would conduct swap operations with financial institutions on Nov 2 that could inject more than 100 billion yuan ( S$19.19 billion ) into the stock market. It will be the third time the PBOC has used the liquidity tool, created two years ago to allow brokers, insurers and fund companies to obtain liquidity for stock purchases. The PBOC also said a re-lending scheme designed to fund share buybacks and purchases would shift from a temporary arrangement to a long-term mechanism. The interest rate of the expanded scheme was cut to 1% from 1.25%. In a separate statement, the China Securities Regulatory Commission urged key index constituents and “dragon head” tech companies to “actively buy back shares” and stabilise market value. The regulator will also prod some newly established exchange-traded funds to “speed up building stock positions”, and encourage fund managers to buy shares in a down-cycle. The new round of PBOC swap operations “sends another strong signal of policymakers’ commitment to safeguarding capital market stability and supporting investor confidence”, said Hao Zhou, a Hong Kong-based analyst at Guotai Haitong Securities. He said global volatility and external uncertainties continued to weigh on investor sentiment. The PBOC said bidding under the Securities, Funds and Insurance Companies Swap Facility would take place on Nov 3 . It said 31 brokers and fund companies had already applied for swaps worth more than 100 billion yuan. The central bank previously conducted such operations in October 2024 and January 2025, injecting a combined 105 billion yuan into the market. The Shanghai Composite Index climbed 1.1% on Nov 2 , its biggest one-day percentage gain since Aug 27. REUTERS

events.title: Omen AI adds liquid know-how in $16 million Aquatic Labs acquisition
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. U.S. data centers use 17 to 19 billion gallons of water to cool their hot-running chips each year — and that number is expected to triple in the next five years, according to The Water Foundation. That’s an expensive and politically tricky proposition for investors throwing billions of dollars at the challenge of scaling up AI. One way to use less water is to do a better job monitoring the cooling fluids, a task that currently involves sending samples away to a laboratory for tests in a multi-day process. Omen AI was founded in 2024 to solve that problem. The company is building a real-time sensor to determine whether valves were failing, or if bacteria growth in the system threatened to choke off water flow. After raising a $31 million Series A in June, Omen is now acquiring competitor Aquatic Labs in a $16 million cash-and-stock deal. The deal came together after Omen founder Zach Laberge was introduced to Aquatic Labs’ CEO Allan Adams by an investor in the filtration space. Both startups were building real-time water sensors with complementary technology: Omen’s sensors looked for elements in the water, while the Aquatic Labs sensor tests its alkalinity. Putting those two technologies in the same sensor creates a “much richer picture of the water and the fluid,” Adams told TechCrunch, while uniting their vision of automating what had previously been a slow, manual process. The combination unites two classic species of founder: Laberge dropped out of high school to pursue his first company, which did similar fluid analysis for large construction machines that depend on hydraulics. Adams was an academic, trained as a physicist, who spent much of his career developing advanced ocean sensing technology as an MIT professor and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institute researcher before starting his company. Now, with Adams as the company’s chief science officer, the combined teams are working to integrate both technologies into one sensor, which they expect to have on the market by early next year. Omen’s initial sensors will be monitoring chips pulling in 250 to 300 MW of power by the end of the year, worth about $5 to $7 billion, Laberge told TechCrunch, with the hope of being installed on the equivalent of 1 GW of chips by the end of 2027. The added value is in uptime: If the fluid system gets out of whack, data center operators typically choose to dump the water rather than risk damage to their expensive equipment. That means shutting down operations until the fluid system is restored, which costs a lot of money. Monitoring lets data center operators use the same fluid for longer, and minimize the costs of a clean up. Adams hopes to see their technologies have an impact outside of data centers as well, telling TechCrunch that “water goes into data centers, and then it comes out and gets dumped into municipal water, and you want that whole process to happen in a way that’s as safe and responsible as possible — and that means you got to measure stuff.” AI companies once estimated as much as $4 trillion would be spent on AI infrastructure by 2030, but some investors have grown skeptical of the buildout , sending hyperscaler stocks plummeting in recent days. Omen’s team isn’t worried about shifting sentiment though, since their work comes after a data center has been built. “We’re working customers on stuff they’re building today or have already built, and so it doesn’t really affect us because all of those projects were financed 12 months ago,” Laberge said. “Our view is, if there’s tightness, this is still going to be the biggest market in human history, even if you sliced it in half.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Africa needs urban planning investment to deal with rapid city growth
events.summary: Sub-Saharan African cities must invest in urban planning to create jobs for their rapidly growing populations, a new World Bank report said. Africa’s urban population is projected to nearly double to 1.7 billion by 2050, with Luanda, Lagos, and Kinshasa expected to lead the growth. Urbanization suggests a surge in the number of young people seeking jobs, creating the need for policymakers to design environments that can “ concentrate firms , workers, land, infrastructure, services, and connectivity,” the bank said. For example, Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial capital, is one of Africa’s centers of tech and finance, but it still lacks much of the essential infrastructure — like efficient transportation — that make for a modern city. This infrastructure deficit is an “important opportunity” to attract private investment if urban planners make the right decisions about today’s underdeveloped lands, the report said. — Alexander Onukwue

events.title: Ninja’s first-ever microwave just replaced two of my kitchen appliances at once
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. I never thought I’d get excited about replacing my microwave, but the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer has made a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one. Combining a microwave with a built-in air fryer, it’s designed to speed up everyday cooking, give leftovers their crunch back and, perhaps best of all, free up some valuable kitchen counter space. Priced at $449.99, it’s certainly not a budget-friendly microwave. But this is no ordinary machine for heating leftover soup. Ninja has paired a 1,000W microwave with a 1,700W air fryer system, powered by its FusionCrisp technology, which combines the speed of microwave cooking with the golden, crispy results you’d typically expect from an air fryer. Think leftover pizza, chicken tenders, fries, and all those foods that tend to turn sad and soggy in a traditional microwave. Instead, the idea is to get food that’s piping hot and juicy on the inside, with a deliciously crisp, golden finish on the outside. In other words, no more choosing between speed and texture. Of course, microwave and air fryer combinations aren’t entirely new. Brands such as Smeg have already explored the concept, while plenty of modern microwaves come with a range of additional cooking functions. What makes the Ninja Crispi Microwave particularly interesting, however, is its FusionCrisp technology, which is designed to bring both cooking methods together rather than simply offering two separate functions. It comes with a 5.5-quart glass cooking dish and a nonstick crisper plate, which sits on top when you want to air fry and crisp up your food. Another part that makes it stand out is that there isn’t a rotating plate inside, opening up a lot more space to cook more dishes at once. It’s not just about reheating leftovers. For example, if you want to make a pasta bake, the microwave can cook the pasta, while the air fryer crisps up the cheese on top. There’s one thing to consider before buying it, though. Measuring 20.3 x 17.56 x 14.1 inches, the microwave is hardly compact. It takes up a fair amount of counter space, so while it could free up room if you’re replacing a separate microwave and air fryer, it’s not necessarily the ideal solution for a small apartment kitchen. Then there’s the $449.99 price tag. That’s a considerable amount to spend on a microwave, particularly when a basic model can handle everyday reheating for a fraction of the cost. But if you’re someone who regularly reaches for both a microwave and an air fryer, the combination could make a lot more sense. events.title: Drilling imminent at Namibia oil deposit, TotalEnergies says
events.summary: Drilling is imminent at Namibia’s Mopane oil deposit, TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné said, putting fresh capital into the southern African country that has emerged as one of the industry’s most closely watched exploration frontiers. Namibia has attracted other energy majors, including Shell and BP, with a series of large offshore discoveries that promise to transform the nation’s Atlantic coast into sub-Saharan Africa’s hottest oil play . The French company, which took control of Mopane in September, will decide in 2028 whether it should be developed after the drilling. TotalEnergies already operates Namibia’s offshore Venus oil deposit, which is much further along than Mopane, with preparation for development underway. Negotiations with the Namibian government over commercial terms for Mopane have delayed a final investment decision, but Pouyanné said he was “optimistic” that it would be concluded. President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah has prioritized value addition to create “decent jobs … and better lives” for Namibians. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng
