events.title: Tribal Leaders Warned Border Wall Construction Would Disturb Native American Remains. They Were Right.
events.summary: Quitobaquito Springs, a rare Sonoran Desert oasis imperiled by border wall construction, is located within 200 feet of the U.S.-Mexico border in Organ Pipe National Monument outside Ajo, Arizona. Anna Watts Lorraine Eiler stood in the blazing August sun, surrounded by reporters, to offer a warning. The Trump administration was racing to erect a second border wall across Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument, southwest of Tucson. If the bulldozers came, she said, they were bound to disturb the final resting places of her family and Hia-Ced O’odham tribal ancestors. “People used to live here,” the 89-year-old said. Fifteen days later, her fears were realized. ProPublica has confirmed that Native American remains were unearthed in Organ Pipe amid soil overturned by border wall contractors. The discovery, unreported until now, was made on Sept. 8, the National Park Service said in a statement. “Following established protocols, the University of Arizona conducted an assessment and confirmed that the remains are human and align with tribal cremation practices,” the agency said. The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act governs the steps agencies must take following an inadvertent discovery of Native American remains on federal land. Those steps include halting any activity that contributed to the discovery until tribal communities are consulted. “The National Park Service is committed to respecting tribal rights and traditions,” the agency went on to say, adding that it was “working diligently to identify the culturally affiliated tribe and ensure the respectful return of the remains, so the tribe may observe their religious and cultural practices.” Eiler was alerted to the discovery by a cultural affairs specialist with the Tohono O’odham Nation, a larger tribe whose reservation is east of Organ Pipe, and later by the Organ Pipe superintendent’s office. Her family discussed what to do next. Ultimately, they decided to hold off on reburying the newly unearthed remains until construction in the area stops, fearing the work will disturb more sites. “​​Who knows what more will come up,” Eiler said in an interview. “They’re going to find remains wherever they dig.” Hia-Ced O’odham elder Lorraine Eiler stands in the shade of a giant saguaro cactus in Organ Pipe National Monument in 2022. Roberto “Bear” Guerra Customs and Border Protection contractors have bulldozed a wide swath of vegetation parallel to the international divide. The agency has fashioned staging areas for heavy equipment by knocking down, uprooting and attempting to transplant select specimens of the monument’s native plants. Eiler was told the remains were found by a park service archaeologist near the base of a saguaro cactus that was still standing. In a statement, CBP said it was advised of the discovery six days after it was made, that its cultural resource specialists examined the area and found no other remains, and that “no additional construction has occurred at this location to date.” The discovery comes amid tensions between the Department of Homeland Security and tribal communities in the Sonoran Desert. In April, border wall contractors bulldozed through a large, well-marked earthen etching, known as the Las Playas Intaglio , that was believed to be at least 6,500 years old. (CBP said the incident was accidental .) Soon after, the department awarded a $1.3 billion contract for construction of a 62-mile border wall across the entirety of the Tohono O’odham Nation. The tribe is fighting the project in federal court and has erected “no trespassing” signs to keep border wall contractors off its land. As ProPublica recently reported, DHS has responded by deploying masked federal agents as escorts for its work crews and conducting aerial surveillance of tribal members. The head of CBP has justified the need for a wall by describing the reservation as “one of the most dangerous smuggling and trafficking corridors on the Southwest border.” Verlon M. Jose, the tribe’s chairman, expressed gratitude that the park service had notified his office of the discovery, but mourned the fact that it was necessary. “When you have mass destruction and disturbance of land taking place where there are clearly sacred sites, cemeteries and other areas of cultural importance, these types of discoveries are bound to happen,” Jose said in a statement. “Every time this happens it is a wound to the heart of all members of the Tohono O’odham Nation — these are our ancestors, our family members — whose remains are being desecrated.” U.S. Rep. Adelita Grijalva, who appeared with Eiler and the chairman at the August news conference, blasted the government for failing to heed their warnings. “Tribal leaders and elders have warned DHS about the devastating consequences of bulldozing through their ancestral lands, beginning with the destruction of the Las Playas Intaglio,” she said in a statement. “For months, those warnings have fallen on deaf ears. Now, we are seeing exactly what they feared: sacred sites destroyed and ancestral burial grounds desecrated.” James T. Watson, curator of bioarcheology in the Arizona State Museum at the University of Arizona, analyzed the remains recovered in Organ Pipe in the field. While he was not authorized to discuss the details of his findings without park service approval, Watson said in an email that he confirmed the remains were human. The evidence suggested they were cremated in a manner consistent with precolonial practices in the region dating back 1,500 years, he wrote.  Under NAGPRA, the graves protection act, Native American remains inadvertently uncovered on park service lands must be immediately secured, Watson explained, and the superintendent of the jurisdiction must notify “all relevant lineal descendants” with “potential cultural affiliation or ancestral ties to the land.” “Work in the immediate discovery area must remain suspended for at least 30 calendar days,” he wrote, while the park service consults with tribal representatives “to determine the disposition and physical treatment of the remains.” Workers clear desert flora to make way for construction of a double border wall in Organ Pipe National Monument. Anna Watts In a region as rich with archaeological sites as the American Southwest, the inadvertent disturbance of Native American remains occurs with some regularity. What sets the discovery in Organ Pipe apart are the extraordinary powers the Department of Homeland Security wields to expedite wall construction in the borderlands. Following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Congress passed the Real ID Act, which included a provision empowering the secretary of DHS to waive any law that might slow border wall construction. In the two decades since, DHS has invoked its powers 66 times, with 60 of those instances occurring under President Donald Trump’s two administrations. events.summary: At Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026, Hang Seng Bank will showcase AI-enabled innovation and partnerships designed to enhance customer experiences while supporting Hong Kong's development as an international innovation and technology centre [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hang Seng Bank will bring AI-powered wealth management, digital banking, investment innovation and an interactive table tennis experience to Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 as it makes its debut with a dedicated exhibition booth at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre on November 2 and 3. Six interactive experiences will showcase innovation across Retail Banking and Wealth Management, Commercial Banking, Markets and Securities Services, Hang Seng Indexes and the bank's partnership ecosystem. One example is Hang Seng's e-Passbook, Hong Kong's first service of its kind, launched in April 2026 with the needs of elderly customers in mind. Another demonstration is a Proof of Concept exploring the potential of bond tokenisation to make fixed-income investments more accessible to retail investors. Tokenisation holds the potential to enable fractionalisation of an underlying bond into smaller digital tokens, lowering the minimum investment required. It may also help streamline transactions and enable faster settlement. Visitors can follow a simulated demonstration investment journey, to experience the conversion of traditional bond into digital tokens. Elsewhere at the booth, visitors can take on a humanoid table tennis robot as part of an AI-wealth management experience. The game introduces visitors to AI-powered personalisation already available through the Hang Seng Mobile App, which provides tailored financial insights and suggestions based on customer profiles and preferences. Its Wealth Overview page and Goal Planner also help customers review their finances and plan ahead. The table tennis connection draws on Hang Seng's more than 35 years of support for local sporting talent. Supporting businesses and investment decisions Hang Seng will also showcase digital services designed to support businesses at different stages of development. An interactive installation takes visitors through an SME owner's journey, with three steps triggering videos covering remote account opening and daily operations, business expansion and wealth management. The bank's capabilities include digital payment solutions, a cross-bank cashflow analysis platform, Hang Seng SME Business Loan, Hang Seng TradePay, alternative data-backed financing and business mobile investment trading.Investors, meanwhile, can explore ThemeFinder, a Gen-AI-enabled solution co-developed by Hang Seng Indexes with an AI innovator from Cyberport's community. The technology identifies thematic investment trends and accelerates index development, improve the efficiency of identifying listed companies and processing relevant data by up to 5 times. The solution also helps maintain consistency across index operating processes and supports data traceability. Visitors can experience how thematic investment themes can be identified in the markets, create simulated personalised indexes and compare their performance against the Hang Seng Technology Composite Index. The showcase will also feature the Hang Seng Technology Index Family and HK-US index series, which combines Southbound Stock Connect-eligible Hong Kong tech stocks with major US-listed tech companies. Connecting Hong Kong's innovation community Its Living Lab programme with HKSTP, for example, launched a second cohort in April 2026 focused on AI applications in retail and commercial banking, providing technology ventures with opportunities to test solutions in banking environments. Such collaborations can move ideas from exploration and pilot programmes towards safe deployment, turning technological advances into solutions that can benefit customers at scale. With deep roots in Hong Kong, Hang Seng is connecting people, ideas and expertise to make banking more accessible, personalised and responsive to changing customer needs.

events.title: More than 400 jobs to be affected under Mater Pathology changes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts More than 400 jobs affected as Mater moves to external pathology providers More than 100 positions at Mater Pathology will be lost the next two months, a spokesperson said. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) More than 400 positions are expected to be affected at Mater Pathology in Brisbane and Springfield as the hospitals transition to an external pathology provider. A spokesperson for the healthcare provider blamed rising costs for the decision. More than 100 positions will be lost in the next two months, with most of the remaining positions ending in 2027. Mater has outsourced its pathology services in a move that will affect more than 400 staff. The announcement was made today, just a month before Christmas. The healthcare provider has blamed rising costs, saying Medicare subsidies have not kept pace with increasing financial pressures over the past decade. Mater says the transition to external pathology providers will affect more than 400 part-time, full-time and casual employees over the next 12 to 18 months. A spokesperson said the change will have no affect on patients. ( ABC News: Mark Leonardi ) Under the new model, pathology services at Mater's Brisbane and Springfield hospitals will be delivered through specialist providers, including Sullivan Nicolaides Pathology and Pathology Queensland. The change will not affect Mater hospitals in Townsville, Mackay, Rockhampton, Bundaberg or the Gold Coast, which already rely on external pathology service providers. A Mater spokesperson said the decision would have "no impact on the high-quality care Mater patients receive". "The pathology model Mater is adopting is used by private hospital operators across Australia and will allow more resources to be directed to the clinical care of our patients. "We are deeply grateful to our Mater Pathology people," the spokesperson said. "This decision is not a reflection on their capability, professionalism or commitment." events.title: Democrats question if X is giving Polymarket preferential treatment
events.summary: Senate Democrats are accusing Elon Musk’s social media platform, X, of giving prediction market Polymarket preferential treatment. “Typically, X allows users to report an ad for a myriad of reasons; however, when attempting to report Polymarket’s ads through the standard X interface, users are denied the option to do so,” Sens. events.title: Elections pose next test for Venezuela
events.summary: Venezuela’s next big test will be whether it can turn the Trump administration’s plan for elections into a genuine transition to democratic rule. And with the US midterms over soon, the issue will soon face renewed interest from Washington. Interim Venezuelan President Delcy Rodríguez held a rare address last week in which she vowed to hold elections — an ambitious promise for a government still navigating political upheaval following the US’ arrest of President Nicolás Maduro in January. But no election date has been set, as opposition leader María Corina Machado emphasized in her own remarks shortly afterwards. Meanwhile, Rodríguez is already signaling an interest in working with Washington, despite some of her public rhetoric, tapping former opposition aide Oliver Blanco as foreign minister. — Shelby Talcott

events.title: Election ‘war rooms’ enter the AI age
events.summary: Both OpenAI and Anthropic will have “war rooms” dedicated to ensuring their platforms provide accurate information about the midterm elections, a first for both companies. The concept of a tech platform “war room” dates back to 2018, when Meta stood one up for the first time amid concerns about the proliferation of election-related misinformation. The AI age has supercharged those threats, which now include deepfake videos and AI-powered search results spreading incorrect information. Case in point: Last week, Google’s AI Mode wouldn’t respond to a query about who won the 2020 election, which the company said they were working to fix . “Teams across the company work year-round on strengthening our election-related safeguards and enforcing our policies. Ahead of the election, we have a dedicated war room monitoring our platform for misuse and ready to quickly respond to any incidents,” an Anthropic spokesperson told Semafor. These efforts will be made more difficult by AI’s unpredictable nature, recent cybersecurity issues, and the tendency of AI search tools to reflect back results users want to see. Former Meta director of public policy Katie Harbath told Semafor that war rooms are “built for dealing with the things we can’t necessarily predict going wrong and you need a quick, established process in terms of triaging.”

events.title: Leading progressive wants Democrats to think big post-midterms
events.summary: A leading progressive lawmaker says his party colleagues need to think big and dare President Donald Trump to veto Democratic bills if they take the majority. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, is pushing for votes on bills to tackle “price gouging, that crack down on utility rates going up, that crack down on politicians profiting off their jobs” — and though he acknowledged some might become law, “if Donald Trump vetoes them, then that’s exactly the platform upon which we beat JD Vance or whoever else in 2028.” House Democratic leaders have sketched out some early priorities for their potential majority, like restoring lapsed health insurance subsidies or reversing cuts to Medicaid; the path beyond that is fuzzier. But the scope of House Democrats’ ambitions will depend on how many seats they pick up, and on Senate control, too. Casar bristled at recent comments by Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who said that Democrats should table bigger policy questions until the 2028 campaign, since Trump is still in the White House and likely to veto their legislation. He argued that pushing the envelope was necessary for Democrats to prove to voters they care. “I don’t want to waste our majority by negotiating down to Trump’s level,” Casar said. And if Democrats take the Senate as well on Tuesday, party-line legislation to circumvent the filibuster should be on the table, Casar said. “We should do a reconciliation bill, or multiple reconciliation bills, and dare Trump on those issues. We should also push for policies that are 80% popular across the country and dare Senate Republicans to vote against them,” Casar added. Some incoming progressive lawmakers have threatened to withhold votes for Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries in a speaker election unless he commits to progressive policy goals. Casar sidestepped a question on that prospect. “I’ve worked very regularly with Leader Jeffries, and I am a supporter,” he said. “Everybody’s vote, of course, is their own, and I would let each member speak for themselves on that question.”

events.title: How Trump's iron grip on the Republican Party put the Senate in play
events.summary: The News Americans are angry about war and prices, and a president’s second midterm is always difficult — but a series of decisions by President Donald Trump has made Republicans’ Senate majority ever-more vulnerable. The mark Trump made on the midterms began in the summer of 2024, when he selected former Ohio Sen. JD Vance as his running mate. Since then, the president’s personnel and political decisions have reshaped the Senate battleground from what looked like an impenetrable red wall into a toss-up. His decision to pick Vance opened up a special election in Ohio that will by the end of this week cost the GOP hundreds of millions of dollars and potentially a Senate seat. Trump’s party-boss mentality in North Carolina, Texas, and South Carolina has further contributed to the yawning battleground. He endorsed Rep. Mike Collins in Georgia’s Senate race against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff — a contest that never really got off the ground after Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, whom Trump tried to take down in a primary in 2022, passed on the race. Ossoff is favored to win. And party insiders blame Trump’s tariffs and war with Iran for creating a volatile Senate map that has left seats in red states like Nebraska and Kansas vulnerable. Republicans could hold the chamber — or lose as many as a half-dozen seats on Tuesday. “Every negative for the GOP this cycle is a downstream effect of Iran,” said a person close to the White House. Republicans can lose up to three seats and still keep Senate control. Trump’s zeal on the campaign trail is undeniable and he helped direct huge sums of money into the midterms, albeit later than many Republicans would have liked. He spent the last weekend capping off a breakneck fall campaign schedule stumping in Iowa and Kansas, two places where the GOP was strongly favored to win a few months ago but now is struggling. “President Trump has a 97% endorsement record and he remains the best turnout machine for our base voters,” said Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre. Trump is hosting nearly 20 tele-rallies in the last days of the campaign, in addition to his almost-daily travel for rallies over the past month. The White House has sought to emphasize the administration’s accomplishments on issues like the border, crime, and US investment and manufacturing, as they look to encourage low-propensity voters to turn out for Republicans. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” White House spokesman Davis Ingle said. But his moves to reshape the party in his image over the past two years also often showed little regard for conventional political risk assessment. Trump created two special elections with decisions to put Vance as his vice president and Marco Rubio, a popular former Florida senator, as his secretary of state. On Tuesday, Democrats are underdogs in Florida after nominating democratic socialist Angie Nixon to face appointed GOP Sen. Ashley Moody. The race is more competitive than expected but not a five-alarm fire like Ohio, where Vance’s replacement, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is in a precarious position. The longtime preference of Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was to run for governor, according to multiple people familiar with internal party deliberations. He was instead appointed to the Senate and Vivek Ramaswamy ran for governor; Ramaswamy now trails Democrat Amy Action. A campaign spokesperson for Husted said that he “is completely focused on retiring Sherrod Brown once and for all this Tuesday.” “Public polls in the national media have gotten Ohio wrong every election cycle since 2016,” one Ohio GOP operative argued. drama in the south A year after selecting Vance, Trump tangled with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., over healthcare cuts included in the tax cut law, prompting Tillis to retire. Tillis told Semafor afterward that Trump’s backing might not have helped anyway: “I’m not sure that his endorsement would have helped me in a general election in North Carolina next year, to be quite candid.” Trump quickly cleared the field for former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, avoiding a costly primary, but Whatley’s candidacy crumpled against his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in an interview last summer that Tillis was “established” and “knew how to run and win in North Carolina,” while also praising Whatley as a candidate who could win with Republicans united behind him. In recent weeks, however, Republicans essentially ceded the race as the battleground map expanded to places like Texas. Thune and many sitting GOP senators had hoped to convince Trump to back Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. But Trump gave Cornyn the cold shoulder after the Texas Republican’s remarks questioning Trump’s viability heading into the 2024 election cycle. Trump instead backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, who won the nomination. Paxton is trailing in most polls while receiving the most air support of any candidate. “Texas was an unforced error, I think, on the part of the president,” Cornyn told Semafor in previously unreported comments earlier this year. “We spent a lot of money trying to win the nomination, but the promise was that if I won the nomination, then that would be a layup in November. That’s all off the table.” Had they been nominated again, Cornyn and Tillis may have had tough races too, but most Republicans now believe they would have been closer. Paxton could still win, but the race undoubtedly opens up a shocking vulnerability in Republicans’ red wall. So too in South Carolina. After the death of his longtime ally, Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., Trump backed Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., who most senators thought would be an interim senator. Instead, Trump helped launch Graham’s run for a six-year term, even as several other prominent Republicans mounted their own campaigns. Graham defeated conservative Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., in the primary runoff this summer with Trump’s help, but Graham is now in a toss-up race with Annie Andrews, who is outraising her by astronomical margins. Norman barely lifted a finger to help Graham and the race has gotten closer and closer, prompting intervention from the Senate Leadership Fund, a GOP-aligned super PAC. “There’s an incredibly divided Republican Party in South Carolina,” Andrews told Semafor in September. She added that polling clearly showed “that Darline was going to be easier for me.” Room for Disagreement Republicans say some of Trump’s impact has been positive. events.title: The agentic web is here
events.summary: In 2001, a decade after he invented the World Wide Web, Tim Berners-Lee articulated a new vision. Together with two colleagues, he published an article in the magazine Scientific American in which he outlined what he called the “Semantic Web” : an internet designed to be navigated by autonomous software agents that could address our every need, without requiring us to muck about with browsers and search engines ourselves. To illustrate what this might look like, Berners-Lee and his colleagues told a story about a pair of siblings who use their agents to automatically research and book physical therapy appointments for their mother, making sure they would be covered by insurance and fit their busy calendars.  At the turn of the millennium, this vision seemed far-fetched: Google had only been online for a couple of years, and most people were still on dial-up connections. But a quarter-century on, the dream of autonomous software agents that use the internet and carry out tasks for us has finally been realized. New tools such as Meta’s blockbuster Muse agent, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s  are being given access to people’s email inboxes and bank accounts,  Meanwhile, in a series of worrying incidents, agents created by OpenAI broke free of their sandboxes and caused havoc online.   Just as the rise of smartphones sparked the development of a more atomized and attention-grabbing internet, the advent of powerful AI systems heralds a new era: We’re facing not the semantic web but the agentic web. This new web is developing out of sight and in ways that might not be entirely within our control. As it grows, the agentic web will inevitably transform the human web—and whether the human web survives this transition is anyone’s guess. For Berners-Lee’s original vision to work, internet users would have had to annotate the pages they built with special tags so that a software agent could understand each element’s meaning—say, “street address” for the part of a physical therapy office’s web page that indicates its location and “appointment types” for the list of services. And so the idea never really caught on. “It’s a lot of labor,” says Eni Mustafaraj, a professor of computer science at Wellesley College. “And the benefits of that were not obvious.” For the next two decades, then, the internet remained a place that put humans first, with the odd Twitter reply bot or web scraper to round things out. Large language models changed that. Unlike the agents that Berners-Lee was imagining, today’s LLM-based agents don’t need any tags to understand which part of the text on a clinic’s site is its address and which details the services it offers. They can search for and process text far faster than any human, and agents with multimodal capabilities can even interpret screenshots of websites and click on specific elements such as hyperlinks and drop-down menus.  They’re also just a way more intuitive means of finding information and accomplishing tasks online. Rather than poring over pages of Google results to find a budget-friendly product dupe or a half-remembered meme, why not have Claude or ChatGPT peruse dozens of sites in just a few minutes, guided only by your vague query? Or go one step further and use a personal assistant agent like Muse to hunt down a restaurant reservation or book a flight.  As agents flood online spaces, this new user base is changing the web for good. Time magazine, for instance, is publishing versions of its articles that are easier for agents to parse and has started selling ads targeted at them. Companies from Etsy to Expedia have partnered with the major AI firms to build tools that allow agents to interface seamlessly with their services. Despite these early efforts, it’s still tough to tell exactly what forms the agentic web will take and how it will change our online experience. Depending on how it’s designed and who controls access to it, we could be in for something that’s as open and customizable as the web of the early 2000s, only far easier to use. Alternatively, we could be reduced to viewing much of the web through tiny portholes controlled by a few dominant platforms, as independent sites and creators struggle to survive the shift. And as this summer’s series of OpenAI security incidents suggests, the agents might even build their own online networks and resources—whether we want them to or not. How this plays out also depends on us: which parts of our online lives we’re happy to delegate to our agents and where we will still demand a human-centric internet. “There’s a lot we don’t know yet about how users want to use [agents],” says Ajit Varma, head of Firefox at Mozilla. But whatever does happen, the changes will be big. “It’s probably on par with getting a mobile phone,” he says. “I think things are going to change very dramatically.” Building a web for agents There are two ways to approach building the agentic web. The first involves training agents to use browsers like humans—scrolling, clicking, typing—and letting them loose on the web that we’re all used to. The second requires building tools that allow agents to interface with the internet via text and code, their preferred media. That possibility offers more separation between the human and the agentic web: designers can create different experiences for those who use text commands and those who use browsers. When Siva Reddy, a professor of computer science and linguistics at McGill University, began studying LLM agents in 2024, he focused on the first option. “At that time, we thought it should be that the best agent in the world is probably an agent that can use a browser,” he says. Such an agent would integrate seamlessly with the preexisting human web, and its owner could easily supervise it by watching as it navigated familiar interfaces. The frontier AI companies were already developing these “computer-use agents.” But they didn’t work terribly well—at least not at first. “There’s a lot of moving pieces [on the web], and they are not really optimized for automatic consumption,” says Xing Han Lu, a graduate student in Reddy’s lab at McGill. We humans are naturals at interacting with graphical interfaces using a keyboard and mouse, but agents are not. PINGNAN LU So Reddy and Lu pivoted toward the second, tool-based approach. In the summer of 2025, they expounded on this view in a preprint paper envisioning a new kind of web interface that would allow agents to interact with websites just as effectively as we do. Such a full-featured version of the agentic web doesn’t yet exist, but it is emerging in smaller ways. For example, if you open up Claude, ChatGPT, or Muse, you’ll find an option to add a wide variety of “plug-ins” or “connectors” that your agents can use: Gmail connectors allow your agent to triage your inbox, and Instacart plug-ins let your agent do your grocery shopping. events.title: Asian shares are mixed and US futures advance, while oil prices retreat
events.summary: Asian shares are mixed ad oil prices have retreated, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran HONG KONG -- Asian shares were mixed and oil prices retreated Monday, falling sharply on renewed hopes for progress in diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran. U.S. futures advanced after U.S. stocks fell Friday to their worst day since June as investors dumped technology- and artificial intelligence-related stocks. Japan’s Nikkei 225 gave up early gains, slipping 0.3% to 63,081.86 as some major technology companies fell. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index rose 2.2% to 5,859.08. Samsung Electronics added 1.8%, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix jumped 3.8%. Technology stocks have been volatile as investors worry that the AI buildup may prove to be a bubble. Apple is due to report its latest earnings results later in the day. Last week, earnings reports from Google parent Alphabet Inc. and Amazon rattled markets and raised fresh questions over whether their massive AI-related spending will bring profitable returns as quickly as hoped. While recent developments do not necessarily mean that the AI boom is beginning to unravel, the debate is entering another phase, Sunil Tirumalai at UBS Global Research wrote in a recent note. Investors have become “distinctly more nervous about a handful of companies with weaker balance sheets or bigger financial commitments,” he said, rather than the technology sector as a whole. “Some cracks have appeared,” said Tirumalai. “Increasingly, the question will be whether all the money being spent on it can generate adequate financial returns.” Over the past month, the Nikkei 225 has fallen more than 7% and the Kospi dropped more than 16%. Taiwan’s Taiex was 0.7% lower, with leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., shedding 1.7%. Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Hong Kong’s Hang Seng gained 0.5% to 23,411.49. The Shanghai Composite index was up 1.1% to 3,638.03, despite China reporting over the weekend that its factory activity returned to contraction territory in October indicating that the economic momentum may have slowed. China’s central bank and its securities regulatory body met with financial institutions Monday to discuss ways to support the markets, according to Chinese media reports. The Shanghai Composite index has fallen 14.6% in the past year. In Australia, the S & P/ASX 200 lost 0.6% to 8,856.50. On Friday, Wall Street’s benchmark S & P 500 fell 1.8% and the technology-heavy Nasdaq composite declined 2.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 1.1%. Investors are watching for the outcome of Tuesday’s U.S. midterm elections . Voters across the political spectrum have shown increasing concerns about AI and data centers , along with inflation and other key issues. Oil prices dropped more than 2% early Monday, with Brent crude, the international standard, down 2.8% to $110.24 per barrel. Benchmark U.S. crude gave up 3.1%, to $100.85 a barrel. Iran’s top diplomat said in an interview shared on his Telegram channel over the weekend that Iranian negotiators were in Qatar for talks on a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. meets several conditions. However, he said no direct talks were being held with the U.S. The final outcome of the diplomatic efforts to avoid a return to all-out war depends on answers provided by the United States to the “Iranian questions,” he said. In other dealings early Monday, the U.S. dollar rose to 157.83 Japanese yen from 157.49 yen. events.title: Asia’s factories lose steam as AI glow meets war’s economic chill
events.summary: Manufacturing activity slowed in China, indicating the drag from Iran war may be offsetting gains from robust global demand for AI chips. Asia’s factory growth slowed in October, especially in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, even as chip and AI demand stayed strong. The Middle East war is lifting fuel and food prices, hurting spending and confidence, while China’s price competition is also pressuring exporters. The IMF warned Asia’s growth may ease in 2026 and 2027, and Japan’s central bank said an AI slump could hit exports, production and financial markets. TOKYO – Factory activity across Asia continued to expand in October, but growth slowed in major chip exporters, private surveys showed on Nov 2, suggesting the AI boom may be losing momentum as markets start to question the sector’s profitability. The data points to growing strains on export-led economies, as prolonged conflict in the Middle East keeps fuel and food prices elevated, hitting consumption and business confidence, even as demand for chips and artificial intelligence-related goods remains resilient. Manufacturing activity slowed in China, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, the surveys showed, indicating the drag from the US-Israeli war on Iran may be offsetting the benefits from robust global demand for chips and AI-related goods. “Strong chip and AI demand had masked soft spots in Asian and global economies. But that’s becoming hard to sustain with the Middle East war dragging on for so long, pushing up fuel and food prices,” said Toru Nishihama, chief emerging market economist at Dai-ichi Life Research Institute in Tokyo. “High inflation is hurting Asian consumption. Intensifying price competition from China is also weighing on rival exporters like Japan and South Korea,” he said. The RatingDog China general manufacturing purchasing managers’ index (PMI), compiled by S&P Global, stood at 52 in October, exceeding the 50-mark that separates growth from contraction but falling from 52.1 in September. The reading followed official data released on Oct 31 showing China’s factory activity shrank in October, marking the third contraction in four months. “The PMIs suggest that China’s economic activity lost momentum in October following September’s pick-up. Manufacturing softened a touch, but foreign demand still looks resilient,” said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics. “More worrying was the sharp reversal in construction activity and expectations, suggesting that firms have become less confident that fiscal support will provide a substantial boost over the rest of the year.” Japan’s PMI eased to 53.3 in October from 54.1 in September, a survey by S&P Global showed, marking the slowest expansion in seven months as output and new orders lost momentum. South Korea’s factory activity grew in October at the slowest pace in eight months on weaker output and demand, with the PMI falling to 51.3 from 53.9 in September. Taiwan’s PMI stood at 54.9 in October, down from 56.7 in September. Other economies showed factory activity expanded in October at a faster pace than the previous month, including Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia. India’s manufacturing growth slowed in October as domestic demand eased and hiring weakened, though a surge in export orders helped cushion the slowdown. Asia has outperformed many other regions as manufacturers benefitted from brisk demand for chips and AI-related goods. But the International Monetary Fund (IMF) has projected Asia’s economic growth to moderate in 2027 , and warned of heightening risks from the Iran war-induced energy shock and a potential correction in the AI boom. The IMF said it now expects Asia’s economy to grow 4.8% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, higher than projections made in April but still slowing from a 5% expansion in 2025. While Japan has been among the beneficiaries of the AI boom, the central bank warned the technology also poses risks to the country’s long-term economic outlook. “If growth expectations for AI decline substantially, a tightening of global financial conditions, accompanied by a rapid repricing of stocks and a sharp slowdown in the race for AI development, could significantly hurt Japan’s economy through a plunge in exports and production,” it said. events.title: Alstom shares plunge after it cuts guidance, plans overhaul in second warning
events.summary: Alstom’s anticipated positive free cash flow was revised to an expected cash burn of €1.5 billion (S$2.1 billion). Alstom cut full-year guidance after delays in German projects hurt margins. It now expects about 1% adjusted Ebit margin and a €1.5 billion cash burn. Problems in Coradia Max orders caused penalties and a “domino effect” across other projects. Chief financial officer Bernard Delpit said the project’s gross margin is now negative. The company will review its organisation, cut costs, and seek about €2 billion of debt reduction through more asset sales. It reports full results on Nov 17 and a capital markets day in 2027. Alstom cut its full-year guidance and announced a deep overhaul after delays in key German projects led to penalties and hurt margins, plunging the French train maker into a fresh crisis. Its stock slumped as much as 27% in early Paris trading on Nov 2, after the company slashed its profit margin, cash flow and train car production targets for the fiscal year. The shares have lost more than half of their value in 2026. Alstom now expects an adjusted Ebit margin of about 1% for the fiscal year, down from 6.5% previously, it said on Nov 2 . An anticipated positive free cash flow was revised to an expected cash burn of €1.5 billion (S$2.1 billion). Alstom also downgraded its train car production target for the period to about 4,000 units from as many 4,500. The latest warning is tied to the Coradia Max orders, a series of projects including regional trains ordered by German states such as Baden-Wurttemberg and Lower Saxony that were meant to be the company’s biggest ramp-up in 2026 . The delays in one of the Coradia Max projects, caused by problems in the final development phases, had a “domino effect” on other German projects, leading to penalties that weighed on margins, chief financial officer Bernard Delpit said on a media call. The Coradia project’s gross margin is now negative, according to Delpit. The problem was detected after chief executive officer Martin Sion, who took the helm in April, sent out teams to deal with struggling projects, Delpit said. The CEO found that “not only were there engineering issues, but the organisation surrounding project management was neither efficient nor effective”, Delpit said. Alstom is now tackling a broader review of its organisation to improve execution and accountability, to lower costs and to make processes simpler. It also will carry out a new plan to slash debt by about €2 billion, which will include further divestments. “We have identified the assets and are beginning the process,” Delpit said on the call, when asked about the group’s possible future divestments. He declined to elaborate on details, saying it was too early. The company already stunned markets in April by withdrawing its financial guidance due to slow progress related to various projects, prompting a share slump. The group has been seeking to shore up its balance sheet after the troubled US$5.5 billion (S$7.03 billion) acquisition of Bombardier’s rail business in 2021. The group’s former CEO, Henri Poupart-Lafarge, had completed a previous €2 billion plan to slash debt. Alstom is due to report full fiscal results on Nov 17 and hold a capital markets day in the second quarter of 2027. BLOOMBERG

events.title: China’s top three airlines head for full-year losses as fuel costs rise
events.summary: China Southern Airlines, which returned to the black in 2025 for the first time since 2019, is set to slip back into the red. China’s top three airlines are heading for full-year losses as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit third-quarter results. Air China, China Eastern and China Southern all posted sharp profit falls, with China Southern swinging to a loss and all three losing money in the first nine months of 2026. Analysts said airlines remain under heavy pressure because fuel costs have more than doubled, competition is intense, and profits may stay weak into the fourth quarter. BEIJING – China’s three biggest airlines are on track for full-year losses after posting far weaker third-quarter results than in 2025 as surging jet fuel costs, weak domestic fares and typhoon disruptions hit what is normally their most profitable period. Air China and China Eastern Airlines are heading for a seventh consecutive annual net loss since the Covid-19 pandemic, according to analyst estimates compiled by LSEG. China Southern Airlines, which returned to the black in 2025 for the first time since 2019, is also set to slip back into the red, the estimates showed. Air China’s third-quarter net profit fell 92.6% from a year earlier to 270.6 million yuan (S$52 million). China Eastern posted a net profit of 64 million yuan for the quarter, down 98.2% from 2025. China Southern swung to a third-quarter net loss of 609 million yuan from a net profit of 3.84 billion yuan in 2025. All three airlines reported losses for the first nine months of 2026, a period in which they were profitable in 2025. The third quarter, which covers the peak summer travel season, is traditionally the strongest for Chinese airlines and set a high base for year-on-year comparisons. But all three carriers said the steep rise in jet fuel prices had a negative impact on their results. The price of jet fuel has more than doubled since the United States and Israel launched a military campaign against Iran in late February. Chinese airlines hedge far less of their fuel than many Asian and European peers, leaving them more exposed to swings in oil prices. Domestic fares were weak in the third quarter amid intense competition, including from high-speed rail. Huatai Securities estimated Air China’s yields, a proxy for airfares, fell 5% during the period, leaving it unable to recoup higher fuel costs. “Chinese airlines are expected to remain in net loss into the seasonally weaker fourth quarter given the impact of spiking jet fuel,” said Nathan Gee, head of Asia-Pacific transport research at BofA Global Research. Gee said third-quarter earnings had come in slightly better than “very low expectations”. Checks suggested domestic fares were rising at double-digit rates year-on-year after the October Golden Week holiday, as airlines kept a lid on capacity. But fuel “remains the big headwind”, he said. “Chinese airline margin remains under extreme pressure from spiking jet fuel and soft consumption demand,” Gee added. Airlines are trying to boost flying hours per plane to control costs, but big cost cuts will be difficult, he said.

events.title: Shift Left Is Becoming A System-Level Problem
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation. Fragmented workflows with disconnected tools and models are allowing bugs to escape even though individual components have been verified. Agentic AI may improve coordination across disciplines, identify bottlenecks, and optimize tool usage, but it cannot replace fundamental processes such as simulation and emulation. Experts at the Table : Semiconductor Engineering sat down to discuss why shift left is pushing beyond verification to system-level validation, and where AI can and cannot help, with Frank Schirrmeister, executive director of strategy programs and system solutions at Synopsys ; Ronen Laviv, vice president of business development and strategic partnerships at Hiveware; Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco ; Ashish Darbari, founder and CEO of Axiomise . What follows are excerpts of that conversation. To view part one of this discussion, click here . L-R: Silvaco’s Berg; Synopsys’ Schirrmeister; Axiomise’s Darbari; Hiveware’s Laviv. SE: The focus of shift left in design has largely been about verification. But increasingly it’s also about validation, right? Darbari : Yes, and it’s influencing huge decisions that could make small companies go bankrupt if they get it wrong. We’ve seen meetings with architects, designers, UVM leads, emulation leads, FPGA and software leads, and VPs, where they’re all looking at bug escapes and asking, ‘Why did this happen?’ The architect is saying, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ The designer is saying, ‘We didn’t know that.’ The software team says, ‘It’s supposed to be this.’ And we’re sitting there as formal verification people thinking about communication and the model not being accurate, and I don’t know how well we’ll be able to solve this unless we bring the software into the development cycle. Schirrmeister : It’s not only software. It’s all the other aspects, like multi-physics. EM, thermal, and mechanical, which all have to be integrated. To look at this differently, there are hurdles that I cannot fix in this project. But perhaps I can fix it in the next one. It’s a labyrinth. We have models that are digital twins that are irrefutable, because we’ve measured them against the real thing. We can’t overcome those. We are dependent on the application. It may be more vertical, it may be more horizontally stacked to fit into a certain form factor, like a phone or a data center. But it’s like a video game where you have these things popping up. I want to package it this way, but the packaging guy says we can’t do that, at least not today. Maybe a year from now. All of this needs to be taken into consideration as part of your model. Dabari : Absolutely correct. Laviv : Shrinking times for packaging or power estimation or simulation, or even emulation — isn’t that something we could look at? We’re shifting left using AI in order to do stuff earlier. Berg : Verification traditionally has been the longest and most expensive part of doing a design, and it would be nice to say we can take everything and shift it all left. There are chunks that are being shifted left and verified, and that’s good. But how to shift everything left is something we’re still learning. Darbari : If we pick up historical data from packaging and thermal, why can’t we start building models to say, ‘This happened last time. This time it could be done better.’ Berg : You can do that based on inference. Darbari : But we don’t have a tool that ties everything together in one frame. ‘This is the model of functional safety, security, power, packaging, thermals. Go build it.’ Berg : We have different aspects of that, and we, as an industry, are working slowly but surely to integrate all of those. But we don’t have a single workflow that does that. And it really is a workflow, not just a single tool. Laviv : Nowadays, with AI knowing everything with its skills and touching everything, there is kind of a common database for verification and emulation and all the physical stuff. It might benefit customers if they have access to everything is there to be used, potentially even cross-companies. Schirrmeister : There are certain things you can shift left, and others you have to wait for. Certain things are irrefutable. Yes, you can make them faster, but you can’t bypass them. You can be smarter about how you use them. You can figure out which things should be done in emulation, which should be done in simulation, and which should be done with FPGA-based prototyping. We have customers telling us that if they find something in simulation that should have been found in formal, or simulation beforehand, they’ll review why that happened. Laviv : Why not look at bottlenecks in formal, in verification, in emulation, and see if you can handle those bottlenecks in a way that would open the flow for faster AI? Schirrmeister : There are two views here on this whole AI stack. I’m a firm believer that the underlying portions of the stack will still be required. They will be used in different ways by the AI objects, but you don’t take away the characterization, the simulation, the emulation. You get smarter about how to use them. But at the end of the day, you need to build the emulator. That takes some time. You need to get the design into it. And there is a certain number of things which you cannot overcome. You can make the tool flow more productive, but the underlying engines still need to execute, and there are limits to how fast they can become. Darbari : We need to put all of these things in a singular context because if the manufacturing, or the physics, the heat, or the functional, are all sitting in separate context windows, and the software is sitting somewhere else, then you don’t have a complete picture of what this whole device will look like. I was coding for one project and I remember asking a designer, ‘What would happen to this processor if there was more than one outstanding transaction? Could you discard the later ones?’ And he said, ‘We’ll just discard them.’ Everything was exhaustively proved, and while I was taping, the software teams were running their own stuff. But a bug got missed. The software team had a completely different understanding of how they were going to drive the SoC. So they found a trace, and they said, ‘We are losing transactions.’ There was a complete misalignment between what the architect and the designer thought they were building, so they had to patch it at the end of the day. That’s what worries me now, because things are getting so much more complex. We’re putting all of this in the hands of an agent, but who is the master at the top leve

events.title: Putting AI To The Test
events.summary: There are an increasing number of new EDA companies these days, and this is great news. The industry needs some new vitality, new thought leaders, people willing to take risks. The same goes for established companies that cannot go outside their existing comfort zone while meeting next quarter’s financial goals. But sometimes, new startups forget the risks associated with semiconductor design. While they may be able to point to an improvement in time to market, or meeting better performance goals, they fail to understand how small that particular step is in the whole process. Today, a number of companies want us to believe that AI can do everything. Some point the way to automating design, others to verification, and some even claim it can do both at the same time, from the same source material. No, it can’t. While some of it may be possible in the future, it is far from that point today. What many of them fail to do is show proof. One example, one design, one piece of IP is not proof. When verifying any new tool or methodology, you always need to hold back a test set to apply at the end. In this case, with AI, it has to be something it has never seen before, never been trained on. That is the only thing that can provide a fair, unbiased result. As soon as you tweak your tool to do well on that test case, it is no longer a true test. This is why I was delighted to receive communications from Vikash Kumar, senior verification architect at Arm. He has 15+ years of semiconductor industry experience and is the author of the book “AI-Assisted Hardware Verification: Cognitive Verification Architecture with the VEGA Framework.” What he shared with me was his independent work on the quality of existing LLMs for the creation of testbenches. More than 20 years ago, Certess introduced the industry to mutation analysis. If you inject a bug into the design, does the testbench find it? They used the traditional stuck-at fault model and sophisticated statistical analysis to reduce the total number of faults required. The results were a slap across the face to many companies that thought they were doing a good job, only to find out how poor their testbenches were. Vikash’s approach is different. “The setup was simple — hand AI a spec and the RTL, tell it to verify and report back when it is confident the design is clean, and check what it actually found. I hand-seeded realistic, design-representative functional bugs, which keeps the ground truth clean. I know exactly which bugs were planted, so detection is measured against a known set rather than an impression.” I asked Vikash why he chose to insert bugs rather than using the stuck-at model, which has been the industry go-to since the ’80s. “The whole question with AI verification is whether it comprehends design intent well enough to catch the subtle, intent-level bugs, and that is exactly where it struggled — the misses clustered in data-path, encoding logic, and functional corners, not in anything a stuck-at pattern would have flagged.” He started with 25 hand-coded designs spanning bus protocols, DMA engines, ECC memory, control and peripheral logic, and concurrency scenarios. The RTL has never been made public. Into those he inserted 806 bugs. The models were given a specification based on published protocol standards. Three frontier AI models were chosen: Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.4, and GLM-5.2. “Without human intervention or predefined time limits, each model generated testbenches, developed coverage goals, executed simulations, identified and corrected RTL defects, and iteratively refined verification until independently declaring sign-off. All defects were seeded upfront, although some became observable only after earlier corrections.” Here are his key findings: Claude Opus 5 detected 79.2% of seeded defects, GPT-5.4 detected 76.2%, and GLM-5.2 detected 62.8%. Even the highest-performing model missed 20.8% of seeded defects, which is approximately 168 bugs. All three models reached 100% of their self-defined verification goals and declared sign-off despite remaining functional defects. In this audit, particularly high miss rates were observed in ECC memory, GPIO, and AXI DMA designs. Some missed defects involved ambiguous specifications. The agents proceeded without requesting clarification and ultimately declared verification complete. Even the best model, Claude Opus 5, did not detect roughly 168 defects. GPT-5.4 missed about 192, and GLM-5.2 missed close to 300. Perhaps even worse is that Vikash ran each model three times, and each run produced different results. But he is very optimistic about the results. “The impressive part is how much AI caught on its own,” he says. “The important part is how much it missed, and that’s where the engineer still matters.” In a similar manner, ChipAgents just released its new build-a-chip-bench tool. It goes from a workload specification to GSD. The company ranked five models. The best, Claude Fable 5.1 achieved a score of 16.6%, whilst the bottom of the pack was GLM-5.3 with a score of zero. These results look dire, but the biggest failure was their lack of understanding of performance constraints. I believe this will be an even bigger problem when it comes to writing software that has to be cognizant of the underlying hardware and its performance beyond raw speed. Real-time systems deployed within physical AI need predictable latency, at low power, over a broad range of operating conditions. None of this data is available for training today. I will finish with another comment Vikash made: “You can automate the work of verification. You cannot automate the responsibility for it.” The post Putting AI To The Test appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Investor scrutiny of the AI spending boom is rising, but Big Tech is unlikely to give up
events.summary: Given that the bulk of chip manufacturing capacity is in Asia, the AI boom’s fate has the potential to redefine the region’s economic outlook. Investor scrutiny is rising over Big Tech’s huge AI spending. Alphabet fell 13% after reporting US$51.4 billion capex and negative free cash flow, despite 25% revenue growth. Big Tech says it must keep buying compute and chips to stay competitive. Scaling Laws, custom silicon and lower compute costs are driving more data centre and chip investment. Asia’s chip exporters are watching closely because AI demand supports trade and growth. Analysts say spending should stay high, with supply still tighter than demand and more sell-offs possible. SINGAPORE – As tech titans continue pouring massive amounts of money into data centres and equipping them with ever more expensive chips, growing investor scrutiny on the AI build-out is pulling down stock prices and pushing up borrowing costs. The selling pressure isn’t just pounding hard on Big Tech; their most consequential partners in the global AI supply chain, semiconductor chipmakers, have also suffered. Hence, investors and policymakers in Asia’s top chip-exporting nations, including Singapore, are watching Wall Street’s attempt to reset the AI trade with measured trepidation. The International Monetary Fund recently noted that global trade rose 8.3% between 2023 and 2025 – a figure that would be closer to 4.6%, or nearly half, without AI-related products. The Monetary Authority of Singapore’s latest Macroeconomic Review said Singapore’s technology-related sectors accounted for around 75% of overall year on year GDP growth in the third quarter of 2026. On the face of it, the question investors are asking seems plain: Can Big Tech can afford the AI buildout? The market evidently doesn’t think so. Google’s parent, Alphabet, for instance, saw its stock drop by as much as 13% , erasing US$500 billion (S$639 billion) in market capitalisation, following its third-quarter 2026 earnings report released on Oct 28. Even as Alphabet posted strong revenue growth of 25% and a doubling of Google Cloud revenue, its stock was hammered after it reported US$9 billion in negative free cash flow, driven by a massive US$51.4 billion in capital expenditure, mostly on AI infrastructure. Free cash flow is the money left with a company after paying day-to-day operations and maintaining or expanding physical assets. So why aren’t companies that are leading the charge on AI giving in to the demand for fiscal discipline? For tech firms investing in AI infrastructure, including computing and memory chips, sufficient compute capacity is a must. This capacity is the single most important driver of AI capability, speed and competitive advantage. In the tech world, the concept is known as Scaling Laws. A framework of predictable mathematical relationships in AI that shows how a large language model’s performance improves – it gets smarter and makes fewer mistakes – as the resources driving it increase over time. According to the Center for Governance of AI, a non-profit research organisation, compute capacity is also the primary gatekeeper of AI diffusion, acting as the bridge that transforms elite lab research into affordable, ubiquitous commercial tools. Economic experts refer to this process as compute deflation, which reflects the rapid, sustained drop in the cost per unit of processing power, memory and AI inference. As the falling cost of compute replaces the cost of labour and production, it exerts downward pressure on the general price of software and tech-enabled services. That’s why some AI hyperscalers are also designing their own high-performance AI accelerator chips – specialised semiconductor hardware designed to process AI, machine learning, and deep-tech learning workloads much faster and more efficiently than standard chips. Big Tech is also investing in chips The shift towards custom silicon is reshaping the entire cloud computing industry. To break free from Nvidia’s hardware monopoly and drastically lower operational costs, all major cloud hyperscalers – including Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure – have aggressively built out their own proprietary chips. Alphabet disclosed in its third-quarter earnings report that more than 100 significant Google Cloud customers – including Anthropic and Apple – are now running AI using Google’s own tensor processing units, an alternative to Nvidia’s AI chips. Consumer tech platforms are also designing custom silicon – Meta’s MTIA, or Meta Training and Inference Accelerator, chip family, for instance – to power their internal AI tools and ad engines. This competition in semiconductor chips and devices aims to break old hardware monopolies and force down pricing.

events.title: Binance users withdraw $3.6bn after largest-ever crypto hack
events.summary: Published 2 November 2026, 00:26 GMT Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history. The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets. Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack . The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack. Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added. Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance. The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack. Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed. Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. AI discovered a massive cyber-security flaw - here's what happened Published 22 October The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them. The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions. The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue. Watch: What we know about Binance's $6.3bn hack and what to do if you're affected Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally. events.title: MAS sets aside $30m to help insurers build expertise in funding major projects
events.summary: MAS is also proposing changes to the capital insurers must set aside against investment risks, reducing requirements for investments where the risks justify this. MAS will set aside $30 million to help insurers build skills in financing major projects such as power grids and data centres, using funds from the Financial Sector Development Fund. It also plans lower capital rules for some project investments, if risks are lower. The public consultation runs from Nov 2 to Dec 18. At the Singapore reinsurance conference, industry players launched a data centre insurance scheme and an AI risk handbook, showing new growth areas and new risk concerns. SINGAPORE – The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) will set aside $3 0 million to help insurers build expertise in investing in major projects such as power grids and data centres. The central bank is also proposing changes to the capital insurers must set aside against investment risks, reducing requirements for investments where the risks justify this. Minister for National Development Chee Hong Tat announced the measures o n No v 2 at the 2 2nd Singapore International Reinsurance Conference at Sands Expo and Convention Centre. The event, organised by the Singapore Reinsurers’ Association (SRA), drew more than 4, 300 delegates representing 85 countries and territories, according to the association. Reinsurers provide insurance to insurance companies. Chee, who is also MAS deputy chairman, said insurers could play a bigger role in financing Asia’s growth, alongside protecting businesses and communities against risks. The $30 million, from the Financia l Secto r Development Fund , will help defray the costs of building dedicated investment teams, training staff and engaging professional services to establish and expand these investment activities in Singapore. Across ASEAN, more than U S$200 billion (S$256 billion) is needed annually for projects ranging from roads and ports to renewable energy and telecommunications networks, Chee said. Yet, past studies put such investments at only around 1 % to 2% of insurers’ assets, although this share has been growing. “High-quality infrastructure assets can generate stable, long-term cash flows that align well with insurers’ long-dated liabilities, particularly those of life insurers,” Chee said. This means income from these projects can help insurers meet payments owed to policyholders years later. MAS proposes extending lower capital requirements to qualifying debt investments in these projects that have credit ratings, subject to conditions. Investments with features that reduce risk, such as stable contractual revenues, could qualify for further reductions. MAS also proposes lower requirements for certain rated investments backed by pools of assets, subject to conditions including repayment priority, ease of trading and structural safeguards. The public consultation runs from Nov 2 to Dec 18. Chee said industry players are developing a Singapore-based insurance facility for data centres, with US $200 million in initial capacity. An insurance facility is a pre-arranged agreement where several insurers join their underwriting ability to cover particular types of risks. Participants include MSIG, Gallagh er Re, SCOR, Samsung Re and the Cybersecurity Association Singapore. The facility is expected to cover construction, operational, supply chain, design and cyber risks. Separately, SRA launched a handbook at the conference to help reinsurers assess risks associated with artificial intelligence. The guide addresses issues including the reliability of data and AI decisions, dependence on external providers, and how AI affects decisions on insurance coverage and claims. Minister for National Development and deputy chairman of the Monetary Authority of Singapore Chee Hong Tat speaking at the Singapore International Reinsurance Conference on Nov 2. SRA ch airman Glen Rid dell said: “AI is creating new opportunities across the insurance value chain, while also introducing new considerations for the risks insurers and reinsurers assume.” Reinsurers need to understand how AI affects the risks they cover and claims outcomes, he said. “This handbook provides practical, principles-based guidance to help reinsurers assess these considerations and incorporate them into reinsurance decision-making.” The conference runs until Nov 5, with discussions covering geopolitical and economic shifts, disaster protection and the skills needed as technology changes the insurance industry.

events.title: What to look for if you’re buying a smart lock in the UK
events.summary: Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . More people are fitting keyless devices to their front door – but are they worth it and do they affect your insurance? A s the nights draw in, thoughts turn to home security. A growing number of British homeowners are choosing to upgrade their front doors with tech-enabled “keyless” smart locks, which allow them to be opened by phone, fob, fingerprint or a number pad. But you need to make sure you have the right lock for the door – and that your insurance isn’t invalidated by installing it. They allow you to get into your home without a key, instead using a code, a phone, a fingerprint, a voice assistant such as Siri or facial recognition to give you entry. Some can be operated remotely via wifi so that if a tradesman calls to do work, you can let them in wherever you are. Many offer a combination of several options. In South Korea, and some Scandinavian countries, they are becoming the norm, says Steffan George of the Master Locksmiths Association (MLA), a UK trade body. In the UK they are more common on offices, but interest is increasing. The types vary in complexity. Some have the smart feature and a handle in one unit that fully replaces an existing door handle. Others are made up of a small unit which can be fitted on an existing lock, sitting on top of it, opening the door when activated. This type essentially turns a traditional lock into a smart one. And there is a third type where the existing mechanical lock cylinder is swapped for an electronic one, which opens the lock once activated. Some allow for a physical key to be used in an emergency. They range from less than £100 to well over £1,000. Shane Hales, of HalesLocks in Sidcup, Kent, puts the starting price for a good quality version at between £200 and £250 for the unit. Getting a professional to fit them will add to the cost. Look out for the Kitemark on the faceplate to ensure that it meets security requirements set by the British Standards Institution. Sold Secure, an agency which judges the performance of locks, has a certification called SS504 . To qualify, locks are tested for physical security, technical performance and cybersecurity. Hales highlights the Black X (about £200) and the Ultion Nuki (£339) as two well-regarded units. George says that a smart lock is unlikely to last as long as a traditional one, which “will last 20 years easily with just a little bit of lubrication”. Hales adds that, in his experience, smart locks will last for five to six years before they need to be replaced . In the UK front doors are made from a variety of materials, including UPVC, timber, and a composite of different types. Checking the lock works with whatever type of door you have is vital. Many US imports will be unsuitable for British doors because of differences in the locking cylinders. Lots of lockmakers have guides on their websites so you can check whether their product would work for your home. For example, Yale has a “smart lock compatibility checker” which uses a visual guide on what your lock looks like to recommend options. You can email in pictures of your existing fitting and door to some installers and manufacturers, and they will advise what is suitable. Retrofit smart locks are usually installed on the inside of the door and work with the existing cylinder – the barrel in which you insert the key. They have a motorised unit inside which connects to the lock and turns it open. To install one yourself, you will need basic tools. Most people will also want to choose a lock that has been designed to be easy to install, with no modifications needed to the door itself. Things get more complicated when wiring, drilling or carpentry is needed to get the lock to fit properly, or if the door you have is UPVC, composite or non-standard. Checkatrade, the tradespeople’s recommendation site, says installation costs vary; it puts the labour at between £63 for a basic keypad lock and £210 for a Z-wave-enabled lock, a communication system similar to Bluetooth and wifi. If you are considering getting a smart lock, it is important to run it by your home insurer to be sure that what you buy adheres to its standards. The Association of British Insurers (ABI) says you should check the terms of your policy before making any changes. “Some home insurers have specific requirements for the type of lock you use to protect your home, and your provider will be able to advise you,” says its general insurance policy adviser, Charlie Inwood. Your insurer may also require that the lock is put in by a professional. Hales says people should always get professional advice. “There is no one size that fits all doors. For that lock to be compliant, it needs to fit properly, and if it’s not fitted properly, then you know you could leave yourself open to problems.”

events.title: Billionaire Sergey Brin is building political infrastructure that will last beyond his $102 million fight against Prop 40
events.summary: Google cofounder Sergey Brin spent much of his career on the sidelines of electoral politics. But a proposed California wealth tax has turned the billionaire into one of the state’s most powerful political financiers, prompting him to build an organization that can continue shaping state policy long after voters decide on the measure that initially mobilized him. Brin has contributed $102 million to Building a Better California, a political organization that has become the central vehicle for Silicon Valley billionaires seeking to influence California’s political direction. The group has raised hundreds of millions of dollars from wealthy tech executives, venture capitalists, and business leaders—channeling money into ballot measures that extend beyond the immediate fight against Proposition 40 .
