events.title: How HSBC is investing in Hong Kong to build the future of finance — and why now
events.summary: As Hong Kong FinTech Week 2026 approaches, HSBC is investing in the city’s talent, technology and partnerships to turn advances in AI, blockchain and tokenisation into banking services for customers in Hong Kong and beyond [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] Hong Kong has been a home market for HSBC since the bank was founded 161 years ago. It is now also a base for the bank’s AI investment and delivery, with capabilities developed in the city intended for use across other markets. The city is also expanding the regulatory and market infrastructure needed to support digital finance at scale. HSBC returns as a Strategic Partner of Hong Kong FinTech Week x StartmeupHK for the fourth consecutive year as technologies discussed for years begin to find a commercial footing. “Our vision is simple. Empower our colleagues to use AI to create a personalised experience for each customer, and to deliver it safely, in real time and at scale, all while keeping human judgement, decision-making and accountability at the core.” AI is a core part of HSBC’s technology strategy. In Hong Kong, the bank already has a team of 150 AI specialists and plans to double the team within two to three years. HSBC will also establish a global AI institute in Hong Kong, expected to begin operations in early 2027. It will initially focus on AI, post-quantum cryptography and blockchain technology, with a view to applying these technologies across HSBC’s operations. In addition, HSBC has technology and AI specialists in other key locations, innovating to address bank-wide opportunities globally. From capability to customer outcomes HSBC has used AI for years in automation, data analysis and services for employees and customers. Its focus now covers an end-to-end view of AI across the bank’s operations and customer services. Banker Assist, for example, combines HSBC’s internal data with trusted external information to provide relationship teams with more detailed client insights. The bank has also rolled out HSBCnio here in Hong Kong, a digital, AI-enabled solution for corporate and institutional clients. It brings transaction-banking functions into one connected experience and allows clients’ own AI tools to access authorised bank accounts and transaction information on a read-only basis. HSBC is also working with technology companies including Mistral AI, Google, Amazon and Microsoft, with governance, resilience and risk management built into its approach. Building innovation people can trust HSBC recently tested two use cases within the Hong Kong Monetary Authority’s GenAI Sandbox, covering customer accessibility and anti-fraud capabilities. The first is a generative AI-powered sign-language translation solution that explores ways to make banking services more accessible for customers who use sign language. The second focuses on deepfake detection and ways to identify manipulation as criminals use increasingly sophisticated techniques to imitate people, documents and communications. The two use cases show different sides of responsible innovation: improving access to banking services and strengthening protection against new forms of fraud. The infrastructure that moves money, assets and information is also evolving towards always-on, data-rich and increasingly programmable digital rails. Tokenised deposits, digital bonds, stablecoins and central bank digital currencies can support faster settlement, improved liquidity, lower operational friction and better traceability. For retail customers in Hong Kong, HSBC is launching HSBC RedCoin, its first Hong Kong dollar-denominated stablecoin, for 3.3 million customers through PayMe. It is designed to support peer-to-peer and peer-to-merchant payments using HSBC’s technology and security infrastructure. Later this year, HSBC also plans to add stablecoin wallet functionality to the HSBC HK Mobile Banking app and enable customers to subscribe to tokenised investment products through HSBC RedCoin, including a soon-to-be launched share class of HSBC’s HKD money market fund. HSBC Gold Token is another case in point. Since its launch in 2024, the tokenised gold service has recorded 390,000 trades with a total traded value of US$2.5 billion. For corporate clients, HSBC has launched Tokenised Deposit Services, starting in Hong Kong and expanding across Asia, Europe, the US and the Middle East. The service supports 24/7 cross-border payments and real-time settlement across a range of currencies, and has also been applied to corporate treasury management and capital-markets settlement. HSBC is also facilitating interoperability across networks and platforms through active participation in the HKMA’s Project Ensemble and other industry initiatives. For institutional investors, HSBC Orion provides a concrete example of tokenisation in capital markets.

events.title: Where Dems eyeing the White House are putting their midterm chips
events.summary: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro 's chances of being a presidential contender in 2028 are riding on his winning reelection in a landslide Tuesday. New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's future hinges on whether a fellow progressive can carry a swing state, for once. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has to show that his congressional redistricting gambit worked for Democrats — and he needs to beat back a state wealth tax proposal supported by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Driving the news: Democrats eyeing White House runs have spent the past year preparing to emerge from Tuesday's midterms with momentum, and an argument for a 2028 candidacy. They want Democrats to do well — but to each, some races are especially important. Some have focused their time and money on particular contests for ideological reasons, or a desire to show strength in their home states. Others have hedged their bets across the nation, so that Tuesday is unlikely to be a huge victory or a significant defeat. Here's how the top potential Democratic contenders for president have placed their bets in this week's elections — and what success or failure will look like for them. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez A great night: AOC has wagered just about everything on the Senate race in Michigan, where she's said that a win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would "break open the entire political calculus in America" and show that "anybody can win anywhere." She's weighing whether to run for president or the Senate, and much of her electability argument for a national campaign hinges on an El-Sayed victory. Progressives are desperate to establish that one of their own can carry a presidential battleground state. Ocasio-Cortez has contributed $1 million to help El-Sayed and stumped for him at several events. An El-Sayed victory "would prove to the country, and the world, that competent, courageous progressive populists can win in the most competitive swing states in America," said Bhavik Lathia, a left-wing strategist from Michigan. "The implications for 2028 would be enormous." AOC would get bonus points Tuesday if other progressives she's supporting — such as House candidate Randy Villegas in California and Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Florida — win their swing-seat races. Worst-case scenario: If El-Sayed loses, many progressives think AOC would be less likely to run for president. That's why she's widely viewed as having more on the line Tuesday than any other potential Democratic contender for president, followed by Shapiro. Josh Shapiro A great night: Shapiro needs to win so big Tuesday that it makes Democratic presidential primary voters see his technocratic "get shit done" brand of governing as the party's best bet to take down the GOP in 2028. Shapiro is less known nationally than many 2028 hopefuls, and that has been by choice. He's largely focused on Pennsylvania this year, even as would-be rivals for president crisscrossed the country. A blowout in America's biggest swing state could help him stand out. A good night for Shapiro would be defeating Republican Stacy Garrity by double digits and carrying three Democratic House candidates — Janelle Stelson, Bob Brooks and Paige Cognetti — across the finish line to defeat Republican incumbents. He'd have a great night if his coattails were so long that he pulled a fourth Democratic House hopeful, Bob Harvie, to victory — taking down GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who's known for surviving difficult electoral cycles. Shapiro would get extra credit if he helped Democrats win a trifecta in Harrisburg for the first time in decades by flipping control of the state Senate. Worst-case scenario: If only one or two Democrats in his state flip House seats or he wins by less than 10 points, Shapiro's setup for 2028 would fall short. Andy Beshear A great night: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who moonlights as chair of the Democratic Governors Association, put his chips this year on helping his party take control of a majority of the nation's governorships. Beshear would earn bragging rights if Democrats flip the two governors' seats needed to do that. He's eyeing the races in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. "I am laser-focused on these governors' races," he told us, arguing that the results will help determine what's possible in the 2028 presidential contest. "Rob Sand wins Iowa, Iowa's in play. When Amy Acton wins Ohio, Ohio's in play," Beshear said. Worst-case scenario: Beshear made enemies among some Latino Democrats this year when the DGA rebuffed calls to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor. If Hinojosa loses to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott by a razor-thin margin or pulls an upset, Beshear's decision-making will come under heavy scrutiny — and he could have a problem with some Latino leaders in a 2028 campaign. Gavin Newsom A great night: Newsom won over many MS NOW moms and "resistance" liberals across the country when he responded to President Trump's push to create more GOP House seats in other states by fighting back with a successful voter proposition to do the same in California. His goal has been to gain five Democratic seats from the change to help Democrats take back the House. That's his bar to clear Tuesday. Some political insiders now think Democrats could gain 20 or more House seats across the country, so Newsom's contribution might not be as decisive as once thought. Newsom would score a political win if a proposed billionaire wealth tax on the ballot in his home state, which he opposes, fails. Worst-case scenario: If California voters approve the tax or Democrats flip fewer than five House seats there, it would diminish Newsom's California clout. Jon Ossoff A great night: A long-running knock against Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has been that he won his seat in 2021 by riding his fellow Peach State Sen. Raphael Warnock's coattails. Ossoff has the chance this year to prove he doesn't need Warnock, who isn't on the ticket. He's on his way to doing just that, with polls showing him comfortably leading GOP challenger Mike Collins. But to have a truly great night, Ossoff needs to show that he has enough sway in his state to help pull Democratic gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms to victory. events.title: AI can make tech CEOs’ lives easier. What about everyone else?
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Dazzle AI CEO Marissa Mayer recently became the latest tech CEO to face criticism over seemingly out-of-touch comments extolling the usefulness of AI. In Mayer’s case, that involved asking an AI tool for help with a school-assigned description of her daughter . For OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, that’s included suggesting that parents create personalized podcasts for their kids’ drive to school and also declaring that he could not imagine parenting without ChatGPT . Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has even suggested that it will become increasingly acceptable to meet your social and romantic needs through AI . This all led TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling to wonder if AI executives are simply too out-of-touch to build products for normal people — a crucial question with Anthropic set to go public just as Wall Street begins losing its appetite for heavy AI spending . On the latest episode of the Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I chatted with Amanda about why industry leaders can sometimes seem so tone deaf. Kirsten wondered if this is more of a marketing problem or a product problem. Amanda’s answer: “A little bit of both.” She also argued that the tech industry is increasingly pushing a future “where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring,” adding, “And call me old-school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society.” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Anthony: There’s a lot of societal skepticism about AI, this feeling that the people running these companies don’t have our best interests at heart, that they’re out of touch. And so, you would just think, “Maybe don’t make statements like that,” because of course, people are going to see them very skeptically. I think [CEOs] are trying to walk this delicate balance. On the one hand, there’s a tremendous financial incentive for them to make the case that you should use this technology in every aspect of your lives. But when you make that case, it actually [doesn’t paint] a very appealing picture. In some cases, it’s downright dystopian. Kirsten: Anthony, if they took your advice, we would have nothing to talk about on this show. But I will say this: There’s this whole idea of ChatGPT and other AI tools making your life easier when it comes to personal relationships. And in many of these cases, it just seems to overcomplicate what would be, like, observing your child. That might be hard for some people, the people who are building these products, and it doesn’t necessarily relate to everyone else out there in the world. It can just seem so incredibly disconnected when you see these quotes. To me, it always comes back to — who are they speaking to? Are there people out there who can relate? Maybe there are. Amanda: Other use cases we’ve seen people mention are, like, the Bumble CEO Whitney Wolf Heard has made comments about, “Well, what if we had AI concierges, your AI dates the other person’s AI. And then if the AIs have a good date together, then they introduce the people.” Or in The New York Times article, Marissa Mayer mentioned, “Well, what if my AI could coordinate with my husband’s AI” and stuff like that. And I think that it feels like people are trying to over-optimize out of just having conversations with people. I’ve already seen that happen in my generation, where I do notice in myself that if I’m ordering takeout, it feels weird to call a place. I’m just so used to, “Well, obviously you can do it online and you don’t have to talk to anyone. And I feel like there’s just going to be more of these things, where basic human interaction gets more and more optimized out of actually occurring. And call me old-school, but I think that humans being able to talk to each other is probably a net positive for society. Sean: Yeah, but what’s the ROI, Amanda? How much revenue can you generate off of a conversation that somebody’s having in meatspace? Amanda: That is the thing, though. Dating is really inefficient. It sucks that you have to go on a bunch of dates with different people. You might waste an evening and be like, “Well, that was a bust.” And so you can see why people are [wondering,] “What if you didn’t have to go on dates? What if your AI could go on dates for you?” But there’s just something not human there. And then also, you are outsourcing the decision of who you are going to date to a computer that you are trusting knows you better than yourself, which I don’t think is true. Kirsten: One thing that I think is worth going back to, and I sort of hinted about this earlier: Who are they talking to? Who is their audience for all these optimizations, in your view? Is it a product problem, or is it a messaging problem?

events.title: Insurance unaffordable for flooded homes almost two years on from disaster
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Insurance unaffordable for north Queensland homes flooded almost two years ago Michelle Yates said her home was still being repaired after flooding in February 2025. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Home owners are struggling to obtain or afford insurance in north Queensland which is still recovering from devastating floods in early 2025. Policy holders in the town of Ingham say their insurance was not renewed after the event or had substantial premium increases. The Insurance Council of Australia says the floods generated $327 million in insured losses, and some claims were still being negotiated. Michelle Yates still hasn't finished rebuilding her kitchen or replacing water-damaged floors in her farmhouse near Ingham nearly two years after devastating floods struck north Queensland. A 15-month payout negotiation with her insurer and ongoing trades shortages have slowed the recovery. Another wet season is looming over the region and bringing a new challenge with it. The north Queensland town of Ingham flooded in the first week of February 2025. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) "We have no insurance," Ms Yates said. "Sure Insurance cancelled our policy altogether because we were flooded." Michelle Yates lives on acreage in the Hinchinbrook Shire north of Townsville. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) It is one of several instances where Sure Insurance sent a non-renewal notice to policy holders who were flooded during the 2025 event. The 2026 notices, viewed by the ABC, stated that Sure Insurance had changed its underwriting guidelines and would not offer insurance if a property made a flood claim in the past five years or had a risk of damage in a one-in-20-year flood. A spokesperson for Sure Insurance said it provided cover to one-in-four insured Ingham properties and that underwriting guidelines were reviewed regularly. "To determine our ability to provide ongoing cover at a price that is fair," they said. Ms Yates, who owns her home, says she's still looking for an affordable alternative. Without insurance home owners like Ms Yates would endure the entire cost of rebuilding or repairs in the event of damage to her property. Ingham broker Kieran Volpe said many residents were struggling to afford rising insurance premiums. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Ingham-based insurance broker Kieran Volpe said some providers were not offering cover to high-risk properties while others "priced themselves out". "We are seeing, quite commonly, quotes coming in at $10,000, $15,000 or even $20,000 in those high-risk flood areas," Mr Volpe said. Matthew Porter said his home insurance increased 74 per cent in 12 months. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) Matthew Porter bought a home in Ingham after the 2025 floods knowing it had suffered superficial flood damage in the lower, unoccupied level during the event. When his Allianz Insurance policy was due to be renewed this year the premium increased by 72 per cent. "We thought that was quite expensive and there would be something cheaper," Mr Porter said. "To our shock it was at the cheaper end." He said he opted to stay with the policy but found the increase "ridiculous". A spokesperson for Allianz said the frequency and severity of weather events in Ingham had increased in recent years and so had the cost of claims. "Premiums must reflect the genuine cost of insuring a property against these risks to ensure we can continue to pay claims when customers need us most," they said. The 2025 north Queensland floods generated $327 million in insured losses. ( ABC News: Baz Ruddick ) The Insurance Council of Australia said anyone who had received a non-renewal notice from their insurer or a significant premium hike should ask for an explanation, shop around or speak to a broker. "Insurance remains available in Ingham, but in areas exposed to repeated, severe flooding premiums will reflect that risk," a spokesperson said. "The most effective way to bring them down is to reduce the underlying risk, that requires greater investment in flood defences, house raising and more resilient homes." The spokesperson said the council remained involved in individual claims discussions from the 2025 floods and that trades shortages and steep cost increases had delayed recovery. Hinchinbrook Mayor Ramon Jayo said the insurance market was failing in north Queensland. ( ABC News: Chloe Chomicki ) The Hinchinbrook Shire Council has released new data from a community survey on insurance that heard from 305 respondents. The survey found most households within the shire maintained some form of insurance, but that underinsurance was an issue locally.

events.title: Lifelong renter now living in tent with dog after Tasmanian housing struggles
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Salvos Street 2 Home service searches for rough sleepers, amid surging demand for help The only homelessness outreach program in southern Tasmania is a team of just three people who search for rough sleepers and connect them to essential services. Street 2 Home used to operate statewide but had to close in the north and north-west because of insufficient funding. Street 2 Home is pushing for more funding to cater to what it says is a growing number of Tasmanians sleeping rough. It is eight degrees on a chilly Tuesday morning, and the Salvation Army's Street 2 Home outreach team has driven along an off-road dirt track in southern Tasmanian bushland. They are looking for Effie*, a woman living in a tent with her German shepherd, Gus. Annie finds camps of unhoused people. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Street 2 Home is the only homelessness outreach program in southern Tasmania that searches for people sleeping rough, asks if they need help, and connects them to essential services. The program says it is struggling to keep up with demand, as the numbers of people coming onto the street outpace those coming off. With extra funding, it said the program could expand state-wide, having recently closed both its north and north-west operations for financial reasons. Between 2016 and 2021, the number of homeless Tasmanians increased by 45 per cent. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Rental rejections led to the street With a life of renting under her belt, Effie* was not worried about finding somewhere to live after being evicted from her home. "I was unsuccessful for every house that I applied for," she said. Street 2 Home says it is struggling to keep up with demand for its services. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) She said the difficulty of finding a home or emergency accommodation with a dog meant she had no choice but to pitch a tent and was soon noticed by a passer-by who contacted Street 2 Home. They have visited her regularly since. "I've got the hand warmers and body warmers … my darling friend from [The Salvation Army] brings me those," Effie said. Gus watches from inside a car. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) Burden on homeless to find services themselves For a region with roughly 2,500 people experiencing homelessness, the Street 2 Home team of just three people is stretched to capacity. Program lead and outreach worker Chris Allen said many other homelessness services were based online, and this put the burden on the individual to seek out help themselves. Chris Allen is the team leader of the Salvation Army's Street 2 Home and Beyond the Wire programs. ( ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke ) "[People sleeping rough] might not have heard about a lot of the programs and a lot of the services that are designed to actually help them," he said. "Most of them won't know how to use a phone, or they don't have internet. They don't know how to look up those services and find them." People who sleep rough are often not aware of the services there are to assist them. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) Success stories few and far between What used to be a state-wide operation was scaled back to the south due to a lack of funding. In September last year, the program shut its doors in northern Tasmania, and in June this year, the north-west met the same fate. Street 2 Home says many people have complex mental health issues, addictions, low literacy and other barriers to securing housing. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) There is no limit on the number of cases or people the team supports, but this leaves it stretched thin. "The more people we come across, the less time we can spend with each individual," Mr Allen said. He said success stories were becoming rarer over the years. "We've had fewer [people getting into housing] this year than we had last year," he said. Housing waitlist times in the state have reached roughly 1.7 years, as of August this year. Mr Allen said the focus was on making it as comfortable as possible for the person experiencing homelessness, while they worked to help them find housing. In Tasmania, people deemed priority applicants can wait up to two years for public housing. ( ABC News: Owain Stia James ) "If our details are attached to [an application], we'll go out, we'll get [the person] on the phone … and we'll make sure they make it to those appointments, so they don't miss that property," Mr Allen said. Homelessness Australia director Catherine Robinson said outreach services offered "critical" human connection that online services lacked.

events.title: Trump has frank call with Netanyahu about next move in Iran war
events.summary: President Trump had a candid phone call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Saturday about the state of U.S. negotiations with Iran and how quickly to return to combat, according to one Israeli and one U.S. source. Why it matters: The sources said Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump, for now, wants to let negotiations play out — a strategy Netanyahu is concerned about. The Israeli source said the call was "tough," while the U.S. source described it as "direct." The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office declined to comment. Driving the news: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterms. Last week Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about the possibility of restarting negotiations . It was the most senior-level outreach by the U.S. to Iran in several months. Trump told reporters on Saturday that negotiations with Iran are "going fine" and noted he is not "in much of a hurry." While the Iranians want to make a deal, the president said they "are not very reliable. ... They make a deal and then they back out." At the same time, Trump said the U.S. still has to "take care" of one or two nuclear sites in Iran. "We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly," Trump said, referring to a suspected nuclear site built into a mountain. The Wall Street Journal first reported the Trump-Netanyahu call, but did not describe its contents. State of play: Qatari mediators met with Iranian officials on Sunday for the third consecutive day in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that there is no agreement yet and stressed that a deal depends on the U.S. answering Iran's questions. "We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," he said.

events.title: Thousands of public EV chargers may be unusable
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Thousands of public EV chargers are coming, but they could be unusable This kerbside charger in Bondi is used about once a week, as it's usually blocked by non-EVs. ( Supplied: Plugshare ) A program targeting high-density areas will more than double the number of public EV chargers. But many of the power pole-mounted chargers could be inaccessible to EV drivers. Data shows chargers without dedicated parking are often blocked by petrol and diesel cars. Many electric vehicle (EV) drivers know the frustration of rolling up to a public charger and finding a petrol car parked in the way. Getting "ICEd" by an internal combustion engine (ICE) car means expensive charging infrastructure goes unused and EV drivers waste time finding the next available plug. Now, neighbourly conflict over blocked chargers may be coming to a street near you. From 2027, the federal government's Accelerating EV Charging Program will see about 14,000 EV chargers installed on power poles in high-density areas in cities where residents have limited access to off-street parking. Pole-mounted chargers installed under the program will fully charge a typical EV in about eight hours. ( Supplied: Ausgrid ) Under the program's rules, installers aren't required to negotiate with councils for dedicated EV-only parking. Many in the EV industry expect the vast majority of kerbside chargers will be "undedicated", meaning they won't have EV-only parking. Data shared with the ABC suggests many newly installed chargers, partly funded through households paying higher power bills, will end up being obstructed and remain largely idle. As a result, the program's modelled emissions reductions may be wrong. Tension over parking and EV charging in congested areas About a quarter of motorists don't have off-street parking, making it difficult to charge an EV at home. In inner-city areas, the proportion is much higher. But setting aside precious parking for public EV charging can be unpopular, with EVs only accounting for about 3 per cent of cars on the road. Tensions created by high EV uptake and lack of off-street parking are already apparent in Sydney's eastern suburbs. This undedicated EV charger on Curlewis St, Bondi, has been used four times in the past 12 months. ( Supplied: Plugshare ) In the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas, more than half of residents live in apartments and EV ownership is more than three times the state average. The area has 320 public charging ports, of which 90 are undedicated and sit mostly unused due to obstruction, Anthony Weinberg, program manager for the EV charging program across the three councils, told the ABC. "Utilisation of these spots is about 5 to 10 per cent of the dedicated spots," he said. A dedicated charger on Ocean St, North Bondi, has had 988 sessions over the past year. A kilometre away, on Glenayr St, an undedicated charger of similar power has racked up 40 sessions. Another, on nearby Curlewis St, has had just four charging sessions in 12 months. "A lot of the dedicated ones are getting between two and three sessions a day, and the undedicated ones are getting a session every two days," Mr Weinberg said. "We won't install an EV charger now unless it has dedicated parking." Other councils report a similar pattern. Sydney's Inner West Council found its 78 chargers with dedicated parking were used four times more than the 68 chargers without, according to an internal report tabled in May. The report recommended "Council gradually transition non-dedicated EV charging spaces to dedicated charging spaces". Inner West Council did not respond to requests for comment. Questions over program's modelled emissions reduction The Accelerating EV Charging Program will support emissions reductions of 9.8 million tonnes of CO2, worth $802 million in value, according to modelling by the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW). The idea is more EV chargers will drive EV ownership, which will mean fewer ICE vehicles on the roads. The modelling estimates the program will fund about 14,000 new chargers, and each charger will support 30 EVs, or about 420,000 EVs in total. Most of Australia's existing 11,000 public chargers have dedicated parking, like these at Bondi Beach. ( Supplied: Waverley Council ) This estimate could be overly optimistic, according to a separate analysis of charger utilisation in the Waverley, Woollahra and Randwick council areas by Ross de Rango, director of Vehicle Charging Solutions Australia.

events.title: India's opposition parties stage new protest against the country's election chief
events.summary: It's the latest display of public dissent against PM Modi’s government. NEW DELHI -- India’s opposition parties on Sunday renewed calls for the resignation of the country’s election chief , staging a new protest in the latest display of public dissent against Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government. The protest, called by opposition bloc INDIA , drew tens of thousands of demonstrators, some carrying musical instruments and waving various flags, as they chanted slogans against the central government's policies. Several opposition parties of the alliance, formed in 2023 to unseat Modi, mobilized their cadres from different states for the protest. The demonstration came weeks after a police crackdown on protesters in New Delhi. Led by Rahul Gandhi, leader of the main opposition Congress party, and backed by the youth “Cockroach” movement , the protesters called for the safeguarding of India’s democracy while demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a contentious voter roll revision. The protesters gathered at Ramlila Maidan, a sprawling public square in New Delhi, after police last month withdrew Jantar Mantar from the list of officially designated venues for demonstrations. The historic observatory had long served as the capital’s main protest site. Addressing the rally, Gandhi said that India has faced vote theft for years. “I am telling every citizen and every youth of India that Gyanesh Kumar will have to relinquish his position. Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail,” he said in Hindi. Gandhi also accused the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, the ideological parent of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, of tightening its grip on state institutions, from the education system to investigative agencies. “Because of this, farmers, laborers and youth are being denied their rights,” he said. Authorities deployed thousands of police and paramilitary soldiers and mounted extensive surveillance, with more than 200 security cameras, drones and body-worn cameras at the venue and along the protest route, officials said. The ongoing review of voter lists has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, threatens to disenfranchise millions more, and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say The Election Commission and Modi’s administration deny the allegations and say the revision is intended to remove duplicate and ineligible entries. Human Rights Watch on Thursday said that the accusations over the voter roll revision raise “serious questions about the fairness of future Indian elections.” “The authorities should immediately scrap the voter roll revision process that has denied India’s most marginalized people their right to vote and other government services,” said Elaine Pearson, the group’s Asia director, in a statement. For weeks, the call for Kumar’s resignation has been a rallying cry for opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party seeking to challenge Modi’s Hindu nationalist BJP. Opposition parties, mainly the Congress, say the governing BJP has undertaken systemic manipulation of the electoral process, accusing the party of “vote chori,” or vote theft. Modi hasn't publicly commented on the protests. Some of his party leaders have dismissed the demonstrators as “anarchists” and suggested, without offering evidence, that they are backed by foreign powers. In July, protests led by the youth “cockroach” movement forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister , a rare setback for Modi, who has been in power for more than 12 years. The movement began as an online satirical campaign this summer after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites. Suresh Sharma, a protester from northern Haryana state, said that the country’s system needed reform because democracy was being throttled. The process of voter roll revision needs to be scrapped, Sharma said. “We demand that Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar resign and be arrested,” he said. 1 dead, 6 injured in 'targeted' shooting at California Halloween store 24/7 coverage of breaking news and live events

events.title: TechCrunch Mobility: A new, bigger AV boom is here
events.summary: Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now. Founder Summit begins Nov. 4, 9:00 a.m. ET. Get your pass savings & deals before it starts. REGISTER HERE. Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility ! I’ve joked here and on the Equity and Autonocast podcasts that the autonomous vehicle industry feels a lot like 2016, at least in terms of the buzziness surrounding the sector. But a recent conversation with Trucks VC partner Puneeth Meruva has me rethinking that comparison. There’s evidence that 2026 is even hotter — at least by certain measures — than those frothy dealmaking days of 2016 and 2017. Trucks VC, which specializes in early-stage investing, has fielded pitches from 81 new autonomous vehicle startups so far in 2026 — two-thirds more than last year and enough to surpass the boom years of a decade ago. The VC firm argues in a new blog post that we’re in the midst of a second, even bigger AV wave fueled by technological breakthroughs. Yes, I’m talking about AI. “For a long time AV companies were trying to go from what was AV 1.0 to AV 2.0, which is kind of this holy grail end-to-end architecture for AVs,” Meruva told me. “And I think the foundation models now provide a technical architecture that makes those end-to-end systems possible.” These foundational models are particularly good at generalizing across different environments and scenarios, potentially making AVs cheaper and faster to deploy. The arrival of powerful open source models like Nvidia’s Alpamayo and Qwen’s general-purpose vision-language-action models has made it even easier for startups to get off the ground. The barrier to entry is lower than ever before. Meruva said Trucks is consistently seeing startups deploy within a few months and with less than $1 million raised. (And while Meruva wouldn’t name names, the firm has invested in some of them.) Of these 81 startups that pitched Trucks VC, I mistakenly assumed most would be applying their AV tech to construction, warehouse, agriculture, and mining. And yes, those were in the mix. But what surprised me was the growing number of startups pitching pure-play robotaxi businesses. And many are positioning themselves as direct competitors to Waymo. As wild and galaxy brain-thinking as that may sound, Meruva thinks there is room for smaller players. “In this world, smaller, more niche autonomy companies can compete — maybe they’re not competing with Waymo on a global scale, but maybe they’re competing in specific regions or specific types of routes,” he said. And Meruva doesn’t see the pace flattening. He expects even more AV startups to pitch the firm next year. Regular readers of this newsletter know we’ve been closely following Slate Auto — breaking the original story on Jeff Bezos’ investment way back in April 2025. But the company it spun out of is what got our attention this week. Re:Build , a Massachusetts-based manufacturing accelerator, raised $2.1 billion to “expand Re:Build’s capacity to manufacture hard tech products and launch new industrial startups.” The investment was led by General Catalyst and JPMorganChase’s Strategic Investment Group. Other investors weren’t disclosed. The company, which was co-founded by Amazon’s former commercial CEO Jeff Wilke, has billed itself as “America’s answer to Shenzhen.” Bedrock Robotics raised $600 million in a funding round that values the autonomous vehicle technology startup at $4.1 billion. CapitalG and Emergence Capital co-led the Series C round. New investors US Innovative Technology Fund (USIT), Bessemer Venture Partners, and Temasek participated in the round, alongside existing investors 8VC, Georgian, Valor Equity Partners, Xora, Eclipse, Perry Creek Capital, and Nvidia. DoorDash has agreed to acquire Instacart for $17 billion. Meanwhile, DoorDash noted in its third-quarter earnings that it has, so far, only received a few hundred orders from AI agents . PreScalar , a San Francisco-based startup developing software and testing infrastructure for factories, raised $7 million in seed funding co-led by Dynamo Ventures and BMW i Ventures, with participation from Blue Wire Capital, Uplift Ventures, and Antler. The startup was founded last year by a trio who had stints at Cruise, Google, Rivian, and Waymo. Elroy Air , a startup developing autonomous heavy-cargo drones for defense, rapid response, and commercial logistics, hired Jeremy Hux as its CFO in preparation for going public. Ford announced two new EV chargers that will allow its forthcoming Fathom pickup truck to serve as a battery capable of delivering power to the home or grid. GM is embracing hybrids now. Times sure have changed! The U.S. automaker is also trying to move past the driver data-selling controversy from several years ago.

events.title: Virgin Media O2 set to cut thousands of jobs to reduce costs
events.summary: Thousands of Virgin Media O2 staff are facing redundancy as the telecoms firm attempts to save money in the face of billions of pounds of debt and tougher competition. The broadband provider has not finalised the number of roles to be cut but it is likely be a sizeable chunk of its 16,000-strong workforce, the BBC understands. Virgin Media O2 has billions in debt on its balance sheet and is tackling both smaller providers as well as giants like BT, which has agreed a deal to acquire rival TalkTalk, which Virgin Media O2 has firmly opposed. The company declined to comment. Prospect, a union which represents Virgin Media O2 staff, said the cuts were "disappointing and very unsettling". Noel McClean. deputy general secretary at Prospect, said the union was "committed to supporting our members through what is a difficult time, as well as also working with employers to explore ways to mitigate the number of redundancies and ensure retraining and redeployment of staff affected". The majority of the affected staff are in roles that are not customer-facing and a number of senior leadership changes are already under way, the BBC has been told. Virgin Media O2 is also expected to review its use of contractors and suppliers in conjunction with the job cuts. As of 30 June, Virgin Media O2's total liabilities stands at £27.2bn while it holds assets worth £45.9bn, according to the firm's latest accounts. Meanwhile, the company is dealing with fierce competition from cheaper "altnets" like Hyperoptic, Community Fibre, Gigaclear and YouFibre. Virgin Media O2 had attempted to respond to this growing threat by buying altnet competitor Netomnia for £2bn via nexfibre, a joint venture owned by Virgin Media O2's owners. However, the Competition Markets Authority (CMA) has provisionally found competition concerns in the deal , external , with a final decision to come in December, sparking anger from Virgin Media O2. In October, Virgin Media O2 called the BT's agreed takeover of TalkTalk a "stitch-up" that had allowed its rival to "tighten its grip" over the market. BT said its deal provided "a safety net" for TalkTalk customers as their broadband provider faced collapse without the takeover. On Friday, BT's share price jumped 7% after the Financial Times reported Virgin Media O2 was close to agreeing a deal , external to use its rival's fibre broadband network. events.title: Global energy giants gather in Abu Dhabi as Adipec prepares for record exhibition
events.summary: Some of the world's biggest energy companies will converge on Abu Dhabi on Monday as Adipec prepares to stage what organisers say will be its largest exhibition yet, bringing together industry leaders, ministers and investors amid heightened concerns over energy security and global supply disruptions. The four-day event, running from November 2 to 5, is expected to feature a record 2,260 exhibiting companies, including 54 national and international energy companies, as well as more than 40 government ministers. Organisers expect more than 239,000 attendees from more than 170 countries, with all 16 exhibition halls at Adnec Centre Abu Dhabi booked, prompting them to build additional structures and relocate the opening ceremony to accommodate demand. BP, Shell, TotalEnergies, Eni, ExxonMobil, Chevron and Occidental Petroleum are among the major energy companies listed as exhibitors, alongside technology and industrial groups including Siemens, IBM and Microsoft. “The industry's commitment to Adipec is clear,” Christopher Hudson, president of organiser dmg events, said. “We have a record-breaking 2,260 exhibiting companies, with the exhibition venue fully sold out and additional structures built to accommodate demand.” The gathering comes as governments and companies reassess energy supplies, infrastructure investment and trade routes following months of disruption to global oil and gas markets. Energy security, AI, electricity demand and the financing of new infrastructure are expected to dominate discussions. Energy giants showcase new technology Several major companies have independently confirmed their participation, outlining plans to demonstrate technologies designed to improve operational efficiency, strengthen infrastructure and reduce emissions. US oilfield services company Halliburton said it would showcase advanced drilling and completions technologies, production optimisation systems and AI-powered tools. Its chairman and chief executive, Jeff Miller, is scheduled to address the conference on Tuesday, discussing how energy companies can navigate volatility while maintaining profitability. Industrial automation group Emerson has also confirmed its attendance, with plans to demonstrate AI-enabled software, autonomous operations and advanced instrumentation aimed at improving reliability and project execution. GE Vernova, the US energy equipment manufacturer, said it would showcase advanced gas turbines, electricity grid modernisation and carbon management technologies. Schneider Electric, meanwhile, will focus on autonomous operations and AI-driven technologies. Research released by the French company ahead of Adipec found that 76 per cent of surveyed Middle East energy leaders had increased investment in autonomous technology over the past year. SLB, another major US oilfield services group, plans to demonstrate AI-enabled drilling, reservoir management and digital technologies aimed at improving production efficiency. Industrial software company Aveva will showcase digital twins and connected industrial intelligence, while Honeywell is expected to demonstrate AI-driven autonomous upstream operations. The technology focus comes as energy companies increase their AI spending , with an Adnoc and Microsoft study finding that 89 per cent of surveyed energy leaders had raised investment over the past year. However, the industry's growing reliance on AI presents challenges of its own, with a separate Adipec survey finding that 81 per cent of energy executives believe electricity demand from AI will exceed existing forecasts. Abu Dhabi's Enersol, the energy technology investment platform jointly owned by Adnoc Drilling and Alpha Dhabi Holding, will also highlight technologies developed and manufactured in the UAE. Asia's growing influence Asia will send its largest delegation yet , with 353 companies and six national pavilions representing China, India, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore and South Korea. Participants include China's Sinopec, CNPC and CNOOC, battery manufacturer Catl, Malaysia's Petronas and Japan's Inpex and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. The record Asian presence follows major disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical route for global oil and gas supplies. Before the war, nearly 90 per cent of crude oil and condensate shipments passing through the waterway were destined for Asia, according to the US Energy Information Administration, with China accounting for 38 per cent. The disruption to shipping earlier this year triggered what the International Energy Agency described as the largest supply disruption in oil market history. For Asian energy buyers, Adipec offers an opportunity to engage with Gulf producers on supply security, infrastructure investment and long-term partnerships. “Asia is at the centre of global energy demand growth,” Abdulmunim Al Kindy, chairman of Adipec 2026, said last month. Mr Al Kindy has also highlighted how Adnoc's contingency planning helped maintain production during the Iran war. The opening day's programme will feature an address by Dr Sultan Al Jaber, Minister of Industry and Advanced Technology and managing director and group chief executive of Adnoc. Adipec 2026: Opening ceremony A ministerial discussion on energy security will bring together UAE Energy Minister Suhail Al Mazrouei and his counterparts from Germany, Turkey and Egypt. Other executives scheduled to speak include BP chief executive Meg O'Neill, Siemens chief executive Roland Busch, Baker Hughes chief executive Lorenzo Simonelli and Inpex chief executive Takayuki Ueda. The exhibition also follows Adnoc's announcement of Dh60 billion in manufacturing opportunities for UAE suppliers, aimed at strengthening domestic supply chains and reducing dependence on imports. Commercial agreements will also be in focus. Last year's Adipec recorded 49,131 agreements worth $53 billion, according to organisers, with further announcements expected during this year's event.

events.title: You should pick your credit card perks like Warren Buffett picks his stocks, TD Bank exec says
events.summary: If you’re a Boglehead like myself, you can talk endlessly about the compounding powers of the three-fund “lazy portfolio”: some bonds, some domestic stocks, and some international ones. Set it and forget it; never look at it again until you need to. If you don’t feel comfortable with the three-fund portfolio, you might want to get a financial advisor who can pick specific stocks for you for an AUM. The opportunity cost is in your head: For a low-expense ratio, you can have some ETFs that fit the three-fund portfolio, or you can shove all decision-making onto an advisor who will charge more to manage your portfolio. All it means is someone or something will be managing your money, and depending on the amount of effort and work you want to put into it, you can pay a higher fee and get it done for you for potentially higher rewards (although FAs rarely beat the market returns of ETFs) or grab a low-expense ratio fund and call it a day. If you’re a Warren Buffett aficionado, you’ll recognize this as his ever-touted “circle of competence,” in which you stick to what you know and leave what you don’t know to those, well, who know. Invest in what you understand and on things that have long-term value, and leave the frequent trading and market volatility to those who know what they’re doing. It seems as if the king of compounding’s philosophy might not just work for investing but also for picking credit cards—and the perks you get with them. And so it makes the same sense with credit cards too: you can grab a high-annual fee card that comes with all these perks and so-called “freebies,” or if you don’t want to shuffle through a rolodex that explains credit card maxxing, you might just settle on a simple no-fee card with cash back bonuses. At least that’s according to Chris Fred, TD Bank’s head of credit cards and unsecured lending, who said sometimes, points chasing (or “churning,” as those in the know call it) might prove too difficult for the average person. “Just like Warren Buffett says to buy the index fund, a good flat‑rate card often wins out over all the fancy bonus categories,” Fred told Fortune. The concept is simple, à la Buffett: If you know what you’re doing, you are fully encouraged to open several cards, each with various amounts of points or cash back per category. If you don’t, you should stick to the “circle of competence” and opt for a blanket cash-back card so you’re not trying to day trade at the checkout counter. How do you maximize credit cards points? Churning, although a fairly new (within the last three decades) concept with regard to credit cards, might be as old as personal finance itself. You might remember the App-O-Rama days of the aughts, in which people tried to fool financial institutions by opening multiple credit cards at once so as not to tank one’s credit score with each pull. In 1999, David Phillips brought churning to the mainstream by taking advantage of a pudding promotion to earn over 1.25 million frequent-flier miles. (For what it’s worth, credit card perks had just started—take a blast from the past and go though the 2003 web page of Amex’s offerings to see the beginnings of credit card perks). In the 1900s, banks would encourage folks to open savings accounts with a free $100 or so deposit. And even in the 700s and onwards, people were purchasing silver coins at face value and turning them into the mint in England for new coins, worth more than their initial purchasing price. Long story short, churning, in various forms, has been around for a while. In the credit card world, the r/churning subreddit boasts nearly 30,000 weekly visitors, and even has a whole FAQ section about dissuading the average person from engaging in churning, offering several reasons that Fred agrees with. “People think, ‘I can always beat that 2%.’ On average, they don’t,” Fred said. Fred referenced TD Bank’s three credit card offerings, which include 2% cash back on everything, and another base 1% cash back on everything in addition to 2% to 3% cash back on select categories. When compared with other card issuers that have cardholders deliberating over which card to use at the pump versus the restaurant table, Fred said, the mental math just isn’t worth it for the average consumer, especially when they never end up beating the blanket 2% cash back they are guaranteed to get with other cards. Take, for example, a premium card that offers 4x on dining but only 1x on pharmacies and basic goods. It offers 3x on groceries, 1.5x on travel, but not transportation. The points on dining and groceries may very well exceed the 2% cash back from other cards, but it would be offset by the 1x and 1.5x elsewhere. Then add in those with multiple cards, and you have cardholders who, Fred joked, would need to constantly refer to a spreadsheet to ensure they are getting the most bang for buck—when a blanket 2% cash back would leave the cardholder without a care in the world knowing they’re getting the most they’ll get. How much are the annual fees? That’s just the points/cash-back debate. Add in the exorbitant annual fees, and it really becomes a race to use all of your cards’ perks. “The higher the fee, the more benefits you tend to have,” Fred said. “It’s a dangerous proposition: You’d better start using those benefits, or it’s going to be really hard to justify the fee.” Some of these cards can cost nearly $1,000, but are marketed as being worth thousands more in perks, only if the cardholder remembers to use it accordingly. Use one card and get a monthly takeout or rideshare credit; use another and get a semiannual hotel bonus or early access to restaurant reservations or exclusive sporting events. These are designed in a way to discourage using them, Fred said. There’s a reason you have to opt into an offer on your credit card’s portal instead of it being automatically applied as a bill credit. And it’s also the reason that keeps customers coming back. “Those customers are sticky. They know they’re spending a certain amount each year in annual fees, so they’re vested,” Fred said. That’s not to mention how some card fees keep going up, and annual fees are climbing on entry-level cards, too. American Airlines announced that it will raise the fee on its Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard to $150 from $99, its first increase since 2018, and the business version of the card will cost $150 as well. But in exchange, cardholders get three times the miles on hotels booked through American’s portal, a credit of up to $120 every four years toward Global Entry or TSA PreCheck, and a $100 annual statement credit for in-flight purchases that replaces the old 25% discount on food and drinks. United and other rivals have raised fees on similar cards, and entry-level airline cards that once cost about $100 are moving closer to $150. events.title: Guarding the Gates of Knowledge
events.summary: A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion. Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must. Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “ I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper ,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses. “He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.” Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it. Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions , Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools. “Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.” If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty . Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity. Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”

events.title: Behind the Curtain: OpenAI's post-election power play
events.summary: Right after Tuesday's midterms, OpenAI will unleash a policy and PR blitz to try to get in sync with the new Washington, including an effort to rebrand data centers as "AI compute campuses." Why it matters: After two years of a friendly White House, AI companies will face a harsher Washington after Tuesday, when Democrats will likely win the House. OpenAI also aims to help frame the AI debate for the big field of 2028 presidential contenders that'll start forming on Wednesday. "You can try to chase the moment, or seek to inform the moment via the power of ideas," OpenAI chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane tells us, calling Tuesday an "electoral portal from one era to the next." Since August, Lehane and his team have been stockpiling policy proposals, some new and some repackaged, to drive urgency and steer the AI debate. It'll all start during the lame-duck session of Congress — the awkward but often consequential weeks between the election and the swearing-in of new members and senators on Jan. 3. This year's lame duck opens Nov. 9. The big picture: Other tech companies are also positioning themselves for a potential blue wave. Meta is taking steps to strengthen its ties with Democrats, Axios' Sara Fischer scooped Saturday . Other big AI and tech players can be expected to do the same. Tech titans who enjoy close relationships with President Trump will be top targets for Democrats, who are eager to ramp up scrutiny and regulatory pressure on the industry. OpenAI's plans, being revealed here for the first time, all involve control — trying to send the message that AI is being built for people, not to displace people. The proposals include: Speed limits: Building on earlier proposals , OpenAI plans to unveil new ideas for mandatory safeguards for the most powerful AI systems — speed limits for AI that will allow humans to keep their hands on the wheel. This'll include a more aggressive congressional drive. "You're going to see us talk more and more about the concept of speed limits," Lehane said. "Our belief is people should always remain in control of this technology. AI should be built by and for people, and people should have more control over how the technology shapes their lives and communities." Data centers: OpenAI hopes to stem the nationwide, bipartisan backlash by offering new community compacts and commitments to smooth the way for future data centers. In addition, the company will try to set a new industry standard by proposing state legislation that gives people a meaningful say in how projects are built and what benefits they receive. In an intentionally provocative rebranding effort, OpenAI will argue that the infrastructure it's building, in contrast to legacy data centers, should be called "AI compute campuses" that can economically transform host communities. OpenAI points to its role in developing a huge data center project that promises to bring thousands of jobs to Pike County in Ohio's Appalachian region. "We think the conversation is good and healthy," Lehane said. "It's democracy in action. Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects." Economic opportunity: OpenAI is developing ideas to help more people see AI as empowering for their daily lives and on the job, including supporting workers through disruption, widening access to education and training, and making it easier to start and grow a business. International cooperation: OpenAI will push for the U.S. to shape global standards with AI built on democratic values. Between the lines: OpenAI is trying to stake out a human-centered "third path" in a debate that often defaults to an artificial binary of doomers vs. accelerationists. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, speaking to the UN Security Council in September, called for an AI approach that leads to a "new Renaissance of creativity and discovery." What we're watching: OpenAI's overtures are aimed partly at 2028 presidential hopefuls, who'll be increasingly vocal about their plans starting Wednesday. "AI is going to be the issue in 2028," Lehane said, calling the midterms a "bit of a movie trailer for what you're going to see in 2028." "I don't think it's going to be good enough just to say 'AI bad,'" Lehane added. "The public gets that this is a much more complex, nuanced conversation. They're going to be looking for whoever their FDR or Lincoln is who's actually going to want to try to lead them through this journey." Lehane said candidates should ask: "How do we start to think about trust? How do we think about the incredible anxiety that exists in modernity? How do we think about the fact that people are profoundly unhappy with where their social contract is, where the American dream is?" The bottom line: The plans for the coming months are just the beginning of OpenAI's effort to inject more urgency in Washington and push the industry on frontier safety. Remember: Every day, AI models get more powerful — and tougher to corral. "Our policy priorities — and urgency, especially on frontier safety — are about meeting the moment in response to the rapidly advancing capabilities," Lehane said. "And we expect that to continue as a new Congress ramps up." Axios' Bradley Olson contributed. Disclosure: Axios has a content licensing and technology agreement with OpenAI, emphasizing expansion of local news coverage. Go deeper : "AI governing the AI world."

events.title: Crypto firm Binance covers 90% of losses after $6.3bn hack
events.summary: Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, says it has covered 90% of the $6.3bn (£4.7bn) assets stolen in a hack on Thursday. The remaining 10% may take longer to source in the required amounts, the company added. Binance has consistently pledged to cover 100% of the losses from what is suspected to be crypto's biggest hack on record and said it has set aside more than $6.34bn in company funds to do so. "Binance will absorb the financial impact of these stolen funds, not our users," the company said in a statement on Saturday. In an update on Sunday, Binance said withdrawals had been restored on several of its networks, after they were suspended following the hack. It previously said withdrawals would be resumed in phases. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said on Saturday that North Korea was responsible for the attack. The FBI said it had observed hackers converting stolen assets into a type of cryptocurrency called Ethereum and that it is expected that the assets will then be converted again using decentralised finance and instant swap services. Two analytics firms previously told the BBC they had robust intelligence pointing to North Korean state-backed hacking unit the Lazarus Group, also known as TraderTraitor - which was specifically named by the FBI - as the likely culprits. Speaking to reporters on Saturday night, US President Donald Trump said , external the US is still unsure who the culprits are. "We're learning about it. We don't know if it's North Korea - but if it is, we'll talk to North Korea about it," he said. Binance said it had replenished the stolen assets using various funds and its own corporate treasury. All holdings of the cryptocurrencies bitcoin, Ethereum and Tether are covered, along with seven other widely-traded crypto assets, the company said. From Bitcoin to Binance: Crypto terms and what they mean The hack is believed to be the largest in history, eclipsing the record of a $1.5bn heist on the Bybit exchange in 2025 - for which the FBI also said North Korea was responsible. North Korea has always denied involvement in these attacks. Binance's initial investigation suggested an engineer's laptop was compromised, which allowed access to unauthorised withdrawals, but a later update said they had uncovered "additional points of breach". Richard Teng, Binance's co-chief executive officer, said the hack was carried out by more than one person, and the hackers used sophisticated methods to hide their tracks, such as a "self-destruct mechanism". On Friday, the company said it had frozen around $3bn of stolen assets after working with law enforcement, intelligence firms and partners. The investigation is ongoing, it added. The US Secret Service said on Friday it is "working around the clock" with private sector partners "to identify, freeze, trace, and recover funds" stolen from Binance. Binance, founded in China in 2017, lets users buy, sell and trade digital assets - it is estimated to have hundreds of millions of users worldwide. Crypto is a digital asset, which doesn't exist physically and is instead accessed via digital wallets or computers. events.title: Australia nears 'largest property downturn in 40 years' as prices plunge
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 'Largest property downturn in 40 years' in sight as house prices fall for seventh time Bidders are nervous at auctions. ( ABC News: Ben Cocklin ) The median value of Australian homes has dropped $63,400 since March. The decline is tracking faster than any past downturn over the past 40 years. Experts predict it will be some time until interest rates start to fall and the market turns. National house prices have fallen for a seventh consecutive month, with the speed of the decline in home values tracking at the fastest pace seen over the past 40 years, according to property research group Cotality. Its latest national Home Value Index (HVI) was down 1.2 per cent in October and is now 6.7 per cent below its March peak, equivalent to a decline of about $63,400 in the value of the median Australian dwelling. The index shows the median national house price now stands at $884,855. Cotality head of research Gerard Burg said the speed of decline was tracking faster than any previous downturn over the past 40 years, with capital city values down 8.1 per cent in seven months. Virtually every suburb across Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide has recorded a drop in values over the past three months as buyers have struggled to get loans because of higher interest rates. Investor demand has also been waning because of the federal government's budget changes to property tax breaks. "This is really a demand-led downturn," Mr Burg said. "That's reduced the borrowing capacity of households, but also increased the repayments for people to make on a mortgage, and it's pushed a lot of buyers to the side." Gerard Burg says house prices will fall further. ( ABC News: Kyle Harley ) Mr Burg is among many economists anticipating higher rates for longer and further house price falls. "The previous record was 2017 through 2019, which stood at 8.2 per cent [falls] across the combined capital cities. Now, at the moment, as of October, the downturn that we've seen over the past seven months is 8.1 per cent, so it looks like we're easily going to push past that mark." Mr Burg said the downturn should be considered in the context of a steep rise in prices before the decline. "But a city like Melbourne has comparatively little further to go and I think we're already seeing that in the dynamics of Melbourne values at the present." People with established mortgages in some cities will be particularly insulated. "However, given the magnitude of the upswing prior to the downturn, most home owners in these cities are likely to be sitting on a significant equity buffer," Cotality said in its release. "For example, a 20 per cent drop in Perth home value from their record high would take the market back to levels recorded in around mid-2025. "Home owners in Melbourne and Sydney aren't in as strong an equity position, with Melbourne home values 7.3 per cent lower than five years ago and Sydney values 1.5 per cent below October 2021 levels. ACT values are virtually unchanged from five years ago." How much further will house prices fall? Home sales have dropped sharply as demand weakens. Cotality puts the number of home sales over the past three months 23 per cent lower than a year ago and 18 per cent below the previous five-year average. With fewer buyers, selling homes has become harder. Auction clearance rates across the combined capitals are consistently tracking below 50 per cent, while private treaty metrics have also weakened. The median time on market, at 39 days, is the highest since August 2020, while vendor discounting, at 4.7 per cent, is the largest since May 2019. Mr Burg said buyers would hold back until the Reserve Bank of Australia indicated a different direction on rates, and that likely would not happen until the latter half of 2027. "The eventual recovery that we do see in the housing market is likely to be more subdued than we've seen in previous episodes," Mr Burg said. "It [the RBA] doesn't necessarily require rates to come down, but [give] the clear signal that that is the direction that they are going to take." Domain's chief economist Nicola Powell said rate cuts might not be on the agenda until well into next year before. "We need something to change to improve buyer confidence. And that isn't going to come at least until we have the discussion of a potential rate cut. And that's unlikely to happen until the latter part of 2027." Nicola Powell says it could be well into next year before rate cuts are on the agenda.
