events.title: Why Florida Republicans are "white-knuckled" about Tuesday
events.summary: Florida Republicans aren't panicking about sluggish turnout for the midterms , but in the words of one GOP elder: "We're white-knuckled." Why it matters: Florida once looked like a much safer Republican bet for the midterms. Losing any statewide race would stun and embarrass its elite Republican residents, starting with President Trump . "I don't necessarily want to be the bearer of bad news, but I don't think the turnout is as strong as we would like to see," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis fretted last week. The biggest GOP concern is U.S. Rep. Byron Donalds' campaign for governor, though most polls show him narrowly leading Democrat David Jolly. Donalds has raised $176 million; Jolly just $28 million. Zoom in : The GOP's jitters are rooted in early turnout data. Republicans led Democrats in early ballots cast by 3 percentage points as of Sunday morning. That's much lower than in the past two general elections — and it's despite a much-bigger Republican registration advantage over Democrats: 11 points. Republican turnout is weakest in parts of the conservative Panhandle and rural North Florida, including many of the 17 counties Donalds lost in the Republican primary. In those 17 counties, GOP turnout is 3.2 points below 2022, compared with 1.1 points below in counties that Donalds won, University of Florida political scientist Michael McDonald found. Between the lines: Republican turnout is made up of more habitual voters, while Democrats and independents are banking ballots from people who don't always show up. That could benefit Jolly if polls underestimate those voters. Democrats already have surpassed their entire 2022 early and mail-in vote totals in 15 counties, compared with four counties for Republicans. Nearly every poll shows independent voters favoring Democrats by double digits, so Republicans need a heavy turnout advantage. About two-thirds of Florida voters typically cast ballots before Election Day, making the early and absentee margins critical. Among voters who waited until Election Day in 2022, roughly 60,000 more Republicans than Democrats have already voted this year, Democratic strategist Steve Schale found. That means some voters Republicans rely on for their Election Day surge in 2022 have already cast ballots — potentially shrinking their usual Tuesday advantage. The big picture: Donalds could enter Election Day down by as many as 500,000 votes, according to internal Democratic and GOP estimates shared with Axios. To overcome that deficit, Donalds could need to win the Election Day vote by a 2:1 ratio. It's a tall order, but Republicans have delivered huge Election Day margins before, notably in 2022. By the numbers: Black and Hispanic voters, who are leaning more toward Democrats this year in Florida polling, are making up a growing share of the early electorate, accounting for a larger share of newly reported ballots. Across racial and ethnic groups , Democrats are voting at higher rates than Republicans. Among active Democrats, 50% of white voters, 39% of Black voters and 34% of Hispanic voters have cast ballots, compared with 35%, 21% and 28% of Republicans in those groups. Young voters show another substantial gap: 25% of active registered Democrats under 30 have voted, compared with just 9% of Republicans. Yes, but: Florida Republicans still outnumber Democrats by 1.5 million, with a larger pool of reliable voters. Florida's GOP is better funded and organized than the state's Democratic Party. Even in 2018, when a blue wave flooded the nation, Florida's red wall held. By razor-thin margins, DeSantis won the governor's race and then-Gov. Rick Scott was elected to the Senate. "We always win Election Day, and we know how to do this," state GOP chair Evan Power said. "A lot of the nerves here are because the last time we had a close election was eight years ago, and people forgot what a close election looks like here." Zoom out: Republicans face a different political climate than in 2018, when Trump was ascendant in the GOP and the economy was improving. Today, Trump's approval with Republicans is lower and gas prices are higher. Republicans worry they could lose 10 to 15 state House seats, jeopardizing their supermajority. In Miami's 27th Congressional District, voting patterns are flashing warning signs for Republican Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar in her race against Democrat Eliot Rodriguez. As for the three statewide Florida Cabinet posts (attorney general, chief financial officer, agriculture commissioner), "no one should feel safe, but there's reason to feel OK," said a Republican involved one of the races. Nationwide , the atmosphere is so bad for the GOP that Texas, Kansas, Alaska, Ohio and even South Carolina look in play. Behind the scenes : The early voting data sent a chill through Republican ranks in Tallahassee last week: What if the polling assumptions about stronger Republican turnout were wrong? "Just a few weeks ago I didn't think I would be feeling like this," a top consultant for one of the statewide races said. "It's not panic. At least not yet." Republicans remain more confident about Sen. Ashley Moody's race against state Rep. Angie Nixon, who's widely seen as too progressive for the red state's voters. Friction point: Republicans have quietly fretted that racism could hurt Donalds just as it may hurt Nixon. Donalds and Nixon are Black. "We're about to run the biggest experiment to see how racist some of our voters are," a longtime Republican consultant said, calling the counties Donalds lost "more culturally Confederate" than the rest of Florida. "During the primary, he underperformed in the Panhandle and if people think skin color didn't play a role in that, they are naive," MAGA influencer Laura Loomer posted Saturday on X.

events.title: Opec+ holds December oil output targets steady as Iran war disrupts supply
events.summary: The Opec+ bloc kept its oil production targets unchanged for December, maintaining September's required production levels as the war in the Middle East continues to disrupt global energy supplies. The group's seven core members – Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Algeria, Russia and Kazakhstan – decided during a meeting on Sunday to “maintain September 2026 required production for December 2026” after reviewing global market conditions and the outlook, a statement said. The group finished unwinding 1.65 million barrels per day of voluntary cuts from 2023 in September. It is keeping a further two million bpd of cuts, agreed to in 2022, in place until the end of the year. It is also reviewing members' production capacity to set quotas for 2027. The seven Opec+ countries “reiterated their collective commitment to achieve full conformity with the Declaration of Co-operation”, the statement said. The producers will continue holding monthly meetings to review market conditions, with the next scheduled for November 29. The joint production targets for the seven members amount to about 31 million bpd for December, unchanged from September, October and November. Saudi Arabia has the largest allocation at 10.478 million bpd, followed by Russia at 9.949 million bpd and Iraq at 4.431 million bpd. Kuwait's target is 2.676 million bpd, Kazakhstan's at 1.628 million bpd, Algeria's at 1.007 million bpd and Oman's at 841,000 bpd. But most members are producing below their targets because of the war. The group reaffirmed its commitment to market stability, although the statement did not announce any additional production adjustments or provide a timetable for increasing output. The Strait of Hormuz , which carried about a fifth of the world's crude oil and liquefied natural gas, has been effectively shut since fighting between the US and Iran started on February 28. The conflict, now in its ninth month, has no clear endgame in sight. Fears are growing that the US might resume hostilities on Iran after the midterm elections, with President Donald Trump saying the war “will be wrapped up soon”. Israeli media reports, meanwhile, claim that the country's military is preparing for the possibility of another round of conflict with Iran, although Mr Trump has yet to make a decision on launching a new military campaign. Attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strait reached their highest monthly level in the Iran-US war in October, with at least 35 attacks reported, according to maritime incident tracking data. Increasing attacks from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia have also added to regional tension. On Saturday, Riyadh said its air defences had “intercepted and destroyed a hostile drone” in the Saudi capital. That followed dozens of Houthi strikes on Saudi assets over the past weeks. Oil prices settled up more than 2 per cent on Friday to hit six-month highs and post a fourth straight monthly gain. Brent was up 2.4 per cent at $117.64 a barrel, after briefly touching $118, while West Texas Intermediate gained 2.08 per cent to settle at $104.12 a barrel.

events.title: Trump's election probes find an opening in Georgia
events.summary: On the eve of midterms, President Trump is facing setbacks left and right in his push to investigate alleged election fraud . But in Georgia, he has an opening. Why it matters: Six years ago, Georgia was at the epicenter of Trump's efforts to overturn the 2020 presidential election. Now the state's own election board has invited his administration to investigate its voting system. Georgia features two high-stakes statewide campaigns: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) against Rep. Mike Collins (R) for Senate, and former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) against businessman Rick Jackson (R) for governor. The big picture: The Justice Department disclosed in court on Friday that the administration has sent letters to officials in California, Washington, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada, asking some states to segregate mail-in ballots from suspected noncitizen voters. A federal judge on Friday issued an emergency order that blocks federal officials from threatening to charge election officials who count ballots from voters the DOJ claims are ineligible. In October, a federal judge restricted the Department of Homeland Security's investigations into suspected noncitizen voters. But Georgia is different . "We've managed with duct tape and bubble gum to be able to bootstrap our way through one last round, but that's not a way of running elections," a Georgia election official told Axios. Georgia's State Election Board asked the Justice and Homeland Security departments to review and potentially investigate the state's voting system and handling of election data. The Sept. 30 letter cited outdated software, threats to ballot secrecy and QR-code ballots it says may violate the Help America Vote Act. A DOJ spokesperson said in response to the letter: "We take seriously allegations that election officials have failed to adequately maintain election equipment and otherwise comply with federal law. We are evaluating the request and will investigate and, if appropriate, bring an enforcement action consistent with federal law." The other side: Georgia State Election Board Chair John Fevrier , appointed by Gov. Brian Kemp (R), opposed the letter and told Axios that a majority of the board now believes it "far exceeded what was in the resolution." Michon Lindstrom, senior director of communications for Georgia's secretary of state, said: "It's unfortunate that the state election board sought to inject chaos in the 11th hour of the election." In 2020, Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger rebuffed Trump's efforts to overturn Georgia's presidential election results. Friction point: Georgia has spent years debating how to address vulnerabilities in its voting system. The secretary of state's office said Georgia's machines haven't been updated since they were purchased in 2019. The state said it's starting a procurement process for new machines for the next election cycle. The state's legislature passed a law in 2024 to move away from a QR-code ballot system to hand-marked paper ballots. This transition was supposed to be implemented by this July, but lawmakers passed a deadline extension. A software glitch on the state's tabulators that could impact ballot secrecy has been known to the state since 2022. But an available fix hasn't been installed. Between the lines: "There are no clean hands in this," the Georgia election official told Axios. "The secretary of state could have fought harder for the funding... [The] legislature could have funded it when the secretary of state asked for it. But ... they all have pissed each other off so much." In 2025, Raffensperger urged lawmakers to reconsider a $47 million voting-machine upgrade, proposing a software update costing less than $15 million or delaying any purchases until the existing contract expired. In 2026, Raffensperger told legislators that there wasn't money for any election upgrades. No upgrades were funded. What they're saying: "Money allocation is ultimately the function of the legislative branch, and any questions about why they did not deem it necessary to fund 'election infrastructure improvements' should be directed to the legislature," Lindstrom told Axios. Fevrier told Axios: "I blame the legislature. If the legislature thought it was an issue, they would have fixed it, and they didn't." The Department of Homeland Security didn't respond to Axios's request for comment. The bottom line: The Trump administration suffered a setback in California on Friday, with an appeals court rejecting its demand to set aside mail-in ballots. But the dispute in Georgia shows that the fight over federal intervention in state elections is far from over.

events.title: Dems and GOP quietly bankroll dozens of third-party spoilers
events.summary: More than 40 third-party candidates in pivotal House and Senate races across the country are receiving support from outside super PACs, many of which have ties to the two major parties, an Axios analysis has found. Why it matters: The sums being thrown around, which total more than $16.5 million, are far greater than virtually any of those candidates have raised or spent on their own. The super PACs have spent an average of $375,000 more than the third-party candidates they are supporting. More than half of the 43 candidates haven't filed any financial paperwork with the Federal Election Commission. While it is a comparative drop in the bucket for a midterm that has already seen billions in ad spending nationally, the money will likely play an outsized role in races that are set to be decided by razor-thin margins. Those races, in turn, will help decide the balance of power in Congress next year. Data: Federal Election Commission; Note: Heikes is a self-identified Republican, but Sen. Dan S. Sullivan is the Republican Party-endorsed candidate in the race; Table: Andrew Solender/Axios The top spenders nationwide have been a pair of obscure groups which, like many of the other "pop-up" super PACs in this story, were formed this month and therefore won't have to disclose their donors until after Election Day. Buckeye Freedom PAC has reported spending more than $3.8 million on ads in Ohio's U.S. Senate election supporting Libertarian Bill Redpath and opposing Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who is in a tight race with Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown. Alaska Values PAC has disclosed spending $3.8 million backing Gerald Heikes, a self-identified Republican running on Alaska's ranked-choice U.S. Senate ballot with Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola. Between the lines : Third-party candidates in Alaska are facing national scrutiny after the New York Times reported that Heikes and another self-proclaimed Republican on the ballot, Dan J. Sullivan, were recruited into the race. Republicans have long accused Dan J. Sullivan of being a spoiler meant to siphon votes from the incumbent senator by confusing voters with their shared name. The "double-Dan" case is unique in that it reportedly included direct involvement from a political operative working with the Peltola campaign, who allegedly used pseudonyms as part of the effort. The Peltola campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee have denied recruiting any third-party candidates into the race. Enough Promises Ohio is another huge spender, putting $2.6 million behind supporting independent Senate candidate Greg Levy in Ohio, per its FEC filings. The group's mailers encourage voters to "join the revolution" and "send a worker to the Senate" by voting for Levy, a member of the Party for Socialism and Liberation who has disavowed the support . The group's FEC filings offer hints as to its partisan affiliation: It shares vendors with several Republican candidates and groups including MAGA Inc. Principled Patriots PAC has reported spending over $600,000 on digital ads supporting right-leaning and Libertarian candidates in 15 battleground House and Senate races, according to FEC filings and Google's Ad Transparency Center. The group's vendor for its ads, Movement Labs LLC, has primarily serviced Democratic clients, filings show. It touts itself as working for "progressive change everywhere." "Washington is spending money it doesn't have. Republicans raised the debt limit $5 trillion. Darline Graham is one of them," says a Principled Patriots' ad in the South Carolina Senate race — part of a $110,000 ad buy. Constitution Party candidate Mark Hackett, the ad continues, "lives here, works here, owes party bosses nothing. Not a Democrat, not a Republican. He'll end the waste, cut spending." "I have spent no money and asked for no help in my campaign," Hackett said in an email to Axios. He said of the PACs supporting him: "I still don't know who they are." Hackett said he will "remain" in the race and suggested he is not concerned about being a spoiler for Graham "since neither Graham nor Andrews have made defunding the wars in Ukraine and Iran an issue." Progressive Champions PAC , a group Republicans used to boost their preferred Democratic primary candidates in several battleground House districts, has quietly resurfaced in a pair of hotly contested general elections. In Virginia's 2nd District, the group has reported spending over $480,000 supporting independent Matthew Baker. One of its mailers, reported by the New York Times , highlights Baker's liberal positions on issues such as abortion. Baker, a self-described "radical centrist," told the Times the mailer makes him "mad as hell" because the group is "only telling half my story" and "trying to use me to trick people." Progressive Champions PAC also spent more than $500,000 on texts and mailers boosting Green Party candidate Shafina Barnett in Michigan's 4th District, according to filings. Our Heritage Matters has reported spending nearly $3.7 million to support third-party candidates in more than two dozen House and Senate races, per FEC filings. Most of the candidates are Libertarians. The group's mailers advertise the candidates as the conservative alternative to the Republicans in each race. Much of its spending is also listed in FEC filings as being in opposition to the GOP candidates. The Nebraska Senate race has seen easily the most separate instances of super PACs boosting third-party candidates — somewhat ironically, given Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts' chief rival is independent Dan Osborn. Outside groups have reported spending more than $450,000 supporting Robin Richards of the Working People Party and $115,000 boosting Mike Marvin of the Legal Marijuana Now Party. One of the candidates, Chuck Conboy of the America First Party, is supported by Principled Patriots PAC. The intrigue: Axios reported last week that the House Democratic campaign arm put messaging guidance on its website laying out how to boost third-party candidates in several key races. It may have come in handy. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee's page on VA-02 — known as a redbox — says white, college-educated men should see that Matthew Baker is "a staunch supporter of the 2nd amendment." Our Heritage Matters began spending for Baker on Wednesday with an initial $18,000 digital ad buy, according to filings. The redbox on Nevada's 2nd District says Republican women in the district should be informed Independent American Party candidate Lynn Chapman "has spent decades fighting for conservative values." Principled Patriots, Our Heritage Matters and another group called Nevadans for Sensible Government have spent a collective $82,000 to boost Chapman's candidacy, per filings, including with mailers touting her opposition to abortion. events.title: Shops looted as German cost-of-living protests turn violent
events.summary: Watch: Protesters clash with police and shops looted in Germany Rioters looted shops in central Frankfurt late on Saturday as clashes erupted in German cities over the cost of living. Besides Frankfurt - Germany's financial hub - there were incidents of violence in Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg, with police saying they used water cannon to disperse protesters who were targeting emergency workers with fireworks, stones and bottles. Thousands joined largely peaceful demonstrations earlier in the day. They were organised by the campaign group Gen Z regelt - meaning "Gen Z takes charge" - to protest against underfunding in schools, the high cost of living, public spending cuts and military service. The unrest in Germany follows similar youth-led mass protests in France, where more than 320,000 people also demonstrated on Saturday. On Sunday, Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told Bild newspaper that overnight police had prevented "violence like that seen in Paris" in recent weeks and called for "harsh punishments" for rioters and looters. Overnight, a large section of Frankfurt's main shopping street was closed off by police. A police spokesperson said many arrests were made in the city. Authorities in Frankfurt, Munich and Berlin reported as many as 18,000 protesters, roughly half of what the organisers had estimated on their website. German media say tens of thousands protested in German cities on Saturday. Gen Z regelt spokesperson Lina Friedrich said the demonstrations were "to fight for peace and freedom, rather than for war and coercion". She said: "What matters most to us is better support for the health and education systems. We are against compulsory military service and we are in favour of a fairer distribution of the burden." Police detain a demonstrator dressed as Batman in Frankfurt Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them? Published 4 days ago On Saturday night Frankfurt police said "violent riots" were occurring in the city centre and that special police units had been deployed. The windows of several shops had been smashed and molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency services, police said. Officials said the windows of a gun shop were smashed and that they had seized two weapons after arresting a suspect. People also broke into other shops, stealing items like trainers. Roman Poseck, interior minister of Hesse state, of which Frankfurt is the biggest city, said that "around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists" had infiltrated the protest in the city. He added that it was "shameful" how the protests had ended. "We all have those images from France in our minds - looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers... France must not be held up as a model in this regard." Police said the situation calmed down overnight into Sunday in the city. People try to break through a window of a Frankfurt shop selling weapons Similar instances took place in other German cities, following largely peaceful demonstrations. In Cologne, police said officers were attacked near the main train station, with bottles thrown and a bicycle launched. Cologne's police chief Johannes Hermanns said it was "deeply saddening that young people who wanted to peacefully demonstrate for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind". A smaller demonstration in the evening in Berlin - following larger protests in the day - resulted in 27 police officers being injured, and up to 56 people temporarily detained, Berlin police said. In Hamburg, people dressed in black set off fireworks and set barricades on fire, with public broadcaster NDR reporting that 120 people were arrested. The protests in Germany took place on the same day as other large-scale demonstrations in Europe. In France, more than 320,000 people took part in a third consecutive weekend of largely peaceful protests in cities across the country, demanding action on the high cost of living and poor public services, especially in the education sector. Thousands of police officers were deployed across the country, and officers fired tear gas at demonstrators in some cities. There were more than 770 arrests across France during the demonstrations on Saturday, roughly half as many as the previous week's protests, the French interior ministry said. Thousands demonstrate in Paris as protests spread across Europe French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said a police officer had been injured by a molotov cocktail and French prosecutors later launched an attempted murder probe. Police in Paris said several hundred rioters had attacked security forces with projectiles. French protest organisers, the Gilet Jaune, or Yellow Vests, have said dozens of protesters have been seriously injured during recent demonstrations across the country, with many hurt by "grenades".

events.title: Hundreds of thousands of young protesters take to the streets across France
events.summary: Thousands of young protesters take to the streets of France for a third weekend. PARIS -- Hundreds of thousands of protesters inspired by frustrated high school students took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education. Youth-led protests were also held elsewhere in Europe , including in Germany and Portugal. France's protests were overwhelmingly peaceful, with whimsical Halloween costumes lightening the mood, but gatherings in Paris and other cities ended in clouds of tear gas and scattered fires set by small groups on the margins. About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country after French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez warned of a “very high risk” of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Paris marches were rerouted to the capital’s edge to protect stores, government buildings and touristed areas in the city center. France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew 550,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers’ turnout estimates are higher. Authorities in France reported more than 560 arrests nationwide by Saturday night. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred marches the previous two Saturdays. In the main Paris march, each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living. Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where “there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats.” An information technology worker protested in solidarity with the students and her mother, who was struggling with a minimum wage job. A gray-haired woman carried a sign reading ‘’The Old are Fed Up Too.'' Halloween costumes reflected the mood. Cléo Farenc, a 30-year-old gallery assistant, came dressed as a beheaded Marie-Antoinette. “It’s about embodying a figure of power who was brought down by the people,” she said. “It’s a very strong symbol in French culture.'' The rallies in France were started last month by high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at the leadership of President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands. On Saturday, the crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Maréchaux, avenues that ring the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city. Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell. Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris. While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Police use tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries . Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say Paris police barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles — neighborhoods popular among young people — from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday. Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement. In Germany, a youth initiative called “Gen Z regelt” — roughly “Gen Z’s got this” — rallied in more than 30 cities “for education, health, climate protection and an affordable life,” and against any return of military conscription. Organizers said that tens of thousands participated in the protests across the country, but official figures weren't immediately available. In Berlin, young protesters gathered at Brandenburg Gate on Saturday afternoon, demanding more investments in education and housing.

events.title: Fight over race questions intensifies ahead of 2030 Census deadline
events.summary: A fight over whether the 2030 Census should stop asking about race and ethnicity has drawn more than 100,000 public comments, according to advocates tracking the federal docket. Why it matters: The change could weaken the nation's most complete snapshot of race — data used in civil rights enforcement and redistricting — just as America grows more multiracial. Catch up quick: The Census Bureau proposed in September to stop asking Americans about their race and ethnicity on the once-a-decade census. The Census Bureau says a shorter form could encourage more people to respond, while greater use of existing government records would reduce the need to ask certain questions. The proposal wouldn't end federal race data: Census could obtain demographic data from government records and other sources and ask about race and ethnicity on the American Community Survey (ACS) and other surveys. But civil rights advocates say that would give the federal government more power to determine people's race and ethnicity , rather than the respondents, leading to inaccurate data. State of play: Census extended the comment deadline from Oct. 13 to Nov. 2. An outside analysis of 52,424 published comments through Oct. 16 found 86% opposed the overall proposal, while 88% addressed removing race and ethnicity questions. This week, an advocacy alert citing Regulations.gov said the docket had topped 108,000 submissions . These comments are not meant to be treated like a survey or poll, but show that people who feel strongly enough to comment tend to be opposed. What they're saying: "If you've ever fought for political maps or explained why race or data matters...it is vital that you tell the Census Bureau what losing that information is going to mean to your work and to your community," said NC Counts Coalition executive director Stacey Carless. The big picture: Race has appeared in some form in every decennial census since 1790, but how Americans identify themselves has changed dramatically. The number of Americans reporting two or more races rose from 9 million, or 2.9%, in 2010 to 33.8 million, or 10.2%, in 2020. Census says improvements in question design, coding and processing accounted for a substantial share of that increase, along with demographic change. The bottom line: The Census Bureau hasn't explained how it would produce detailed racial population counts without asking Americans to identify themselves. The agency already combines information from government and other records to determine people's race and ethnicity when working with administrative data. But its proposal doesn't say whether that system would replace people's own answers in the 2030 Census.

events.title: Dubai's Dewa steps up global expansion push with Shanghai Electric deal
events.summary: The international arm of Dubai Electricity and Water Authority (Dewa) has signed an agreement with China's Shanghai Electric to explore energy and water investments in global markets, as the emirate seeks to expand its footprint in the international utilities sector. The deal covers potential projects in solar and wind energy, battery storage, desalination, green hydrogen and conventional power generation, as well as electricity transmission and distribution. The agreement establishes a framework for identifying, evaluating, developing and investing in projects, including participation in international tenders. “At Dewa International, we are committed to expanding our presence in global markets and building strategic partnerships that leverage Dubai's pioneering expertise in the utilities sector and the global capabilities of our partners,” said Saeed Mohammed Al Tayer, managing director and chief executive of Dewa and chairman of Dewa International. The agreement was signed by Waleed bin Salman, vice chairman of Dewa International, and Shen Bing, president of Shanghai Electric Power Generation Group. The partnership marks another step in Dewa International's efforts to establish itself as a global energy and water infrastructure developer. DEWA International, the global arm of DEWA, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Shanghai Electric to explore opportunities to develop and invest in energy, water and infrastructure projects across global markets. In the presence of HE Saeed Mohammed Al Tayer, MD & CEO of DEWA and Chairman of DEWA International, he MoU was signed by Waleed bin Salman, Executive Vice President of Business Development and Excellence at DEWA and Vice Chairman of DEWA International, and Zhao Hui, Managing Director of Shanghai Electric Group in the Middle East and North Africa. #DEWANews — DEWA | Official Page (@DEWAOfficial) November 1, 2026 Dewa established its international subsidiary in June to pursue overseas projects and partnerships, drawing on Dubai's experience in developing large-scale electricity, water and clean energy infrastructure. The company aims to work with governments, developers and financial institutions to identify investment opportunities and participate in projects outside the UAE. At its launch, Mr Al Tayer said global demand for energy and water infrastructure was expected to exceed $20 trillion by 2035, presenting substantial opportunities for international expansion. Dewa also operates the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park, one of the world's largest solar developments, which has helped establish Dubai's expertise in renewable energy. The utility is continuing to expand its renewable energy capacity, with plans for the seventh phase of the solar park, incorporating large-scale battery storage. Shanghai Electric, a major Chinese power equipment and engineering company, brings experience in developing and supplying technology for large-scale energy projects. The two companies have previously worked together on the fourth phase of Dubai's Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Solar Park, a Dh15.78 billion project. The latest agreement also covers potential co-operation in green ammonia, concentrated solar power and equipment supply for the oil and gas sector. Dewa has previously invested in green hydrogen production , including a pilot facility developed with Siemens Energy at the solar park. However, the partnership remains exploratory, with no specific overseas projects, investment commitments or development timelines announced.

events.title: UAE updates e-invoicing penalties for businesses
events.summary: The UAE Ministry of Finance has issued new rules to update fines for e-invoicing to support businesses and reduce duplicate penalties. Structured invoices are issued and exchanged digitally between a supplier and a buyer and reported online to the UAE Federal Tax Authority . The latest amendments – following a cabinet decision – aim to provide businesses with greater regulatory certainty and reduce administrative burdens by introducing more proportionate fines. A penalty of Dh5,000 ($1,360) applies for an initial accounting violation, followed by Dh5,000 for each month during which the non-compliance continues. Fines are subject to a maximum aggregate penalty of Dh50,000 for these breaches in any 12 consecutive months. Administrative penalties for the issuer's or the recipient's failure to notify the authority of a system failure have also been removed. This change aims to ensure that penalties are applied more appropriately, taking into account the respective responsibilities of the different parties within the e-invoicing system. The changes support the UAE's wider digital transformation objectives and reinforce the country's commitment to implementing a modern tax administration framework. A pilot phase and voluntary e-invoicing adoption launched in July, with a full introduction planned for October 1, 2027.

events.title: Binance to resume withdrawals after covering 95% of $6.3bn crypto heist
events.summary: Binance , the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, is preparing to resume cryptocurrency withdrawals in phases after covering 95 per cent of the $6.3 billion in tokens stolen in what has been described as the world’s largest digital heist . The first phase of withdrawals is scheduled to begin between 6am and 9am GMT on Sunday, covering Bitcoin , ether, BNB, Solana, XRP, dogecoin and other digital assets, Binance said in a post on X late on Saturday. The remaining 5 per cent of the stolen tokens consists of less liquid assets that may take longer to source in the required amounts, the exchange said. https://t.co/pBJaht1UGV — Binance (@binance) November 1, 2026 “Since the incident, our teams have taken precautionary measures to safeguard the platform, conducted security assessments, and worked to verify the readiness of affected services. We aim to restore withdrawals progressively as we complete security and readiness checks,” the Binance post on X said. “Deposit services remain open and are not affected by the incident,” it added. The resumption follows security assessments and precautionary measures taken by the cryptocurrency exchange to safeguard its platform and verify the readiness of affected services. Binance said it would absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds rather than passing the losses on to customers. “As we have said throughout this incident: user funds remain safe,” Binance said. The FBI on Saturday attributed the attack to TraderTraitor , a North Korean state-sponsored hacking unit. Members of the group were observed by law enforcement converting the stolen assets into ether, the FBI said in a statement, adding that it expected further laundering through related technology. Binance said on X that withdrawals were temporarily suspended as a precaution, “while our teams worked to contain the incident loss, assess its impact, restore affected services and complete security checks”. “We did not take this decision lightly. We understand how important reliable access to withdrawals is for our users. However, our priority was to protect users, safeguard the platform, and complete the necessary security checks before restoring services.” Despite its reputation for robust security, the cryptocurrency industry has suffered several high-profile hacks and collapses over the years. In 2014, the Mt. Gox exchange, then the world's largest Bitcoin trading platform, collapsed after hackers stole hundreds of thousands of Bitcoins, alongside a series of technical and operational failures. Eight years later, FTX, then the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, imploded amid revelations of fraud and the misuse of customer funds. Its founder, Sam Bankman-Fried , was later sentenced to 25 years in prison. More recently, the FBI attributed a $1.5 billion theft from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit to North Korea, highlighting the persistent security threats facing the industry.

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Government will not promise net savings in budget update, even as rate rise looms Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said decisions were still being made on the government's mid-year budget update, refusing to commit to delivering net savings. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts ) The finance minister and treasurer have refused to confirm December's budget update will contain more savings than new spending, even as pressure mounts on the federal government to tighten its belt. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Insiders pressures on the budget were growing, and decisions were still being made for the mid-year update. The mid-year economic and fiscal outlook will be delivered in December. Finance Minister Katy Gallagher says growing pressures on the federal budget mean the government cannot promise it will find overall savings in its December update, even as Australians brace for another interest rate rise amid ongoing high inflation. On Wednesday Treasurer Jim Chalmers also refused to commit to net savings in the mid-year budget update following a worse-than-expected inflation figure of 4.3 per cent over the year to September, which lifted expectations of another rate hike when the Reserve Bank meets on Tuesday. The finance minister told ABC Insiders despite pressure being put on the government to rein in its spending, she would not pre-commit to overall savings. "I can't, I don't want to pre-empt the [Expenditure Review Committee] process. We will go through that ... but there is enormous effort being placed, particularly by Jim and myself on the savings side," Senator Gallgher said. "We are doing a lot of work on the savings side but I can’t get ahead of decisions that haven’t been made yet." The minister rejected suggestions the pressure to find savings was causing tension inside cabinet, saying it was healthy for ministers to have "robust" debate and bring different perspectives. Senator Gallagher added that the government's record in each of its previous budgets and mid-year updates had been to deliver overall improvements to the budget, and that in recent budgets its policy decisions had also found more savings than new spending. The Reserve Bank's chief economist said last week that government spending remained a contributor to ongoing inflation, even if the government points to the war in Iran as the "primary driver". Treasurer downplays further fuel discounts Faced with another high inflation result and the likelihood of a rate hike next Tuesday, Treasurer Jim Chalmers calls for "perspective" and points to external factors. The treasurer has previously warned that the cost of borrowing would add billions of dollars in additional costs to the budget, as long-term expectations that global interest rates would remain higher for longer were priced into bonds. Senator Gallagher said other pressures on the budget were also growing, including in health and aged care. She said the government's spending measures in those pressure areas were necessary to rescue a Medicare system "in freefall" and clear processing backlogs for veterans. "If you go back to … the Howard era, you know, they were not dealing with AUKUS, they were not dealing with aged care," Senator Gallagher said. "They weren't dealing with Medicare falling over there, all of these pressures that are coming. So there has to be some acknowledgement of that. We are living in a different world." The government maintains that the budget is helping to tackle inflation . However ahead of his departure to Antigua and Barbuda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese acknowledged that the Reserve Bank only had a single "blunt instrument" in the inflation fight. The remaining levers to reduce demand in the economy rest with federal and state governments. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor told radio station 2GB that the government could do more to avert further rate rises. "The government can commit tomorrow to take pressure off interest rates and inflation, that would send a strong signal to the Reserve Bank [that] they don't need to raise," Mr Taylor said. The Reserve Bank's chief economist Sarah Hunter said last week that state and federal government spending was "definitely" contributing to demand pressures in the economy, before adding that it was not the RBA's place to advice government on its spending. Frontbench minister Murray Watt told News24 demand growth in the economy tripled in the private sector last financial year, while government demand growth halved.

( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) Gladstone Gaol has officially reopened to the public after being closed for four years. Locals are welcoming of the new operators, which they hope will bolster tourism to the town. New licensee, Lantern Ghost Tours, has plans to expand use across the site, including the addition of a café and accommodation. Following a period of closure, one of regional South Australia’s historic landmarks has reopened its doors to the public, with new caretakers leaning into the site’s dark heritage. This year Lantern Ghost Tours licensed the Gladstone Gaol site from the Department of Environment and Water. This weekend, just in time for Halloween, the company opened the doors to the public for the first time, with sold-out ghost tours welcoming thrill-seekers and history enthusiasts alike to the now 145-year-old facility. Naomi Bailey, the project coordinator for Gladstone Gaol, said it was exciting to have people back. "The community really wanted to be here as well, they were showing it through booking of the tours, and the takeaway was the interest. We sold out," Ms Bailey said. Lantern Ghost Tours' Naomi Bailey is the project coordinator for the recently reopened Gladstone Gaol. ( ABC News: Clem Stanley ) "We had to open additional tours, and we've got really strong bookings every Saturday night." Locals also shared Ms Bailey’s excitement to have the Gladstone Gaol’s gates open once again. The Gladstone Gaol in 1929. ( Supplied: State Library of South Australia ) Gladstone Community Development and Tourism Association president David Catford said it was a surprise when the previous operators retired in 2022. "I think that the community has come to realise what it means not having it open," Mr Catford said. Mr Catford said it was a surprise when the previous operators retired in 2022. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) A once-off open day in 2025 was attended by some 1,300 people , which Mr Catford said proved interest in the prison was still there. Sitting on the cusp of the Southern Flinders Ranges and Mid-North regions, authorities in 1879 at the time determined that Gladstone would become home to a new prison, aimed at taking pressure off jails at Port Augusta and in Adelaide. The jail operated in its intended capacity for just shy of 100 years. Opening in 1881, its prisoner intake varied over the years, going from an all-gender prison to male-only, to a military prison during World War II, and later took on a focus more to reintegrate inmates back to society. The jail has reopened to the public after a four-year closure. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) By 1975 – and still not having plumbing in the building – the government of the day closed the facility. Gladstone local and tour guide Steve Schultz said the community acted quickly at the time to preserve the site and its history. "It's been a long battle ever since then to keep it open and at least have it accessible to the public basically," he said. In the years since, the jail's uses have varied, from previous ghost tour iterations, to hosting accommodation and events. Citing a downturn in volunteers after the COVID-19 pandemic, the previous caretakers hung up the keys in 2022. Lindi and Shelley made the trip from Clare on Friday night, with the hope of experiencing something paranormal. Both having fond memories of visits to the jail in its time as accommodation and an events venue, Lindi said its return to the community was "awesome". "I think this is fantastic," she said. Lindi and Shelley were glad to visit the tourist destination again. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) Ms Bailey said the company planned to launch a café on the site, and restoration works that would allow for events and visitors’ further exploration of the site’s history. "We really want to balance the heritage nature of the site and really complement it with events and activities that are coming through," she said. Anthony Van Zeventer was passing by en route to Darwin and was happy to see the site active again. ( ABC News: Arj Ganesan ) Among the visitors on Friday was Anthony Van Zeventer, who stopped by while travelling from Philip Island to Darwin, without realising it was opening night. "I think it's great that the community's got behind it and that they're reopening it again," Mr Van Zeventer said. events.title: FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history
events.summary: FBI sys attack was tied to an entity known as TraderTraitor. New York -- The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history , was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday. The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to “malicious cyber activity” by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and “instant swap services.” Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved. “I’m not concerned. We’re learning about it," Trump said of the case. “We don’t know if it’s North Korea.” Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was. Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months. “It’s bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet,” said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. “However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.” Learjet with 9 aboard crashes in Palm Beach County, Florida: FAA Sen. Chris Murphy hospitalized after suffering a stroke, chief of staff says 2 college students found dead after going missing while hiking, police say He added: “It’s just this cat and mouse game.” On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange , in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack. The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed. ( Reuters: Dado Ruvic ) The FBI has blamed North Korean hackers for the Binance crypto hack. This week, $US6.3 billion ($6.9 million) in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange. Binance says it has enough funds to cover 90 per cent of the stolen assets. The FBI has accused North Korea of stealing $US6.3 billion ($6.9 million) in virtual assets from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, in what is thought to be the biggest crypto heist in history. In a statement, the US bureau said the North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor was responsible for the "malicious cyber activity". On Thursday, $US6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack. The FBI's statement came as Binance offered reassurances it was covering the losses from the hacking attack, saying it has used company funds to buy tokens to replenish 90 per cent of what was stolen. The FBI made the announcement on Saturday, local time. ( Reuters: Nathan Howard ) The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. "The FBI maintains its commitment to protecting the virtual asset community by identifying, mitigating, and disrupting North Korea's illicit cybercrime and virtual asset theft activities," it said. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called Ethereum. Zhao Changpeng is the founder and chief executive officer of Binance. ( Reuters: Benoit Tessier ) The FBI said it expects TraderTraitor would now attempt to convert the assets using de-centralised finance (DeFi) and "instant swap services". "It is expected these assets will then be further laundered," it said. They are the same actors behind a $US1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. 'Cat and mouse game' of tracking assets Crypto expert and chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs Ari Redbord said he expected the hackers would break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months. A crypto expert says he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them. ( Unsplash: Executium ) "However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds. "It's just this cat and mouse game." 90 per cent of assets recovered, Binance says On Saturday, Binance said it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen, to cover 90 per cent of the missing assets. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the company said on X. It said the outstanding 10 per cent consisted of tokens that were less liquid, which meant they might take longer to source in the required amounts. Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but on Sunday it announced that they had resumed. "First batch network now opened in phase one of withdrawals is $BTC bitcoin network," the company said on X. events.title: Fifty years on, Julius Dam continues to sustain outback communities
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Fifty years on, Julius Dam remains a lifeline for outback communities Julius Dam's distinctive multiple-arch and buttress design is the only one of its kind in Queensland. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Julius Dam is marking 50 years since its construction following a devastating drought in Mount Isa. Its unique design has helped secure water supplies for communities and mining operations across North West Queensland. Sunwater expects the dam to continue supporting regional growth, with ongoing maintenance helping keep it operational for decades to come. In 1971, a devastating drought exposed a serious problem in the outback mining city of Mount Isa. Despite having a major dam, the city was running short of water. Lake Moondarra, built by Mount Isa Mines in 1958 on the Leichhardt River north of town, was Australia's largest, privately-funded water scheme at the time. But as the city and its mining industry grew, the drought exposed a need for another reliable water source. The solution was unveiled five years later with the completion of Julius Dam, about 70 kilometres north-east of Mount Isa, at the junction of the Leichhardt River and Paroo Creek. The North-West Star declared "No more water worries" when Julius Dam was officially commissioned on October 8, 1976. ( Supplied: North-West Star ) An engineering solution built for the outback Constructed by Thiess Brothers, Julius Dam required hundreds of workers, including people from Scotland, England and Ireland, some of whom lived on site with their families. Building a structure with a 220-metre spillway in remote Queensland had significant challenges. Hundreds of workers helped construct Julius Dam between 1973 and 1976, overcoming the challenges of building in remote North West Queensland. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Engineers chose a concrete multiple-arch and buttress design that reduced the amount of material needed while maintaining the dam's strength. The design helped overcome the difficulties of building in the outback, according to current operator Sunwater. "Because of its remoteness, because of the difficulty of getting materials in, that's the reason they decided to go with that structure," north region general manager of operations, William Weaver said. Julius Dam's distinctive multiple-arch and buttress design reduced the amount of concrete required for construction. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Sunwater says it remains the only dam of its kind in Queensland. But another feature caught the attention of University of Queensland geotechnical engineering professor Alexander Scheuermann. Professor Alexander Scheuermann says Julius Dam's unique design allows floodwater to flow directly over its structure. ( Supplied: Alexander Scheuermann ) Unlike dams with a separate spillway, Julius Dam's concrete, 18m wide arches allow excess water to flow directly over the structure. "When the water rises higher than the dam is, it simply overtops the dam without harming the structure," Professor Scheuermann said. Storage capacity: 107,500 megalitres (Sunwater) Sources: Original Julius Dam engineering plaque and Sunwater. A reliable water source for the North West Julius Dam can hold 107,500 megalitres of water, equivalent to about one-fifth of Sydney Harbour's volume. While originally developed to supplement Mount Isa's water supply, its role has expanded over the past five decades. The 113-kilometre North West Queensland Water Pipeline, completed in 1998, supplies mining operations including the Ernest Henry copper and gold mine near Cloncurry. Another 38km pipeline was completed in 2010 following a drought, providing Cloncurry with an additional year-round water supply. Lake Moondarra remains Mount Isa's main water source, with Julius Dam providing supplementary water when needed. Julius Dam's built-in spillway allows excess water to flow directly over its concrete arches during periods of heavy rainfall. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) Despite the region's long dry periods, Mr Weaver said Julius Dam had spilled every year for the past decade. He attributed its reliability to seasonal monsoonal and cyclonic rainfall regularly replenishing the Leichhardt River catchment. "What Lake Julius does is it gives you that real assurance and real surety of supply," he said. "And that's allowed Mount Isa and its industry to grow." William Weaver says Julius Dam remains a vital water source for North West Queensland. ( Supplied: Sunwater ) While Julius Dam has operated for five decades, Professor Scheuermann said ongoing maintenance would be essential to its future.

events.title: No more washing up: How Airbnb's new house rules have divided hosts and guests
events.summary: Airbnb host Lisa says her Welsh holiday let was left 'a complete mess' by a group of guests When Lisa Clewes returned to her Welsh holiday let after a group of guests checked out, she was horrified by the mess. Just days earlier, she had met the group in person and helped with their luggage. But after a dinner party, the house was left "in a complete mess" with broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden. "It was really unbelievable. Had I had another booking the same day, I would have had to cancel or delay check-in," says Clewes. She charges a cleaning fee that covers around 75% of the cost of a cleaner and asks guests to empty the fridge, put rubbish in the bins and load the dishwasher. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her property and fears that guests leaving more mess could mean increasing costs But Airbnb's new rules mean hosts can no longer ask guests to do jobs normally carried out by cleaners, including washing and putting away dishes, stripping beds and taking rubbish off site. The updated guidelines, which apply to bookings made globally from 20 November, state that hosts can now set seven standard house rules and add other "reasonable" requests. Clewes says it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property. She fears guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her guests. The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees. She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee. Newhook says the host told them to wash and fold towels, clean the bedding and kitchen, and sweep and mop the floors. She was also warned by the host that their behaviour needed to improve or they could be told to leave, because they had left chairs blocking bins. "We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all." While Newhook likes the home comforts of staying in an Airbnb, she says the combination of relentless rules and rising cleaning fees has taken away much of its appeal. "It is getting to the point where a hotel is cheaper and I know what to expect." Krissi Foskett, 46, from Glasgow, runs a national cleaning company and regularly stays in Airbnb properties so "can see the issue from both sides". Krissi says there's a difference between being a respectful guest and being expected to help run the business you've just paid to stay in During a recent stay in Stafford, she paid a £35 cleaning fee but was still asked to strip the beds, put on a wash, empty bins and carry rubbish down a long track to a recycling area. "I don't particularly mind doing those things, but it did make me question what exactly I was paying the additional cleaning fee for," she says. For Foskett, there is a difference between being a considerate guest – "putting your dirty dishes in the dishwasher" – and being "expected to prepare the property for the next guests". Through her cleaning business, she has also seen the other extreme, with teams arriving to find broken furniture, vomit and pet urine. While she sympathises with hosts facing tight turnarounds and rising cleaning costs, these should not be passed on to guests, she says. "If you're running an Airbnb as a business, professional cleaning is a cost of doing business." Anthony Marsh, who co-owns a cabin retreat in North Yorkshire with his husband, used to list five of their 12 properties on Airbnb, but says the new rules have prompted him to reduce this number to just two. His concern with the changes is that "Airbnb has effectively given guests permission to come and leave properties a tip, and a host can't do anything about it". Anthony and his husband used to list five of their 12 cabins in North Yorkshire on Airbnb... ... but will now list just two in light of the new rules He believes asking guests to wash their pots and put out the bins is hardly unreasonable and, with a small cleaning team and tight turnaround times, he worries extra mess could leave properties unready for the next arrivals. "It's common sense and common decency," he says. His company does not charge a cleaning fee, and Marsh says most guests are respectful. But fees are more common than not. Some 63.2% of Airbnb listings charge a cleaning fee, with an average cost of £55 according to data from AirROI , external . Laura Lewis runs a directory that helps holiday-let owners market their properties and connect with potential guests. Many of her clients also list on Airbnb and she says most are unhappy with the new rules, arguing that asking guests to wash up is a matter of basic respect.

events.title: Country town reliant on backpackers warns visa changes will cripple business
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Manjimup's backpackers and businesses united in opposition to working holiday visa changes Chef Valerie Castro is one of many backpackers living and working in Manjimup concerned about looming visa changes. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) The federal government is pushing ahead with its plan to limit working holiday visas, which include ballots for second and third-year extensions. In communities like Manjimup, in southern Western Australia, businesses and backpackers say the changes are already having an impact. Regional businesses want the changes scrapped to ensure critical workers are not lost. In Paul Fowler's country pub, more than half a dozen backpackers make up over 70 per cent of his workforce. Italian travellers keep business ticking over from the front of house all the way through to his busy kitchen. It is a similar situation at many businesses across Manjimup, 290 kilometres south of Perth in southern Western Australia, with the tourism and agricultural centre heavily reliant on backpacker labour. Seventy per cent of the staff at Paul Fowler's pub are backpackers. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Both Mr Fowler and his workers have backed calls to scrap the federal government's controversial changes to Australia's working holiday visa program. "It's only going to make things harder, and it takes away our ability to function," he said. Before the working holiday visa changes were announced, Mr Fowler bought a second pub in the neighbouring town of Pemberton, which he planned to staff with backpackers. Viola Argenta, Ilaria Dalla Valeria and Mattia Ballarini all work at a pub in Manjimup. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Mr Fowler said that business was now under threat. "We probably go through 50 to 80 workers a year, all backpacking workers, and so without the backpacking staff, we won't have a workforce here at all," he said. Paul Fowler says his pub in Manjimup couldn't run without backpacker labour. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) The federal government's decision to initially slow down visa applications in August was heavily criticised by farming and regional communities across the country . The decision to allocate fewer second and third-year visa extensions prompted WA's Premier Roger Cook to ask federal Immigration Minister Tony Burke to reconsider the restrictions. Manjimup is a regional hub for tourism and agriculture. ( ABC South West: Andrew Williams ) A spokesperson for the Department of Home Affairs said the reduction would ensure the program's long-term sustainability, and it would work with affected industries to access the labour they need. Back in Manjimup, those impacted say the move fails to account for the benefits backpackers provide beyond their first year. Roberto Spadotto wants to build a life in Manjimup. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) Roberto Spadotto came to Manjimup to work as a farmhand, picking avocados and broccoli as part of his visa obligations. After completing his 88 days and being granted an extension, he started managing Mr Fowler's pub along with his partner Giulia Colombo, whom he met while completing his farm work. One-year-old dies in house fire south of Perth Homeowners facing thousands in costs to upgrade from gas to electric Western Australia experienced a roller-coaster of weather in October Learning Auslan a 'life skill' for children "That's where I met Giulia … one of the worst and best days of my life because picking broccoli is very tough, but I enjoyed it and I had a good outcome," he said. After spending about four years in the region, the Italian couple were hoping to put down roots. "I love the area, love the region, never really thought about moving somewhere else," he said. "And now we're planning to stay, settle, and build a new life here in Australia." Fellow Italian traveller Valerie Casto completed her farm work in a seedling nursery, before starting work as a chef once her visa was extended. Valerie Casto says second and third-year visa extensions incentivise backpackers to do hard jobs. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) She said the incoming changes were turning some of her friends off coming to Australia. "Half a year of a farm job can be very, very hard," Ms Castro said. "And some people don't know if it's worth it, if at the end the visa is not granted." Gavin Booth says backpacker workers are already leaving Australia. ( ABC News: Andrew Chounding ) It is an experience all too familiar for truffle farmer Gavin Booth, who produces the valuable fungus on a property in neighbouring Pemberton. He relies on backpackers for sporadic and seasonal work.

events.title: Judge tosses Trump lawsuit against WSJ, Murdoch over Epstein story
events.summary: A federal judge on Saturday threw out President Trump's lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and Rupert Murdoch over the paper's reporting on Trump's ties to Jeffrey Epstein, Why it matters: It's the second time this year courts have blocked Trump's efforts to sue the paper over stories about his relationship with the disgraced financier. As with the first one, courts found the president did not clear the high bar set by New York Times vs. Sullivan for allegations of defamation in critical reporting on public figures. Driving the news: Judge Darrin Gayles of the southern district of Florida issued the 20-page ruling Saturday afternoon, finding that Trump failed to prove the paper acted with "actual malice" by reporting on his links to Epstein. Gayles dismissed the amended complaint with prejudice, meaning it can't be refiled. "We're pleased with the court's decision," a representative of WSJ parent Dow Jones said. Zoom out: Trump first filed suit against the paper and Murdoch in July 2025, seeking $20 billion in damages. At issue was a story describing a "bawdy" letter, bearing Trump's name and given to Epstein for his birthday, which the president insisted was fake. Gayles tossed the initial suit last April, but allowed Trump to file an amended complaint — which was the one he dismissed Saturday, saying it fell short of the burden to prove the paper acted maliciously. What they're saying: "Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false," Gayles wrote. For the record: " President Trump will continue to press forward in his powerhouse lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal and all of the other defendants. The President will continue to hold those who mislead the American People with Fake News and smears accountable for their actions," a spokesman for his legal team said in a statement. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details. Sara Fischer contributed.

events.title: Tusk defends suspension of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal president as protesters gather again
events.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk says his government is acting to restore judicial independence in Poland WARSAW, Poland -- Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Saturday that his government would press ahead with efforts to restore the independence of Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal, as hundreds of protesters gathered for a second night against the suspension of the court’s president . The pro-European government said the suspension is necessary to restore judicial independence, while critics from the opposition have likened it to a “coup d’etat.” President Karol Nawrocki — who opposes the pro-European government — turned back his plane during a flight to Senegal on Friday evening and returned home. On Friday night, he made his way to the Constitutional Tribunal despite the chaos and said he helped the suspended court president enter the building. Police said they detained three protesters on Friday night after some threw objects at officers and tried to break through the security fence around the court. The dispute over the long-embattled Constitutional Tribunal is likely to deepen political polarization in Poland a year before a parliamentary election, further intensifying the standoff between the pro-European government and the national-conservative opposition party Law and Justice , or PiS. Critics in Poland and the European Union accuse PiS, which led the country between 2015 and 2023, of imposing political control over key judicial institutions. Reforms introduced under the PiS government prompted the EU to impose fines on Poland. Tusk’s pro-European government came to power in 2023 with a promise to restore the independence of the judiciary. Since then, its efforts have been blocked by vetoes from two successive presidents aligned with PiS, including Nawrocki. “Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.” Tusk had earlier pledged that his government would ensure the tribunal was again staffed with lawfully appointed judges while acknowledging that his methods may not be to everyone’s liking. The functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal had been impaired for years. The Court of Justice of the European Union, the EU's top court, had said it was no longer an impartial court after PiS appointments. Even after Tusk took power, efforts to balance the court were hampered by Nawrocki and the tribunal's president, Bogdan Święczkowski. On Friday evening, the Constitutional Tribunal’s website announced the suspension of Święczkowski. Shortly after, the protesters — including PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński and far-right politicians — began rallying outside the building. Święczkowski became head of the court under the former PiS government. Tusk has accused him of blocking judges elected by the parliamentary majority from taking up their posts at the tribunal. “Since last night, we’re dealing with a massive constitutional crisis in Poland, the result of an illegal, forceful attempt to take over an important institution,” Marcin Przydacz, a top aide to the Polish president, told The Associated Press. Przydacz said that the president had invited all parliamentary parties to talks on Saturday in an effort to defuse tensions and find a solution to the crisis. The government is a broad coalition made up of Tusk's centrist Civic Coalition, the Left, and two more conservative groupings, Poland 2050 and the Polish People’s Party, or PSL. Representatives of Poland 2050 and PSL, along with several opposition parties, met with Nawrocki on Saturday, while Tusk didn't attend. The president’s camp is hoping that the crisis surrounding the Constitutional Tribunal will erode Tusk’s parliamentary majority. “Everything depends on those political parties who supported Donald Tusk so far,” Przydacz said. Speaking on Saturday night, Tusk compared PiS to a man who steals an elderly woman’s purse and then claims to be the victim when police catch him and take it back.
